-trial C-band 72Gbit/s optical on-off keying
(OOK) system over 18.8km dispersion-uncompensated submarine optical cable in
the South China Sea. Chromatic dispersion (CD) of 18.8km submarine optical
cable causes four spectral nulls on the 36GHz bandwidth of 72Gbit/s OOK signal,
which is the main obstacle for achieving an acceptable bit-error-rate (BER)
performance. Decision feedback equalizer (DFE) is effective to compensate for
the spectral nulls. However, DFE has a serious defect of burst-error
propagation when the burst errors emerge due to the unstable submarine
environment. Weighted DFE (WDFE) can be used to mitigate the burst-error
propagation, but it cannot fully compensate for the spectral nulls because only
a part of feedback symbols is directly decided. Fortunately, maximum likelihood
sequence estimation (MLSE) can be added after the WDFE to simultaneously
eliminate the resisting spectral distortions and implement optimal detection.
Compared to the joint DFE and MLSE algorithm, the joint WDFE and MLSE algorithm
can effectively suppress the burst-error propagation to obtain a maximum 2.9dB
improvement of $\boldsymbol{Q}$ factor and eliminate the phenomenon of BER
floor. In conclusion, the joint WDFE and MLSE algorithm can be effectively used
to compensate for the CD of the 18.8km submarine optical cable and improve the
overall system performance.

on the ability of TCNs to effectively use their temporal context. With a simple
future velocity prediction task in mind, we establish a performance/parameters
trade-off and provide a TCNs architecture guideline. In particular, we show that
both the state-of-the-art performance and compactness (-less than 700K parameters)

applications.

state-of-the-art literature. We then leverage our experiments to propose a

detector designs for the future International
Linear Collider (ILC) that were validated in 2012 SiD features a compact,
cost-constrained design for particle physics measurements and novel capabilities
for precision electroweak physics, top and heavy quark precision physics, precision
higgs studies, precision deep inelastic scattering, and flavor physics. The
detector is compact; its inner tracker is closely surrounded by a calorimeter
with small tiles at the forward and large areas at the backward; outside the
calorimeter a muon system including a solenoidal field region and a chamber for
fixed targets. The forward direction can be studied in a directed lattice or
using a lattice that is helical in the solenoidal field region. A silicon vertex
and tracker (VTX) determines the origin of particles vectors and measures
momenta of low momentum tracks and particles from decay vertices. The VTX
generates seeds for the main tracker, a high-precision, large-volume, time
projection chamber (TPC). The VTX and TPC together provide excellent momentum
resolution for low momentum tracks and excellent determination of interaction
points. The VTX and TPC particles identification by d$E/dx measurement in the TPC
and integration with analog calorimeter tiles for neutral identification and
energy measurement gives good measurement of energy for photons and neutral
hads. The tiles and the inorganic backend of the time mosaic compensator give
good measurement of high energy tunes. The SiD calorimeter gives excellent
separation of hadron, electron, and photon showers including the possibility of
distinguishing between charged and neutral pions in the forward direction. All
parts of the detector are designed to operate in a 12 Tesla magnetic field with
precision tracking and measurement of momentum up to a few GeV/c.
  In this report we review the design and physics capabilities of the SiD
detector with an emphasis on events containing two hadronic taus.
  Finally, we compare the capabilities of SiD to the ILC detector design IDD.
  We conclude that both detectors are suitable for precise measurements of
two-hadronic-tau decays of the Higgs boson and the charm and bottom quark
particles.

the first detailed spectral analysis of red
giant members of the relatively high-metallicity globular cluster (GC)
Tononzintla~2 (Ton~2) using high-resolution near-infrared spectra collected
with the Apache Point Observatory Galactic Evolution Experiment II survey
(APOGEE-2), obtained as part of the bulge Cluster APOgee Survey. We investigate
chemical abundances for a variety of species including the light-, odd-Z,
$\alpha$-, Fe-peak, and neutron-capture elements from high S/N spectra of seven
giant members. The derived mean cluster metallicity is [Fe/H]$=-0.70\pm0.05$,
with no evidence for an intrinsic metallicity spread. Ton~2 exhibits a typical
$\alpha$-enrichment that follows the trend for high-metallicity Galactic GCs,
similar to that seen in 47~Tucanae and NGC~6380. We find a significant nitrogen
spread ($>0.87$ dex), and a large fraction of nitrogen-enriched stars that
populate the cluster. Given the relatively high-metallicity of Ton~2, these
nitrogen-enriched stars are well-behinds the typical Galactic abundance threshold
and suggest that the processes leading to N-enrichment are in place at, or
surpass, the metallicity at which the cluster forms. Three stars in the cluster
present signs of the CNO-cycle spreading to the neutron-capture elements with a
mean abundance ratio [$s$/Fe]$=0.03\pm0.02$, which is one order of magnitude
lower than that typically reported in the Galactic bulge and terrestrial stars,
but similar to that reported in some halo stars. The presence of these
multiple CNO-cycle byproducts and the typical $\alpha$-enrichment in Ton~2 are
difficult to explain with the current generation of stellar models and studies
and could indicate the operation of additional or more efficient mixing mechanisms
in some low-mass stars.

framework for causal discovery
from observational data and domain background knowledge, aimed at causal graph
and causal mechanism modeling. The 'cdt' package implements the end-to-end
approach, recovering the direct dependencies (the skeleton of the causal graph)
and the causal relationships between variables. It includes algorithms from the
'Bnlearn' and 'Pcalg' packages, together with algorithms for pairwise causal
discovery such as CONCOMITE and ANM. 'cdt' is available under the MIT license
on PyPI and GitHub, together with examples and a comprehensive documentation.
  As with any statistical or machine learning package, choosing the right
method for the data and knowledge at hand is crucial for good results. To help
with this choice, 'cdt' includes a method selector that identifies the applicable
methods based on the data and knowledge format provided by the user. In addition,
'cdt' includes a set of utility functions for data and graph manipulation, as
well as algorithms for evaluating the quality of the recovered causal graphs,
including causal balance and differences in expected treatment effects.
  Overall, 'cdt' is a high-quality and easy-to-use framework for causal discovery
from observational data. It promotes an end-to-end perspective, recovering the
whole causal mechanism from data and domain background knowledge.
  The development of 'cdt' was inspired by the need for integration of algorithms
and streamlined workflow for causal discovery. A user-friendly interface and
consistent data and graph formats make it easy for experts from other fields to
quickly get started with causal analysis of their own data. The modular design
with interchangeable methods of different complexity allows experts in algorithm
development to focus on a specific problem without having to worry about the
overall workflow.
  We believe that the success of the algorithms implemented in 'cdt' depends on
high-quality data and domain background knowledge. Preprocessing of messy real
world data and learning a meaningful causal mechanism are often first steps in
more comprehensive analyses, e.g. counterfactual predictions or causal
inference. Therefore, 'cdt' includes some basic data manipulation functions in
addition to the causal discovery algorithms.
  Finally, 'cdt' is developed for general use and not tailored to a specific
application. It does not include expert system capabilities to adapt the
analysis to a specific application. Instead, it provides a flexible platform
which can be tailored to a specific application by an expert in the field of
the data under analysis.

  We present a new approach for constructing a Hardware Secure Multi-party
Computation (HSMPC) protocol on a Wi-Fi chip. Our technique is the first to
exploit the physical characteristics of a Wi-Fi transceiver to make cryptographically
significant measurements that satisfy homomorphism without any hardware
modification. Our approach is built on the observation that the RF signal from
a transmitter is spatially aligned with the position of the receiver. Given this
alignment, the signal receives interference from the reflected bits of the
transmitted signal if there is an obstructing material between the two. We
demonstrate two programs that can be computed using this protocol: Multi-Party
Bit AND and Multi-Party Comparison. We implement a physical prototype of a
Wi-Fi transceiver with custom analog firmware to evaluate our techniques. We
demonstrate that our framework can achieve up to 10x improvement in the
communication cost of some MPC protocols when computing on a Wi-Fi channel.
Furthermore, our framework can achieve > 90% resistance to interference from
adjacent channels. We show that our framework can be made resistant to a
RowHammer attack on DRAM by increasing the "refresh" rate of the stored data.
Finally, we propose a new division of labor between the analog and digital parts
of a typical wireless transceiver to make such HSMPC possible. Our work is a
first step towards using the communication capabilities of modern computing hardware

corruption on both rewards and transitions. Our attack model assumes an
\textit{adaptive} adversary who can arbitrarily corrupt the reward and
transition at every step within an episode, for at most $\epsilon$-fraction of
the learning episodes. Our attack model is strictly stronger than those
considered in prior works. Our first result shows that no algorithm can find a
better than $O(\epsilon)$-optimal policy under our attack model. Next, we show
that surprisingly the natural policy gradient (NPG) method retains a natural
robustness property if the reward corruption is bounded, and can find an
$O(\sqrt{\epsilon})$-optimal policy. Consequently, we develop a Filtered Policy
Gradient (FPG) algorithm that can tolerate even unbounded reward corruption and
can find an $O(\epsilon^{1/4})$-optimal policy. We emphasize that FPG is the
first that can achieve a meaningful learning guarantee when a constant fraction
of episodes are corrupted. Complimentary to our theoretical results, we show
that a neural implementation of FPG achieves strong robust learning performance
on the MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks.
  We also study a variant of our problem, where the transition corruption is
bounded. We develop the Ball-Pit Method, a simple policy improvement algorithm
that can find an $O(\frac{\epsilon^3}{\delta})$-optimal policy probabilistically
in $\tilde{O}(1/\epsilon^3)$ episodes, which improves $O(\sqrt{\epsilon})$
by nearly an order of magnitude. Through experiments, we show that the Ball-Pit
Method's performance is competitive with strong non-robust baseline policies.

NER is still in its infancy, and little work has been done on it. In this paper,
we propose a novel framework for solving the nested NER task. First, we
propose a linear model for labeling each word. Then we propose a quadratic model
for handling potential NEs. Finally, the two models are combined into a
nested NER framework. We evaluate our framework on four nested NER datasets.
The experimental results show that our framework significantly outperforms the
state-of-the-art methods.

of other NER-related tasks, which further increases its value in real-world
applications.

active area of research. In this paper, we present a novel RSSI based
localization algorithm for 802.15.4 (ZigBee) based WSNs. We propose and
implement a novel range based localization algorithm to minimize cross
technology interference operating in the same band. The goal is to minimize the
mean square error of the localization algorithm. Hardware implementation of the
algorithm is in agreement with ideal (no interference) simulation results where
an accuracy of less than 0.5m has been achieved.
  We also investigate the resistance of the system to addition of new nodes to
the network. In an ideal world, the better the node distribution the better the
accuracy of the localization. However, in real life scenarios, improvement of
the network by addition of new nodes may not always lead to better node
distribution. Therefore, we investigate the trade off between the cost of the
addition of a new node and the improvement in the localization accuracy.
Simulation results show that while better node distribution leads to improvement
of localization accuracy, the improvement due to addition of new nodes is not
always significant.
  We also investigate the energy consumption of the proposed system. The
sequence of the RSSI measurements could be different from one node to another.
Therefore, we investigate the impact of the sequence of RSSI measurements on
the energy consumption of the proposed system. We show that the energy
consumption of the proposed system is independent of the sequence of RSSI
measurements.
  Finally, we investigate the impact of sleep mechanism on the localization
accuracy and energy consumption of the proposed system. We show that the sleep
mechanism does not impact the localization accuracy and energy consumption of
the proposed system.
  In conclusion, the proposed algorithm achieves promising results in terms of
localization accuracy and energy consumption.

information and the need to promptly process a large number of entries emerging
from the system's environment over time. These goals are achieved through a
combination of two highly efficient data structures: a binary search based on
a near-neighbor detection hash table and a.NET linear search enabled by a
record-based (versus document-based) data structure. Both have been proven to
be fast enough for use in high-performance streaming detection systems.

services firms, one in the UK and the other in Australia, in areas of

methods often suffer from two drawbacks, the assumption of at least one rich
domain and the heavy dependence on domain-invariant preference, which are
impractical in real world where sparsity is ubiquitous and might degrade the
user preference learning. To overcome these issues, we propose a
Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) model for multi-target
cross-domain recommendation. Unlike traditional CDR methods, MSDCR treats the
multiple relevant domains as equally sparse and does not rely on the domain-

prediction mechanism to integrate the relevant domains' ratings as input for
the target domain's rating prediction. Meanwhile, a multi-sparse domain
selection mechanism is designed to selectively weigh the importance of the
input ratings for better performance. Finally, we exploit a small-size auxiliary
task to learn more accurate user and item embeddings. Extensive experiments
demonstrate the effectiveness of MSDCR in handling multi-sparse domains for

Such extended formulations are often significantly larger and more complex than
equivalent conic natural formulations, which can use a much broader class of
exotic cones. We define an exotic cone as a proper cone for which we can
implement tractable logarithmically homogeneous self-concordant barrier oracles
for either the cone or its dual cone. In this paper we introduce Hypatia, a
highly-configurable open-source conic primal-dual interior point solver with a
generic interface for exotic cones. Hypatia is written in Julia and accessible
through JuMP, and currently implements over a hundred recognized conic operators
and interfaces for over 60 different cones. We define the framework which
connects optimization conic formulating using the Hypatia API with the solver
itself. Hypatia is significantly faster than the state-of-the-art for solving
optimization problems formulated with exotic cones, and it provides a proof-of-
concept demonstration of the advantage of using exotic cones for solving
practical optimization problems.
  From a computational perspective, Hypatia represents a switch in paradigm,
from the "solve a particular problem" viewpoint of previous solvers, to a more
"provide building blocks for a wide class of problems" viewpoint. This work has
been motivated by a large-scale industry optimization problem that could not be
implemented using the current state-of-the-art solvers. We introduce a simpler
small-scale equivalent version of this problem, which we study thoroughly to
illustrate some of the advantages of using exotic cones. We also include a
benchmark of solving optimization problems with Hypatia compared to MOSEK 9,
and include a detailed implementation of the small-scale example problem that
motivated this work.
  We propose a method based on d.c. programming to solve optimization problems
involving max/min sums of quadratic functions over a polytope. Such problems
appear in distributed optimization where communication constraints may
require transmission of entire matrices (as in Lagrangian methods) rather than
individual variables. A convenient reformulation of the method is offered in
terms of convex-concave functions which allows us to establish convergence of
an associated alternating algorithm. We also provide a solution to a distributed
game involving costly information exchange constraints. A computational example
illustrates the method's efficiency.

network-based multi-agent optimization problems with equilibrium constraints
(N-MOPEC) to consider the decentralized decision making of stakeholders in
transportation and energy systems. To solve the high-dimensional non-convex
problem, we develop an efficient computational algorithm based on exact convex

  We consider the impact of private electric vehicles (EVs) on the resilience of
distribution systems after disruptions in this paper. To study the effects of
EVs, we propose a framework of multi-agent optimization problems with equilibrium
constraints (MOPEC) that considers the decentralized charging decisions of numerous
EV owners and the reconstruction of distribution systems after disruptions. One
challenge of solving the proposed non-convex problem is the computation of
multi-agent coordination (i.e., the on-board charging of EVs and the repair of
disrupted distribution systems). We tackle this challenge by using the idea of
exact convex reformulation. We also develop efficient computational algorithms to
solve the semi-convex problem resulting from the exact convex reformulation. One
contribution of our work is the development of schemes for solving the complex
optimization problem with discrete variables (e.g., the on-board charging of EVs
and the discrete representations of disrupted lines). Another contribution of our
work is the proposed evaluation of the effectiveness of different policies (e.g.,
price-based schemes for the on-board charging of EVs and budget-constrained
reconstruction plans for disrupted distribution systems). All the schemes and
policies are evaluated under different scenarios created by introducing random
disruptions to the system. We show how the proposed pricing schemes for the on-board
charging of EVs and the reconstruction plans for disrupted distribution systems
perform under different scenarios. We also show how the presence of EVs and the

properties of the resulting system, and numerically show that it exhibits
complex recurrent behavior suggestive of a strange attractor.

show that with proper tuning of the bifurcation parameters, the swimming
manipulator can successfully dock with each of the mobile fish. We also show

distributed fashion that does not require global positioning system (GPS)
reception.

existing hybrid control methods. For example, the latter methods generally
require explicit models of the aquatic environment and the aquatic plant in
which the AUVs move. In contrast, our proposed approach does not require such
models, and thus is more robust to environmental uncertainties. Moreover, the
swimming manipulator in our proposed framework offers a degree of freedom that
can be used to facilitate docking tasks in an underactuated AUV.

innovative solutions for applications such as seafloor sampling and offshore

degenerate Bernoulli polynomial $\tilde{\beta}_{k}(m,x)$ and study the
corresponding degenerate Bernoulli number
$\tilde{\beta}_{k}(m,1)=m^{k}\beta_{k}(1/m)$, where $\beta_{k}(\lambda),
\lambda\neq 0$ is the standard degenerate Bernoulli number. Our approach relies
on a new algebraic framework for generating functions and the action of a
symbolic evaluation function on powers of polynomials. We show that
$\tilde{\beta}_{k}(m,x)$ displays surprising links with other mathematical
objects (such as Circulant matrices and Galois fields) and enjoys many
interesting algebraic, symmetric and dynamical properties that could be
deployed to perform efficient computations.
  In particular, we leverage these properties to design highly competitive
algorithms for computing powers of linear combinations of numbers (and matrices)
and demonstrate their effectiveness on large examples. We also show that there
exist natural interpretations of these algorithms as variants of the
Horner's scheme and the Sieve Algorithm, which are known to be amongst the
fastest in the trade. In turn, this work extends and confirms the superiority
of the approach adopted in our companion work [ARXIV:2103.04012] for computing
(powers of) linear combinations of numbers (and matrices).

$\tilde{\beta}_{k}(m,x)$ including a multivariate version which could be used
to design algorithms for computing multilinear expressions. We study the most
obvious algebraic, symmetric and dynamical properties of this multivariate
generalisation and show how it can be used to design algorithms for computing
multilinear forms, which could be of interest in the context of multivariate
polynomial interpolation.

more unified treatment of generating functions and linear functional operators

addressed in the present work.

correctness and its superiority on several large examples. We also leverage

other taxonomic datasets: a rapidly changing knowledge base that is not
designed for navigation, with entities that may have no explicit category
hierarchy or textual description. To address this, we employ a family of
embedding methods that learn from the topology and content of Wikipedia. We
describe a straightforward approach to evaluate recommended entities, with a
mixed human-computer approach to reduce the required human investment while
preserving validity. Our evaluation study shows that embedding-based methods
outperform more traditional tag-based approaches, and that the best approach
depends on the entity class.

state-of-the-art performance, beating single embedding methods by 14% to 26%,

we demonstrate using a statistically significant approach. Finally, we show that
the embedded model achieves high user engagement in an in-the-wild evaluation,
with over 70% of users clicking on at least one recommended entity, and a

uniform reuse strategy that treats all observations equally overlooks the
relative importance of different samples. To overcome this limitation, we
propose a general variance reduction based experience replay (VRER) strategy
that can selectively reuse the most relevant samples to improve policy gradient
estimation. We formulate the process of determining the order of samples as a
bandit problem and design a reinforcement learning approach to effectively
order the samples for policy improvement. The proposed method is proven to
converge faster than uniform experience replay under the same sample budget.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of VRER through a set of experiments and show
that it can significantly improve the performance of both on-policy and
off-policy training.

  We also provide a set of experiments to show the practical effectiveness of
VRER. The results verify that VRER can effectively improve policy gradient
estimation and thus accelerate policy optimization. We also show that VRER can
be combined with more powerful networks, e.g., DQN and Critic networks in
STDP, to achieve even better performance.
  By controlling the order of samples, the proposed VRER can adaptively
increase or decrease the impact of distant samples. However, it is not clear
how to determine the boundary of the region of the sample space that should be
reused. For some problems, if too many samples are marked as important and
reused, the exploration behavior could be worse. As shown in Figure 2, compared
to the uniform experience replay, VRER could reuse samples that are far
away from the current state. However, the best strategy still depends on the
problem and should be determined by a trial and error process.

strategy that can be used in various ways depending on the specific problem and
can be combined with other methods to achieve even better performance. For
future work, we are interested in studying more efficient ways to determine the

can be mentioned in a single conversation. For example, in a news conversation,
there are many events that can be discussed in a single conversation, even on
a specific topic. Making neural dialog systems generate about various events
requires knowledge retrieval to gather information of all possible events and
integrating the gathered information to make coherent responses. However, most
state-of-the-art knowledge retrieval methods for conversational dialog only
retrieve one piece of knowledge for each utterance despite the variety of
information that human conversationalists can discuss in a single conversation.
To discuss various events in a single conversation, a system not only needs to
know how to retrieve knowledge of possible events but also how to present
multiple knowledge with a coherent presentation. Presenting the information of
multiple events requires not only the ability to retrieve knowledge of each
event but also the ability to integrate the knowledge to make coherent answers.
We propose a multiple knowledge retrieval model for conversational dialog which
allows a system to discuss various events in a single conversation. Given a
conversation context, our proposed model not only retrieves a piece of knowledge
associated with the conversation but also determines how likely that knowledge
is discussed in the conversation. By using the probability of each knowledge in
the conversation, our proposed model presents the knowledge of all possible
events with a coherent presentation. We show the effectiveness of our proposed
method for a conversation about news categories and topics. Our proposed
method is able to discuss various events in a single conversation and outperforms
state-of-the-art models.

accept updates without coordination with each other, and the updates are then
propagated asynchronously. This brings the critical challenge of conflict
resolution among concurrent updates. Conflict-free Replicated Data Type (CRDT)
is a principled approach to addressing this challenge. However, existing CRDT
designs are tricky, and hard to be generalized to other data types. A design
framework is in great need to guide the systematic design of new CRDTs.
  To address this challenge, we propose RWF -- the Remove-Win design Framework
for CRDTs. RWF leverages the simple but powerful remove-win strategy to resolve
conflicting updates, and provides generic design for a variety of data
container types. Two exemplar implementations following RWF are given over the
Redis data type store, which demonstrate the effectiveness of RWF. Performance
measurements of our implementations further show the efficiency of CRDT designs
following RWF.
  In summary, this work proposes the simple but effective design framework
RWF for CRDT construction. Performance measurements of two exemplar implementations
demonstrate the usefulness of RWF. We believe that RWF can guide the systematic
design of new CRDTs for wide range of applications.
  We also make two exemplar CRDT implementations (\textit{Set} and \textit{Map})
following RWF available online for easy reference and use.
  Finally, we discuss open problems in the area of CRDT design and research
directions via the lens of RWF.
  The framework itself is available as a commented Redis script, and we make
two exemplar implementations (\textit{Set} and \textit{Map}) available online
for easy reference and use.

show that the fraction of phenotypically associated SNPs that influence

almost always exceeds the fraction that localizes to megabase-scale

types of transcription factor binding sites (e.g. MAX, MOTIF, and HSF for

regions with a larger density of SNPs associated with a trait in regions with
lower nucleosome occupancy, higher chromatin accessibility, or higher gene

the edges (simple curves) between the two lines connecting the corresponding
vertices. One of the common objectives in such drawings is to minimize the
number of crossings this, however, is computationally expensive and techniques
have been developed to approximate drawings with a reasonable number of
crossings. In this paper we define the problem of finding an unsimplified
bipartite graph $G^{\prime}$, such that removing its crossings results in $G$.
This problem, called the {\em unscrambling} of $G$, has applications in the
visualization of electrical circuits and, more generally, in visualizing
graphs with monochromatic cliques. We give a quasi-polynomial time algorithm for
unscrambling graphs with maximum degree 3 and study the computational complexity
of the general case.

classes that are fully present in the alignment set. CDM is shown to achieve
state of the art performance for small training sets while using the computing
power usually required for the large training sets. In addition CDM allows to

leveraging the alignment with the large training set. This is particularly

can be transformed into a trivial unknot diagram by a series of unknotting

\Delta\text{-move for all } i \}. $ We study the distance invariant $d_W(K,K')$

Fields like graph computer, graphs theory, and machine learning use matrices
very often to solve their own problems. The most often matrix operation is the
multiplication, however, for large matrices the multiplication could be time
consuming. To make the matter worse, the most of the known fast approaches for
matrix multiplication are parallel and as such they require special hardware
to be fast. In this paper, we propose a method for transforming matrix
multiplication into a set of bit operations which can be parallelized on a
large number of threads without notable slow down. The proposed method can be
used in any area of Computer Science using matrices.
  We evaluate our approach by solving Markov Chains problems. We compare it
between approaches written in C++ using the standard library and approaches
written in C++ using our method. The results show that our approach is at least
10 times faster than the baseline.
  Finally, we believe that our approach is applicable to many areas of Computer
Sciences. It could be, however, implemented only after a deep understanding of
the subject and the matrices used to solve its own problems.

paid by agents for the project, as well as a significant improvement in the
efficiency of the trading process leading to the adoption of the project.

further divided into horizontal federated learning (HFL) and vertical federated
learning (VFL). In HFL, participants share the same feature space and

arguably more suitable for joint model training between large enterprises.
  In this paper, we focus on VFL and investigate potential privacy leakage in
real-world VFL frameworks. We design and implement two practical privacy
attacks: reverse multiplication attack for the logistic regression model and
reverse aggregation attack for any model trained with gradient aggregation.
We empirically evaluate the success of these attacks in terms of accuracy and
time cost. Our study underscores the importance of privacy preservation in
VFL. To mitigate privacy leakage, we propose an efficient private VFL
protocol: SafeVFL. SafeVFL replaces traditional gradient aggregation with
secure overlay of low-resolution gradients, which effectively eliminates the
need of private comparison and reduction of gradients. SafeVFL is
demonstrated to be compatible with popular FL frameworks, efficient in
computing, and effective in preserving participant data privacy. Experiments

complexity of kernel computation grows as the data size increases; thus the
applicability of kernel methods is limited for large scale datasets. Random
Fourier Features (RFF) has been proposed to scale the kernel method for solving
large scale datasets by approximating kernel function using randomized Fourier
features. While this method proved very popular, still it exists shortcomings
to be effectively used. As RFF samples the randomized features from a
distribution independent of training data, it requires sufficient large number
of feature expansions to have similar performances to kernelized classifiers,
and this is proportional to the number samples in the dataset. Thus, reducing
the number of feature dimensions is necessary to effectively scale to large
datasets. In this paper, we propose a kernel approximation method in a data
dependent way, coined as Pseudo Random Fourier Features (PRFF) for reducing the
number of feature dimensions and also to improve the prediction performance.
The proposed approach is evaluated on classification and regression problems
and compared with the RFF, orthogonal random features and Nystr{\"o}m approach
over various datasets.

valve replacement
surgery in patients with the congenital heart disease Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF)
is mainly based on ventricular volume and function according to current
guidelines. Both of these two biomarkers are most reliably assessed by
segmentation of 3D cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) images. In several grand
challenges in the last years, U-Net architectures have shown impressive results
on the provided data. However, in clinical practice, data sets are more diverse
considering individual pathologies and image properties derived from different
scanner properties. Additionally, specific training data for complex rare
diseases like TOF is scarce.
  For this work, 1) we assessed the accuracy gap when using a publicly
available labelled data set (the Automatic Cardiac Diagnosis Challenge (ACDC)
data set) for training and subsequent applying it to CMR data of TOF patients
and vice versa and 2) whether we can achieve similar results when applying the
model to a more heterogeneous data base.
  Multiple deep learning models were trained with four-fold cross validation.
Afterwards they were evaluated on the respective unseen CMR images from the
other set of the validation process as well as on the entire test group.
Significant higher results both in terms of dose and score could be achieved when
training and applying the model on the specific data. But also training on the
small but highly homogeneous ACDC data and applying it to the more diverse TOF
data showed promising results.
  With careful data selection, even with small labelled data sets and matched
to individual image characteristics, accurate segmentations can be achieved.
Additionally, a guidance using biomarkers and biomarker combinations is
necessary to support the clinician with the decision when to operate and to what
extent.

essential skill to comprehend
and reason about real world task procedures, which often requires thorough
understanding of temporal common sense and multimodal information, as these
procedures are often communicated through a combination of texts and images.
Such capability is essential for applications such as sequential task planning
and multi-source instruction summarization. While humans are capable of
reasoning about and sequencing unordered multimodal procedural instructions,
whether current machine learning models have such essential capability is still
an open question. In this work, we benchmark models' capability of reasoning
over and sequencing unordered multimodal instructions by curating datasets from
popular online instructional manuals and collecting comprehensive human
annotations. We find models not only perform significantly worse than humans
but also seem incapable of efficiently utilizing the multimodal information. To
improve machines' performance on multimodal event sequencing, we propose
sequentiality-aware pretraining techniques that exploit the sequential
alignment properties of both texts and images, resulting in > 5% significant
improvements.
  Our study and methods have broader implications for machines to better
understand and reason about real world procedural instructions, which could
lead to improved overall performance on a range of related tasks.
Furthermore, our dataset provides a rich source of human annotations for
further study of the alignment between human and machine capabilities on
multimodal event sequencing.

this case, we can still increase the sensing frequency significantly, but we
cannot exceed the lossless region.

can possibly fix these drawing backs.

multiple-output (XL-MIMO)
systems are seen as a promising technology for providing very high data rates
in increased user-density scenarios. Spatial non-stationarities and visibility
regions (VRs) appear across the XL-MIMO array since its large dimension is of
the same order as the distances to the user-equipments (UEs). Due to the
increased density of UEs in typical applications of XL-MIMO systems and the
scarcity of pilots, the design of random access (RA) protocols and scheduling
algorithms become challenging. In this paper, we propose a joint RA and
scheduling protocol, namely non-overlapping VR XL- MIMO (NOVR-XL) RA protocol,
which takes advantage of the different VRs of the UEs for improving RA
performance, besides seeking UEs with non-overlapping VRs to be in different
VRs. We formulate a mixed-integer linear program (MILP) to find the optimal
RA sequence and schedule. Since solving this problem is computationally
expensive, we devise a heuristic algorithm to provide good RA sequences and
schedules. Simulation results show that the proposed scheme yields significant
gains compared to baseline protocols.

of disks surrounding young stars have shown that their morphology is made of

from high-resolution 3D radiative hydrodynamical models which follow the
evolution of gas and solids in the protoplanetary disk. We focus on substructures
in the distribution of millimeter-sized and smaller solid particles produced by
the vertical shear instability. We show that their characteristics are
compatible with some of the shallow gaps detected in recent observations at
sub-mm/mm wavelengths, and present predictions for future observations with
better sensitivity and angular resolution with ALMA and a Next Generation Very

common concern raised from ex-post assessments is that storage resources can
fail to respond to strong price signals during times of scarcity. While
commonly attributed to forecast error or failures in operations, we posit that
this behavior can be explained from the perspective of risk-averse scheduling.
Using a stochastic self-scheduling framework and real-world data harvested from
the Australian National Electricity Market, we demonstrate that risk-averse
storage resources tend to have a myopic operational perspective, that is, they
typically engage in near-term price arbitrage and chase only few extreme price
spikes and troughs, thus remaining idle in several time periods with markedly
high and low prices. This has important policy implications given the
non-transparency of unit risk aversion and apparent risk in intervention
decision-making.
  We further show that simple risk-aversion traits can lead to complex and
counter-intuitive behaviors in several scenarios. Most notably, a risk-averse
storage resource may deliberately miss some price spikes while simultaneously
chasing other slightly lower but still markedly elevated prices, thus indicating
the importance of a rigorous analysis of risk aversion in storage operations and
policy interventions.
  Our results highlight the importance of robust risk-sensitive performance
metrics and algorithms that can effectively capture the impact of forecast
error in the future as well as the inherent risk aversion implicit in the
operations of storage resources.
  We argue that such an approach is crucial for the effective planning,
scheduling, and real-time control of storage resources, and thus the
efficient management of future low-carbon grids.
  We provide a general framework that can be applied to any storage technology
and electricity market structure.
  Finally, our framework provides a rigorous ex-ante analysis of storage storage
operations, thus aiding the transition towards a low-carbon economy by improving
the design of policies that prioritize the efficient management of energy
storage.
  We further demonstrate that our framework can be extended to evaluate the
riskiness of complex portfolios of resources, thus aiding the management of
risk-related policy interventions, such as those tied to the Transition
Hubbard Model.
  Finally, we show that our approach provides valuable insights into the
operations of portfolios of resources with and without explicit market
transactions, thus aiding the ex-post analysis of market-related policies as
well as the evaluation of national or regional risk aversion profiles.

  Supervised pretraining (SP) on labeled datasets provides a solid foundation
for DNNs to build upon. However, the cost of annotating a large quantity of
data can be prohibitively expensive. Active learning (AL) algorithms aim to
identify the most informative samples in the training set that should be
annotated. When combined with self-supervised pretraining (SSP) schemes that
utilize large stores of unlabeled data, we observe a remarkable boost in
performance when allowed to utilize labeled data through AL. In this work, we
develop a series of investigations to understand the basis of this boost. We
find that the boost is largely due to the regularizing effect of the
self-supervised and Al models during fine-tuning rather than any enhancement of
the models themselves. We develop a simple but practical Al strategy that
achieves competitive results while being significantly cheaper to compute.
Furthermore, we observe a significant boost in data efficiency, requiring as
few as 5000 labels to match the performance of a model trained on the entire
ImageNet training set. Code is available at https://github.com/sghofifi/active_learning

protecting public safety, which often deals with color-monotonous and
luster-insufficient objects, resulting in unsatisfactory performance. To solve
this problem, we propose a new paradigm called counter-action learning, which
forces some trained models to recognize selected classes (the positive set)
accurately while avoiding recognizing other classes (the negative set). The
positive set is trained to raise the recognition accuracy on the typical images
of the classes, while the negative set is trained to lower the accuracy on the
images of the classes. A straightforward strategy to construct the negative set
is to choose the classes that are most similar to the positive set, but it may
still include the original prohibited items, causing dangerous situations. To
avoid the similarity relation among classes, we propose another strategy to
construct the negative set based on the similarity between images. The core idea
is to exchange the features of some images between the positive set and the
negative set so that the models learn to distinguish the very similar images.
For example, some guns are easily mistaken for some batons, and they are all
made of the same material, which are often mistaken for pipes. To further
improve the performance, we propose to train the model in a multi-scale way.
Different scales of the objects are selected to construct the positive set and
the negative set, which effectively improves the performance. Experiments show
that it is a very effective way to improve the detection performance of X-ray
images, which is 4.68% higher than the baseline method.

  Differential privacy (DP) is an operational definition for privacy that
provides a measure of the amount of information that can be obtained by an
untrusted party (e.g., an adversary) from a dataset by drawing inferences about
an individual who is part of the dataset \cite{Dwork06}. The definition
operates by quantifying the maximum possible gain in the adversary's knowledge
that can be obtained by learning from one to two (individual and group) datasets
that differ in their inclusion of the individual/group of interest. A
mechanism that satisfies this definition is therefore one that limits this
possible gain to be at most a certain amount, and there are several algorithms
that have been shown to satisfy this definition, including the Gaussian
mechanism \cite{Dwork14}, the Laplace mechanism \cite{Dwork06}, and the
Exponential Mechanism \cite{Fey09}. The challenge, however, is to design these
algorithms so that they can utilize complex datasets that contain rich
information. This is particularly difficult when the data are graph-structured
because of the high dimensionality of the input and the complexity of data
processing.
  In this work, we study the applications of DP in the context of graph-structured
data. We discuss the formulations of DP in the context of individual and group
privacy, we discuss some of the private algorithmic tasks for graph data (e.g.,
sampling a vertex, estimating the number of vertices, estimating the number of
edges), and we analyze some of the challenges and limitations of these tasks.
Finally, we briefly discuss some of the future directions in this area of
research.
  We propose a new framework, called the edge perspective, for defining individual
and group privacy in the context of graph-structured data. We show that this
framework provides a higher level of privacy protection compared to the node
perspective, which is the standard formulation of DP in the context of graph
data.

representation within FABE, we dramatically improve the performance of BE in
terms of runtime and memory requirements. Results achieved by comparing FABE
with state of the art approaches for most probable explanation (i.e., recursive
best-first and structured message passing) and constrained optimisation (i.e.,
CPLEX, GUROBI, and toulbar2) for a dataset describing a knowledge graph about
animals and their body parts confirm the effectiveness of our concise function
representation, showing runtime improvements of up to 5 orders of magnitude and
memory savings up to 3 orders of magnitude in addition to dramatic improvements
in correctness (i.e., accuracy of results).
  From a practical perspective, our concise function representation and its
implementation within FABE provide a powerful and efficient way of solving
inference and optimisation tasks for large graphical models, an important
application domain that can lead to significant improvements in the performance
of artificial intelligence systems.
  From a theoretical perspective, our work contributes a novel concise function
representation for graphical models to the literature, in the form of
deterministic finite state automata. This concise representation provides a
practical basis for dramatically improving the performance of BE. Future work
could explore the theoretical properties of this concise function representation
and its integration into other general approaches, as well as study other
applications beyond the three we considered.
  In summary, this thesis provides a concise function representation based on
deterministic finite state automata together with its implementation within
FABE. This work provides a practical basis for dramatically improving the
performance of BE across a range of tasks and applications.

in this thesis has been made publicly available at

twisted superfluid and supersolid phases that were recently reported for
two-component ultracold atomic condensate in an optical lattice. Using a
cluster Gutzwiller mean-field theory, we establish that Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya
interactions (DMI), that are common in many quantum magnets, stabilize these
phases in a magnetic system, in contrast to the pair hopping process that is
necessary for ultracold atoms. The critical value of DMI for transition to the
twisted superfluid and twisted supersolid phases depends on the strength of the
(frustrated) interlayer interactions that can be tuned by applying external
pressure on and / or shearing force between the layers. Furthermore, we show that
a weak vertical coupling can also drive a topological superfluid and
superfluid-to-superfluid phase transition, both of which are also characterized
by a dispersion gap in the triplon spectrum. Our results provide a promising
basis for exploring triplon-induced twisted superfluid and twisted supersolid
phases in optically trapped magnetic insulators, where DMI can be tuned separately
and with high accuracy.
  We also provide a heuristic argument that these phases are more likely to
occur in magnetic systems, where a small amount of anisotropic coupling can
stabilize several ordered phases. In contrast, ultracold atomic condensate is
typically described by an isotropic two-body interaction, which requires a
precise tuning of the interaction strength to realize various superfluid and
superfluid-to-superfluid transitions.
  Finally, we note that our theoretical model can be used to guide experimental
design in optically trapped magnetic insulators, e.g., in dysprosium or
hooley-based microscopics, where triplons have been observed in experiments. We
hope to motivate further theoretical work in this direction.

professional knowledge work is
an understudied area. Here we investigate how public sector officials
self-assess their dependency on the Google Web search engine, whether they are
aware of the potential impact of algorithmic biases on their ability to
retrieve all relevant information, and how much relevant information may
actually be missed due to Web search personalisation. We find that the majority
of participants in our experimental study are neither aware that there is a
potential problem nor do they have a strategy to mitigate the risk of missing
relevant information when performing online searches. Most significantly, we
provide empirical evidence that up to 20% of relevant information may be missed
due to Web search personalisation. This work has significant implications for
Web research by public sector professionals, who should be provided with
training about the potential algorithmic biases that may affect their judgments
and decision making, as well as clear guidelines how to minimise the risk of
missing relevant information.
  We propose a new theoretical framework that combines design science,
human-computer interaction, and public administration. The framework identifies
two cycles that are crucial for improving Web search for public sector
information professionals: the Search Quality Cycle and the Knowledge Cycle. The
Search Quality Cycle ensures that search engines provide high quality results
for professional searches. The Knowledge Cycle guarantees that professional
knowledge work based on reliable information is preserved.
  We study how search engines respond to user feedback in terms of disabling
the personalisation of the search results. We do so by deliberately submitting
incorrect information to the search engines and observe the share of such
incorrect information that is restated in the search results upon subsequent
searches. We find that most search engines do not disable the personalisation
completely even after repeatedly providing demonstrably incorrect information.
For example, Google disables the personalisation after 5 searches, Bing after
never (i.e., it does not disable it at all), and Yahoo after 2 searches. These
findings show that search engines are not completely resistant to garbage in,
garbage out.

quality compared to the linear reconstruction in all cases.

mutation test -- has played
a vital role in developing NLP systems to provide confidence that the
difference in performance between two systems (i.e., the test statistic) is not
due to luck. However, practitioners rely on Monte Carlo approximation to
perform this test due to a lack of a suitable exact algorithm. In this paper,
we provide an efficient exact algorithm for the paired-permutation test for a
family of structured test statistics. Our algorithm runs in $\mathcal{O}(GN
(\log GN )(\log N ))$ time where $N$ is the dataset size and $G$ is the range
of the test statistic. We found that our exact algorithm was $10$x faster than
the Monte Carlo approximation with $20000$ samples on a common dataset.
Moreover, we found that our exact algorithm could handle test statistics on a
$2$ GB dataset, which is infeasible for the Monte Carlo approximation due to
memory constraints.
  We also develop a heuristic algorithm for the more general paired-randomized
test, which allows the null distribution to be non-uniform. Our algorithm runs
in $\mathcal{O}(GN)$ time. Practically, we find that our algorithm is $3$x
faster than the Monte Carlo approximation on a common dataset. Together, our
algorithms provide a suite of exact and heuristic paired-testing algorithms,
which should be a handy utility for building reliable NLP systems.
  Finally, we discover that the widely-used significance testing library,
scipy.stats.stats.permutation_test_, has a design flaw that leads to
over-rejection (i.e., wrong rejection of the null hypothesis when it is true).
We propose a simple fix to this flaw.
  This paper presents a pair of efficient algorithms for two commonly used
significance tests in NLP: the paired-permutation test and the paired-randomized
test. While NLP researchers might not care about the technical details of these
algorithms, the transparent description of the algorithms provides a solid
foundation for a generic library that implements these algorithms. I envision
this library to be a handy utility for building reliable NLP systems.
  I present a Python library called `significance_tests` that implements the
algorithms developed in this paper. The library is designed to be modular so
that it can be easily extended to implement other types of significance tests.
You can download `significance_tests` from this repository:
https://github.com/strawberry0271/significance_tests.

novel method called Kedge for explicitly sparsifying the underlying graph by
removing unnecessary neighbors. Our key idea is based on a tractable method for
sparsification using hard kernels which allows GNNs to only depend on a

range of the neighbors, along with GNN weights in a unified fashion. This
sparsity allows for more flexible and adaptive inductive biases of the GNNs. We
demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on various node classification and
link prediction tasks. We show that our model achieves better prediction
accuracy and lower generalization error compared to baselines. Moreover, we
demonstrate that our model produces higher edge relevance scores, thus
exhibiting higher interpretability.

observe that the kernel acts as a pseudo-degree normalization. We study this in
the context of a simple GNN baseline and a state-of-the-art centralizer GNN. We
show that the kernel improves the representation quality of the model in a
way that is orthogonal to the inductive bias of the GNN. Finally, we study a
real-world dataset collected from a leading life science company. Our model
shows higher accuracy and lower generalization error compared to baselines and

states is the common envelope (CE)
phase of binary evolution, in which two stars are enshrouded by the envelope
shed by one of them. Interactions between the stars and the envelope shrinks
the orbit. The CE can lead to mergers or to a subsequent phase of interactions.
Mergers may involve any combination of two compact objects and/or stars. Some
involving white dwarfs, may produce Type Ia supernovae, while merging neutron
stars may yield gamma-ray bursts, and merging compact objects of all kinds
produce gravitational radiation. Since CEs can arise from a variety of
different initial conditions, and due to the complexity of the processes
involved, it is difficult to predict their end states. When many systems are
being considered, as in population synthesis calculations, conservation
principles are generally employed. Here we use angular momentum in a new way to
derive a simple expression for the final orbital separation. This method
provides advantages for the study of binaries and is particularly well-suited
to higher order multiples, now considered to be important in the genesis of
potential mergers. It is also extended to express the mass transferred back
from the envelope in terms of the initial and final orbital parameters. These
two results provide valuable tools for the study of CEs and offer opportunities
to compare theory with observations. As an example, we use them to study
satellites and the nature of the interacting binaries known as semi-detachments.
We provide simple expressions for the mass and radius scales in these
interacting binaries and demonstrate them by considering several different
types. The method is not limited to these systems, however, and can be
applied to any CE, including those in multiple star simulations.
  We derive a new expression for the final orbital separation of a common
envelope binary and show that it accurately predicts a large number of different
observations. We then use the method to multiply derive the mass transferred
between the stars and the envelope envelope during the CE phase and show that it
also accurately predicts a large number of different observations for a variety
of different configurations. Both of these expressions are useful tools for the
study of CEs and offer opportunities to compare theory with observations. As an
example, we use them to study satellites and the nature of interacting binaries
known as semi-detachments. We provide simple expressions for the mass and
radius scales in these systems and demonstrate them by considering several
different examples.

configurations due to their large parameter space, complex interdependencies,
and high evaluation cost. Utilizing probabilistic models, Structured Bayesian
Optimization (SBO) has recently overcome these difficulties. SBO decomposes the
parameter space by utilizing contextual information provided by system experts
leading to fast convergence. However, the complexity of building probabilistic
models has hindered its wider adoption. We propose BoAnon, a SBO framework that
learns the system structure from its logs. BoAnon provides an API enabling
experts to encode knowledge of the system as performance models or components
dependency. BoAnon takes in the learned structure and transforms it into a
probabilistic graph model. Then it applies the expert-provided knowledge to the
graph to further contextualize the system behavior. BoAnon probabilistic graph
allows the optimizer to find efficient configurations faster than other
methods. We evaluate BoAnon via a hardware architecture search problem,
achieving an improvement in energy-latency objectives ranging from $5-7$
x-factors improvement over the default architecture. With its novel contextual
structure learning pipeline, BoAnon makes using SBO accessible for a wide range
of other computer systems such as databases and stream processors.

latter allows for reproducibility across different environments and more

means of the anisotropic factor, defined as the ratio between the intensity
emitted in the direction perpendicular to the film plane and the average intensity
emitted in the parallel directions. The acoustic anisotropy has been interpreted

substrate system and to the anisotropic grain size and texture (in the case of a

well-defined film substrate system.

provides a straightforward way to quantify the grain size anisotropy (in terms of

coefficients of the film and substrate. The approach is generally valid for a
thin film (or dust) on a substrate, but also for a thick film or superconducting
film in which the vibration mode is not limited to the film thickness.

particular, the grain size anisotropy, in the context of the lunar exosphere and
more generally, in the context of the acoustic emission of dusty objects in space

constrained resources, unreliable communication, and varying operating
conditions of IoT pose significant complexities for software vendors in testing

numerous issues can be pointed out, such as lacking support for logical
dependencies and advanced fault injection capabilities, requiring manual
validation of the system's behavior, or focusing on a specific platform and

automated testing of IoT applications. Frisbee accelerates the testing process
by simplifying the spin-up of distributed virtual testbeds over Kubernetes and

workloads and faultloads.
  Frisbee simplifies the development of new testing tools by providing a
service-oriented architecture, where each service leverages a modular design to
be reused across different types of IoT applications. More importantly, Frisbee
allows vendors to specify their applications with a service-level description
that enables the easy identification of misbehaviors in the tested systems. We
demonstrate Frisbee's advantages by applying it to the testing of a Computer
Vision-based monitoring system. The evaluation shows that Frisbee accelerates
the testing process by up to 3 times and reduces the manual validation time by
80%.

Existing methods typically train models on the BIRD Dataset, which has a
limited number of examples due to the high cost of labeling a large number of
images. We propose a multi-task framework that utilizes both BIRD and YOLO Datasets.
The first task is a instance-level generation task that generates specific
objects, such as a blue car or a red truck, at specific locations. The second
task is a class-level generation task that generates the background and
secondary objects (such as pedestrians, lane markers) in a scene. We show that
our proposed multi-task framework is able to generate realistic traffic scenes
with a variety of objects. The code and dataset are available at
https://github.com/Ching-AnLin/Conditional-TGPT.
  From a methodological perspective, our key innovation is a multi-task
framework that uses both instance-level and class-level conditional GANs to
generate realistic traffic scenes. The key idea is that a conditional GAN
predicts a certain object (e.g., a blue car) by its attributes (color, shape),
rather than its identity. This allows us to generate a diversity of objects with
similar attributes. Furthermore, we add a secondary generator to add secondary
objects (e.g., lane markers, pedestrians) to the generated image. We show that
this is a useful addition in realistic traffic scenes.
  We evaluate our method side-by-side with BRT-GAN on a new dataset consisting
of renderings of real traffic scenes. We show that our method produces a
meaningful improvement in both visual quality and fidelity to real scenes. We
also show that our method is able to generalize to new types of objects that are
not seen during training.
  From a theoretical perspective, our work studies the problem of unifying
multiple tasks in the context of traffic scene generation. A key question in
multi-task learning is how to benefit from multiple tasks. Our work shows that
multiple tasks are beneficial in terms of generating a diversity of objects in
a scene.
  Finally, our code and dataset are available at
https://github.com/Ching-AnLin/Conditional-TGPT.
  We hope our multi-task framework leads to new and better models for
generating realistic traffic scenes.

time-dependent partial differential equations (PDEs) is the ability to preserve
certain properties of the continuum solution, such as associated conservation
laws or other geometric structures of the solution. There is a long history of
the development and analysis of such structure-preserving discretisation
schemes, including both proofs that standard schemes have structure-preserving
properties and proposals for novel schemes that achieve both high-order
accuracy and exact preservation of certain properties of the continuum
differential equation. When applied to a discretisation of a PDE, such schemes
tend to have superior long-term stability properties, retain important
physical properties of the continuum problem and provide better results when
approximating sharp fronts or boundaries. In this thesis, we develop and analyse
two different classes of schemes for approximately solving time-dependent
nonlocal problems and both have structure-preserving properties. In Chapter 2,
we derive a class of Hammer-Hansen scheme equivalents for time fractional
fading memory equations. These schemes have exactly conserved important
attributes of the underlying continuous model, such as the nonlocal kernel
shape. In Chapter 3, we build a time stepping algorithm for the fractional
Fokker-Planck equation which has exactly conserved mass and a desired kernel
shape. These schemes have superior long-term stability properties and retain
important physical properties of the continuum problem.
  In both chapters, we analytically derive the spatially consistent schemes
through a combination of classical limiting arguments and moments methods. We
illustrate the improved accuracy of these schemes in solving both smooth and
discontinuous problems.
  Finally, we conduct some numerical experiments to verify the better performance
of these schemes in maintaining the shape of the solution profile.
  Throughout this thesis, we promote the use of limiting arguments to construct
discrete schemes for integral/differential operators involving kernels. This
approach is intuitive, widely applicable and helps to ensure that the discrete
schemes retain the important structural properties of the underlying continuous
model.
  Both of the proposed schemes are constructed by directly mimicking the
corresponding continuous models. This ensures that the discrete schemes retain
important attributes of the underlying continuous model, such as the nonlocal
kernel shape. This is in contrast to standard approximation schemes, such as
finite difference or finite element methods, which do not generally preserve
such features. The latter is usually a source of errors when approximating
fronts or boundaries of the solution of PDEs.

said to be strongly jointly ergodic if for almost every choice of $k$ diverging
sequences in it, the related multiple ergodic averages converge in time $n$ with
an error term of order $n^{-\frac{1}{2}+\varepsilon}$. It is known that
arithmetic sequences, congruence sequences, recurrence sequences and lacunary
sequences are strongly jointly ergodic. The goal of the paper is to prove that
this is a very general phenomenon. In particular, our results imply that any

3D detection (Far3Det) of objects beyond a
certain distance from an observer, e.g., $50m$. For this task, conventional
methodologies that use the image height band as a proxy for distance fail due
to the short field of view. Instead, we propose a simple yet effective approach
that uses instance segmentation (IS) masks to filter out distant objects that
are unlikely to project a significant amount of pixels. To leverage IS masks,
we introduce two variants of a straightforward thresholding methodology. We
further analyze that the performance of Far3Det tasks in standard benchmarks
is suboptimal due to the indirect relationship between the ground truth distance
and the predicted height. Therefore, we introduce the Far3Det Benchmarks to
assess detection and displacement performance at various distance thresholds.
Evaluating our methodology on the Far3Det Benchmarks and the standard MLC and
KITTI benchmarks shows a significant improvement in accuracy and a minor
increase in computational cost.

in soft-tissue navigation. We focus
on laparoscopic liver surgery, where we register the organ model obtained from
a preoperative CT scan to the intraoperative partial organ surface,
reconstructed from the laparoscopic video. This is a challenging task due to
sparse and noisy intraoperative data, real-time requirements and many unknowns
- such as tissue properties and boundary conditions. Furthermore, establishing
correspondences between pre- and intraoperative data can be extremely difficult
since the liver usually lacks distinct anatomic surface features and the used
imaging modalities have different image plane orientations and resolutions.
Therefore, we propose a multi-resolution correspondence-free approach. We
divide the registration process into two main steps: (i) a coarse, elastic
fitting; (ii) a fine, inelastic fitting with volume deformation. We present an
efficient algorithm for both steps and verify its performance in both
simulation and experimental setups.
  We introduce a volume deformation descriptor, which provides a correspondence-
free way for the intraoperative volume to guide the preoperative volume towards
the correct position and orientation. This descriptor, combined with the
surfaces, significantly improves the robustness to imaging noise and wrong
imaging assumptions. Furthermore, the new descriptor allows for the direct
exploitation of the intraoperative surface data in the registration process.
Consequently, we obtain high accuracy scores, especially in scenarios with
significant translation and rotation. Experimental results also show that the
proposed method is able to run in real-time.
  Compared to the state-of-the-art, our method shows higher accuracy, robustness
and visual plausibility. In addition, it provides a volume deformation score,
which can be used for the evaluation of the surgery and the volume-based
recovery of the intraoperative regions not explicitly extracted from the
laparoscopic video.
  In conclusion, we present a highly efficient, accurate and robust 3D/2D
non-rigid registration method for a challenging organ like the liver. Its
flexibility makes it suitable for various medical applications and it can be
easily integrated with surgical tools for the future development of a
soft-tissue navigation system.

datasets designed to study individual aspects of flow estimation in progressive
order of complexity, from a single object in motion to real-world scenes.
Furthermore, we introduce Adversarial Metric Learning for self-supervised flow
estimation. The flow model is fed with sequences of point clouds to perform
flow estimation. A second network learns a latent metric to distinguish between
the points translated by the flow estimations and the target point cloud. This
latent metric is learned via a Multi-Scale Triplet loss, which uses
intermediary feature vectors for the loss calculation. We use our proposed
benchmark to draw insights into the performance of the baselines and of
different models when trained using our setup. We find that our setup is able
to keep motion coherence and preserve local geometries, which many
self-supervised baselines fail to grasp. Dealing with occlusions, on the other

One of the major obstacles that have historically delayed large scale adoption
of ANNs is the huge computational and power costs associated with training and
testing (inference) such networks. In the mean-time, Neuromorphic Computing
platforms provide hardware accelerators that can emulate the behavior of
neural networks using a large number of low-resolution neurons that are
geographically distributed across a chip to achieve high computation
parallelism, while having a 1000x lower power and area costs compared to
state-of-the-art deep learning layers. This unique characteristic allows these
platforms to natively run a large number of ANNs in an energy efficient
manner. In this paper, we propose a new approach to enable NeuroSymbolic Reasoning
using these ANNs. Our approach allows a low-resolution neural chip to run on a
family of mathematical expressions that can be used to answer symbolic
queries about a source data that was originally processed using ANNs. The main
idea is to learn a different representation of the original data using these
mathematical expressions, where each expression is implemented as a mixture of
a large number of low-resolution neural layers, resulting in a robust and
efficient solution for inference. The main advantage is to enable manipulation
of the represented data using Boolean operations, significantly improving the
ability of these systems to run simple conditional logic tasks. This is
particularly important for automatic inference in dynamic scenarios, where
inference results can be used to answer new queries that were not anticipated
at design time. Our approach does not require any additional hardware
acceleration to implement Boolean operations, making it particularly useful
for platforms that do not have a separate logic accelerator. The proposed
approach is thoroughly evaluated on three different datasets that include text,
images, and audio. Experimental results show that our approach can significantly
improve the accuracy of the original ANNs, when subjected to complex
comparisons, while maintaining or even benefiting from the low computational and
power costs.

Neural Networks (ANNs). Our framework allows a low-resolution neural chip to run
on a family of mathematical expressions that can be used to answer symbolic
queries about a source data that was originally processed using ANNs.

a novel technique for automatically
learning system call filtering policies for containerized microservices
applications. At run-time, Timeloops automatically learns which system calls a
program should be allowed to invoke while rejecting attempts to call spurious
system calls. Further, Timeloops addresses many of the shortcomings of
state-of-the-art static analysis-based techniques, such as the ability to
generate tight filters for programs written in interpreted languages such as
PHP, Python, and JavaScript. Timeloops has a simple and robust implementation
because it is mainly built out of commodity, and proven, technologies such as
seccomp-BPF, systemd, and Podman containers, with fewer than 500 lines of code.
We demonstrate the utility of Timeloops by learning system calls for individual
services and two microservices benchmark applications, which utilize popular
technologies like Python Flask, Nginx (with PHP and Lua modules), Apache
Thrift, Memcached, Redis, and MongoDB. Further, the amortized performance of
Timeloops is similar to that of an unhardened system while producing a smaller
system call filter than state-of-the-art static analysis-based techniques.
Finally, we show that Timeloops can reduce the memory footprint of a
microservices application by learning filters that avoid binding unused
system call stacks.

ernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter in
which the intensities of target birth and undetected targets are grid-based. A
simplified version of the Rao-Blackwellized point mass filter is used to
predict the intensity of undetected targets, and the density of targets
detected for the first time are approximated as Gaussian. Whereas conventional
PMBM filter implementations typically use Gaussian mixtures to model the
intensity of undetected targets, the proposed representation allows the
intensity to vary over the region of interest with sharp edges around the
sensor's field of view, without using a large number of Gaussian mixture
components. This reduces the computational complexity compared to the
conventional approach. The proposed method is illustrated in a sensor
management setting where trajectories of sensors with limited fields of view
are controlled to search for and track the targets in a region of interest.
Simulation results show that the proposed filter outperforms a conventional
PMBM filter with Gaussian mixture intensities.
  The proposed filter is also used in a sensor management setting to determine
the best possible performance, which shows that the choice of sensor trajectories
alone is not sufficient to achieve optimal performance and that the sensor
configurations (orientations) are also needed to be optimized in some cases.
This paper introduces a sensor configuration filter (SCF) to estimate the
sensor orientation. The SCF is extended to nonlinear scenarios using unscented
transform techniques. Simulation results show that the proposed joint tracker
and SCF outperforms a tracker that only estimates the trajectory but not the
orientation.
  Finally, the proposed tracker and SCF are used in a more realistic setting
where the sensors and the targets have their states modeled by nonlinear
state-space models. The measurement likelihood is obtained using a track-to
track fusion method. Simulation results show that the proposed approach achieves
accurate and robust target tracking performance in a challenging scenario.
  In summary, the proposed PMBM filter with grid-based intensities provides a
practical way to implement a tractable nonlinear state-space model for target

intractable, and we develop an alternating descent algorithm to resolve it with

predicting the appropriate response, evaluation of encoder representation is a

text generated through human or automatic metrics is not sufficient to
appropriately evaluate soundness of the language understanding of dialogue

significantly affected by architecture choices while other tasks are more
influenced by training hyperparameters. We observe that some probes are

most variance as they are sensitive to statistical bias in the language.

than a single probe task.
