of the key components of SLAM and global
localization in autonomous vehicles and robotics applications. With LiDAR data,
it is possible to extract loop closures by matching scenes that the vehicle has
already visited and globalizing the vehicle trajectory. However, the ins and
outs of LiDAR-based place recognition, especially using point cloud features,
are not well explored. This work investigates the operation of a LiDAR-based
place recognition system and analyzes its performance under different conditions
that could be encountered in a real-world scenario. This work aims to provide
insights for the development of future LiDAR-based place recognition systems and
to contribute to the improvement of SLAM and global localization algorithms.
From the results, it is possible to conclude that LiDAR-based place recognition
can provide loop closures and localize a vehicle trajectory with good accuracy.
However, the system can be improved in the next iteration to address issues
such as geometric transformation misalignment, wrong loop-closure rejection,
and ignored recurring scenes. This work can also be used as a benchmark for the
LiDAR-based place recognition comparison.
  The paper is organized as follows: Section II presents the related work, which
describes LiDAR-based place recognition using point cloud features. Section III
presentes the proposed method, which explains the LiDAR-based place recognition
system operation and the test bed configuration used in the experiments. Section
IV shows the results, which display the loop closures detected by the system and
analyzes the performance in different conditions. Section V concludes the work
and provides final thoughts and future works.

semantic and acoustic features. Inspired by the masking strategy in the speech

and concatenated with those of contextual speech, and further used as
additional model input. The phoneme encoder takes the concatenated phoneme
sequence from neighboring sentences as input and learns fine-grained semantic

semantic features are employed to improve the prosody generation. The model is

multi-field Q-balls lead to a restriction on the sets of fields that can form
non-trivial Q-balls.
  We also comment on the relation between our solution and a similar object
previously introduced in the literature.

constituting a significant fraction of the total energy density of the universe

quenched disorder. This theory shows that such fluids can overcome the
disruption caused by the quenched disorder and move coherently, in the sense of
having a non-zero mean velocity in the hydrodynamic limit. However, the scaling
behavior of this class of active systems cannot be described by linearized
hydrodynamics in spatial dimensions between 2 and 5. Nonetheless, we obtain the
exact dimension-dependent scaling exponents in these dimensions.
Remarkably, the scaling exponents of the polar active fluids with quenched
disorder mimic those of the pure Brownian suspensions in 2 to 5 dimensions.
Finally, our results provide an answer to a long-standing open question of
whether active systems can move in the presence of strong quenched disorder.
This answer is yes, but the physics is somewhat different than what one would
expect from a mixture of active and passive suspensions with quenched disorder.
Such a possibility of coherent motion would not be possible in the absence of
activity.

quenched disorder such as roughness of the surface on which the active particles
move, or orientation dependent interactions, and show that a mixture of active
particles and passive particles with quenched disorder yields unique scaling
behaviors. In this theory, the roughness of the surface or the orientation
dependent interactions are treated as quenched disorders, i.e., they are
treated as random variables that do not change their values in the course of
time. Such a treatment of the hydrodynamic variables is different from the
usual treatment of the disorder in the theory of the statistical mechanics of
randomly oriented or placed particles, where the orientation or placement are
treated as thermal fluctuations that can change their values in the course of
time. The unique scaling behaviors of the polar active fluids with quenched
disorder are derived by linearization of the stochastic momentum equation of the
active particles around the hydrodynamic limit. Nonlinear effects of the

six horizontal layers of plastic-scintillator hodoscopes for determining the
direction and position of the incident cosmic-ray muons. Sandwiched between the
hodoscope planes is a neutron detector filled with 650 kg of liquid
scintillator doped with about 0.06% of Gadolinium by weight for improving the
efficiency of detecting the spallation neutrons. Performance of the apparatus

position of the incident cosmic-ray muons. Each hodoscope plane comprises of 64
x 5 cm x 5 cm large-area plastic scintillator tiles for good position resolution
combined with fine-grained segmentation for excellent timing resolution. The
choice of using large-area tiles was motivated by the relatively low flux of
cosmic-ray muons at large latitudes like Hong Kong. With a total of 384 tiles in
the six planes, the time-of-flight (TOF) and proton charge information can be
combined for determining the momentum of the muons with reasonable resolution.

in this paper.

collection. The choice of using a pair of mirror-finished reflective foils for
light collection was motivated by the relatively large filling volume of each

TESS have demonstrated that
planets are ubiquitous. However, the success of these missions heavily depends
on ground-based radial velocity (RV) surveys, which combined with transit
photometry can yield bulk densities and orbital properties. While most Kepler
host stars are too faint for detailed follow-up observations, TESS is detecting
planets orbiting nearby bright stars that are more amenable to RV
characterization. Here we introduce the TESS-Keck Survey (TKS), an RV program
using ~100 nights on Keck/HIRES to study exoplanets identified by TESS. The
primary survey aims are investigating the link between stellar properties and
the compositions of small planets; studying how the diversity of system
architectures depends on dynamical configurations or planet multiplicity;
identifying prime candidates for atmospheric studies with JWST; and
understanding the role of stellar evolution in shaping planetary systems. We
present a fully-automated target selection algorithm, which yielded 103 planets
in 86 systems for the final TKS sample. Most TKS hosts are inactive,
solar-like, main-sequence stars (4500 K < Teff < 6000 K) at a wide range of
metallicities. The selected TKS sample contains 71 small planets (Rp < 4 Re),
11 systems with multiple transiting candidates, 6 sub-day period planets and 3
planets in the habitable zone. The TKS sample and procedures presented here are
ideal for statistical studies of exoplanetary science.

Edwards, in preparing and executing these observations. We are also grateful
for support from the Keck Observatory 90-night proposal review committee and
from NASA's Exoplanet Science Institute (NESI) for partial funding of this
work.

imaginary chemical potential (anti-Hermitian parameter) and their associated
polaritonic circuits. We consider a two-mode Dicke model as the basic circuit
and obtain closed-form expressions for the eigenvalues and eigenstates. We
observe coherent super and subradiance, as well as the phenomenon of
quantum disentanglement, in the two-mode Dicke system. Furthermore, we explain
how the described phenomena can be implemented in a polariton microcavity.
Using the two-mode system, we construct a switch on or off, a logic gate, a
gateway, and a bridge. We also show how to control the number of photons in the
cavity. We conclude that the Dicke model represents a minimal and effective
scheme for quantum optics and photonics.

classifications of conjunctive queries by their fine-grained complexity only
apply to queries without self-joins. We study how self-joins affect enumeration
complexity, with the aim of building upon the known results to achieve general
classifications. We do this by examining the extension of the known
characterization of the linear-time-enumarable self-join-free queries, which
states that such a query is linearly enumeratable if it has a polynomial
processing power. We show that this characterization does not hold for
self-joins. Moreover, we give a sufficient and necessary condition for
self-joins to make a query nonlinearly enumeratable. Finally, we give an example
of a self-join-enhancing fragment of conjunctive queries which is contained in
the fragment of linearly enumeratable queries, but which is not closed under
repeated self-joins.
  We also examine the restriction of queries to fixed-degree self-joins. We
give a characterization of queries with self-joins of degree greater than 2 by
their enumeration complexity. We show that a query with fixed-self-joins of
degree greater than 2 is linearly enumeratable if it has sublinear processing
power. We complement this by a hardness result showing that even simple
fragments of conjunctive queries with self-joins of degree 2 are nonlinearly
enumeratable under a very restricted notion of hardness.
  Finally, we give a characterization of queries with binary self-joins by
their enumeration complexity in terms of the number of processors available for
evaluation. This characterization is interesting because it shows that even
very simple queries with self-joins (e.g., those containing only one self-join
and otherwise only unary atoms) can have nonlinear enumeration complexity if
the degree of self-joins is 2.
  All of our results follow from a general lemma giving sufficient and
necessary conditions for the enumeration complexity of queries with self-joins.
This lemma is interesting because it shows that even very simple queries with
self-joins can demonstrate rich and interesting enumeration complexity. It is

observations) and is built-up in the inversions. This means that even if we

to the square of the meson-meson scattering amplitude at the pole of the
resonance. Therefore, we start with calculating the scattering amplitude of two
mesons at different energies to continue the story to get the decay width. The
total cross section at different energies are calculated and the energy at the
pole of the resonance is determined using the Mhoedas-Fadely rule. Using the
energy at the pole of the resonance, the scattering amplitude at the pole of
the resonance is calculated to get the decay width.

section of $\rho\rho$ scattering at different energies are calculated using the
Effective Lagrangian method in Universal Chromomagnetic Driven (UCMD) model.
Using the total cross section at different energies we determine the energy
value of the pole of the resonance $W=2m_{\rho}$. Using the scattering
amplitude at the pole of the resonance we determine the decay width of $\rho$
meson.

measure the $\pi\pi$ to $\rho\rho$ transition form factor. Measurement of this

sections of $\rho\rho$ at different energies have been calculated using the

of the resonance $W=2m_{\rho}$ from the total cross section we have calculated
the decay width of $\rho$ meson.

Component Analysis ('FastICA') method ('m-ar-K-FastICA') for feature
extraction. The kernel trick has enabled dimensionality reduction techniques to
capture a higher extent of non-linearity in the data; however, reproducible,
open-source kernels to aid with feature extraction are still limited and may
not be reliable when projecting features from noisy data. The m-ar-K
functionality, implemented in C++ with the R ('Programming Language for
Statistical Computing') rmutil package in mind, provides a robust, reproducible,
and efficient solution by leveraging the arctsinh kernel transformation steps.
This kernel is transformable into a linear input space formulation, which is
practical for ensuring reliability over the range of input patterns, thus
providing a more accurate representation of the original input space. The
m-ar-K-FastICA method was tested against the FastICA standard implementation
available in the R 'fda.usc' package, along with the 'FastICA' R package, for
feature extraction from both synthetic data and real-world datasets with and
without noise contamination. The presented method proved to perform equally or
better than the comparison methods in recovering the true number of sources and
to yield improved accuracy when employed as a precursor step for supervised
classification and unsupervised clustering.

estimation in flux measurements, especially for the shorter exposure times.

can accurately retrieve the noise parameters. Finally, we propose a method to
directly constrain the correlated noise parameters from the data, without the
need of a statistical fit. This method is simple to implement and can be used

precisely measured APOGEE abundances to ~0.1 dex for Na, V, and Ce. The
correlations of residuals reveal a complex underlying structure, including a
correlated element group comprised of Ca, Na, Al, K, Cr, and Ce and a separate
group comprised of Ni, V, Mn, and Co. Selecting stars poorly fit by the
2-process model reveals a rich variety of physical outliers and sometimes
subtle measurement errors. Residual abundances allow direct comparison of
different elements by identifying the relative additional scatter they introduce
beyond the "delayed" component. We use residuals to visually and quantitatively
identify the APOGEE DR17 iron-peak elements: Ni, V, Mn, Co, Cr, Ce, and the
combined measurements of the correlated element group. We visually and
quantitatively identify the main sequence (MS) turnoff (MSTO) dichotomy in the
[{\Delta}V/H]-[Mg/H] plane, which separates the more abundant light elements in
the population of long-lived red clump (RLC) stars. We use residuals to
quantitatively measure the relative position of the MSTO dichotomy in the age
sequence of disk populations. We find that the dichotomy is more extreme in
younger (~6.6 vs ~7.3 Gyr) populations. The amplitude of the dichotomy decreases
with age in a manner consistent with a simple chemical evolution model. We
speculate that the 2-process paradigm, the correlated element group, and the

world.In China, COVID-19 has caused severe consequences. Moreover, online
rumors during the COVID-19 pandemic increased people's panic about public
health and social stability. At present, understanding and curbing the spread
of online rumors is an urgent task. Therefore, we analyzed the rumor spreading
mechanism and propose a method to quantify a rumors' influence by the speed of
new insiders. The search frequency of the rumor is used as an observation
variable of new insiders. The peak coefficient and the attenuation coefficient
are calculated for the search frequency, which conforms to the exponential
distribution. We designed several rumor features and used the above two
coefficients as predictable labels. A 5-fold cross-validation experiment using
the mean square error (MSE) as the loss function showed that the decision tree
was suitable for predicting the peak coefficient, and the linear regression
model was ideal for predicting the attenuation coefficient. Our feature
analysis showed that precursor features were the most important for the
outbreak coefficient, while location information and rumor entity information
were the most important for the attenuation coefficient. Meanwhile, features
that were conducive to the outbreak were usually harmful to the continued
spread of rumors. At the same time, anxiety was a crucial feature causing rumors
to continue to spread.

neural network. Many loss functions have been designed to date, making a
correct choice nontrivial. However, elaborate justifications regarding the
choice of the loss function are not made in related work. This is, as we see
it, an indication of a dogmatic mindset in the deep learning community which
lacks empirical foundation. In this work, we consider deep neural networks in a
supervised classification setting and analyze the impact the choice of loss
function has onto the training of the network. While certain loss functions
clearly perform worse than others, our experiments indicate that under the
right parameters, all considered loss functions converge to comparable accuracy
values. This suggests that the choice of the loss function is not as crucial as
is commonly assumed in practice. To further support this claim, we leverage
proximal methods which allow us to drop the stochasticity from both the data
and the optimization. This way, we can analyze the loss functions at their most
basic form. We observe that all the considered losses are equivalent up to some
constants which have a direct effect onto training. This observation, however, is
completely missed in the unified loss functions currently being used. To that
end, we propose a new family of losses for supervised classification which can
improve upon the currently used ones in specific scenarios. Finally, we provide
a loss aggregation method which allows us to learn multiple losses at once. This
is achieved by means of a hash function which turns the cross-entropy, a
typical aggregator of multiple losses, into a proxy label. All the code used in
this work is available at https://github.com/AmanPriyanshu/DynamicLoss.
  From the results, we observe that the one-size-fits-all mindset regarding the
choice of the loss function is not justified. Different losses are indeed
needed in specific scenarios which is highlighted by the losses we propose.
Along with that, we leverage a method that allows us to learn multiple losses at
once by learning a hash function to aggregate them. This further highlights the
flexibility of modern deep learning models which can learn any function
whatsoever (up to approximations) with the right initialization and architecture
design.

  Imitation learning (IL) learns from demonstrations to acquire new skills in
a much shorter time compared to pure reinforcement learning. However, the
quality of the learned policy depends highly on the quality of the teacher's
demonstrations. In this paper, we propose training a policy using the
likelihood of the teacher's action choices to be higher than a certain
threshold to become robust to noise. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our
approach in three challenging imitation learning problems - a 7 DoF robotic
simulation task, a 16 DoF multi-fingered robotic manipulation task and the
Pybullet benchmark. Our results show that by learning the teacher's noise
policy, our approach can significantly improve the performance of the policy
relative to traditional IL approaches.
  We also provide a theoretical analysis of our algorithm and prove that our
method is guaranteed to increase the performance relative to the noise-free
policy with high confidence, thus indicating that our algorithm is able to
reduce the influence of noise in the demonstrations.

continuous phase
modulation (CPM) is quite robust to channel impairments such as phase and
Doppler shifts. Its implementation is on top of that simple. It consists in
multiplying the received baseband signal by its conjugate and delayed version
of one symbol period. However it suffers from a signal-to-noise ratio gap
compared to the optimum coherent detection. In this paper, we improve the error
rate performance of the conventional differential detection by using a delay
higher than one symbol period. We derive the trellis description as well as the
branch and cumulative metric that take into account a delay of $K$ symbol
periods. We then derive an optimization criterion of $K$ based on the minimum
Euclidean distance between two differential signals. We finally determine
optimized delays for some popular CPM formats whose values are confirmed by
error rate simulations.

detection. Moreover it is quite robust to channel impairments such as phase and
Doppler shifts. The main drawback of the conventional differential detection is
the SNR gap compared to the optimum coherent detection. In this paper, we improve
the error rate performance of the conventional differential detection by increasing
the delay between the received and local signals. Let us note that this approach
is different from the differential space-time designs [6, 7] that maximize the
minimum determinant of the differential transmission matrix. As it will be seen
hereafter, our approach leads to a simplified trellis description and a
simplified optimization criteria.

a solution to increase the delay of the conventional differential detection and

in Section IV.

the formation of coalescing black-hole (BH) - neutron-star (NS) binaries, such

investigate the effects of natal kicks and the NS's radius on the synthesis of

increased merger detection rate of BH-NS systems ($\sim 2.3$ yr$^{-1}$), 5 to

compactness NSs increase the merger detection rate by $\sim 40\%$, due to more
efficient BH+NS mergers with low-mass NSs. We anticipate that detailed
core-collapse simulations incorporated into population synthesis models will
lead to an increased detection rate of electromagnetic counterparts of
BH-NS mergers.

binary evolution, the NS's spins, and the mechanical effects of the supernova
explosion.

supernova explosions in binary evolution studies.

models should be updated according to the latest constraints and simulations.

models with post-core-collapse NS and compact object evolution.

comparison labeling is expensive and time consuming, constituting a major

improve how effectively human time is used in these approaches by batching
comparisons together, rather than having the human label each comparison
individually. To do so, we leverage data dimensionality-reduction and
visualization techniques to provide the human with a interactive GUI displaying
the state space, in which the user can label subportions of the state space.
Across some simple Mujoco tasks, we show that this high-level approach holds
promise and can greatly increase the efficiency of human learning, while
simultaneously yielding better policy performance.
  Which specific comparison-learning approaches can be improved through batching
of comparisons? To answer this question, we provide an empirical framework
comparing several popular approaches, which reveal that while there is some
variability in performance, all of the methods we try can benefit substantially
from batching of comparisons, across several simple Mujoco tasks. These findings
then guide a hypothesis testing framework to determine which methods are
significantly better than others when given access to large datasets that allow
for batching of comparisons.
  Finally, we provide a set of baselines and data analyses to help understand the
ground across which we are trying to improve. That is, are the improvements we
see due to specific algorithmic differences, or are they a result of a more
general increase in data efficiency? To answer this question, we compare the
learning curves of our comparison-learning methods against a set of baselines,

what is observed is a gradual enhancement of dc conductivity as the voltage is

given voltage of dc drive is strongly dependent on an applied magnetic field.

fluctuations responsible for coherent current flow are smoothed by fluctuations
in the order parameter. This inconsistency leads us to conclude that the
coherent quantum phase slip mechanism is not at work in these samples.

these NbN nanowires is the nonequilibrium threshold switch.

from a host to a susceptible person is
governed by complex turbulent airflow, and physics related to breathing,
coughing and sneezing, mechanical and passive ventilation, thermal buoyancy
effects, surface deposition, masks, and air filtration. In this paper, we study
the infection risk via airborne transmission on an urban bus using unsteady
Reynolds-Averaged Navier--Stokes equations and a passive-scalar model of the
virus-laden aerosol concentration. Results from these simulations are directly
compared to the widely-used well mixed model, and show significant differences
in the concentration field and number of inhaled particles. Specifically, in
the limit of low mechanical ventilation rate, the well-mixed model will
over-predict concentration far from the infected passenger, and substantially
underpredict concentration near the infected passenger. The results reported
herein also apply to other enclosed spaces.
  From a numerical analysis perspective, one of the outcomes of this work is the
development of robust and efficient schemes for solving the unsteady RANS equations
in time-harmonic turbulent flows. The current production schemes for solving
time-dependent Navier--Stokes equations, such as implicit second- and fourth-order
schemes and explicit third- and fourth-order schemes, suffer from significant
turbulence-radiation artifacts and have a lower than desired rate of
acceleration. We present and verify a novel implicit second-order scheme that
conservatively solves the spatially-finite-volume discretization of the
time-dependent Navier--Stokes equations in a manner that is both robust and
efficient (it achieves a 100x speedup over the dense solver in a
code-used-by-the-industry). It has been used thousands of times in industrial
computations. A related but simpler scheme that is also robust and efficient for
unsteady RANS simulations is presented and verified. Both schemes have been
thoroughly tested on a large set of both experimental and numerical datasets.
They provide nearly exact agreement with the finest-scale direct numerical
simulations as well as experimental data in the literature. The schemes are
also tested on a realistic bus flow that agrees well with experimental data.
Finally, the schemes are tested on a pair of counter-rotating cylinders and a
separation bubble on a plate, which are both widely-studied flows that are
important for assessing scheme performance. Again, the schemes produce nearly
exact agreement with DNS.

Broadbent and Lord (TQC'20), is an
encryption scheme with the following attractive feature: given a ciphertext, an
adversary cannot create two ciphertexts both of which decrypt to the same
message as the original ciphertext. We revisit this notion and show the
following:
  - Reusability: The constructions proposed by Broadbent and Lord have the
disadvantage that they either guarantee one-time security (that is, the
encryption key can be used to generate only one encrypted message) in the
plain model or they guarantee secure instantiation of unclonable encryption
from trapdoor-permutations. We construct unclonable encryption schemes with
secure key-generation (that is, the user can generate as many encrypted
messages as he wants using the same key) in the random oracle model. This
construction is conceptually very simple and follows from a straightforward
reduction of the problem of constructing public coin (semi-honest) multiparty
computation protocols which was studied extensively in the work of Ben-Or,
Cohen and Gonen (STOC'04). We show how simple modifications to this construction
give us unclonable key exchange protocols, which too are of independent interest
and achieve, to the best of our knowledge, the first formal treatment of the
issue of deniability for key exchange games.
  - Combinatorial properties: The constructions of unclonable encryption schemes
proposed so far all rely on the use of combinatorial objects (constructing
suitable permutations or bipartite graphs) and a probabilistic argument to
ensure security (in either the random oracle model or the plain model). Our
constructions, on the other hand, give a purely combinatorial construction of
unclonable encryption which does not need any probabilistic argument. This is
because we use a technique of "brute force" hashing of messages (with
negligible probability of a collision) to ensure security. This approach is
conceptually very simple and, as mentioned above, follows a straightforward
reduction to constructing public coin multiparty computation protocols.
  - Lower bounds: Finally, we show a lower bound on the number of keys that can
be used for a one-time unclonable encryption scheme in the plain model. This
lower bound is simply a direct reduction of the problem of unclonable encryption
to that of a key exchange game (which is a very standard topic in crypto) and

(PET) imaging limits its
usage in the studies of radiation-sensitive populations, e.g., pregnant women,
children, and adults that require longitudinal imaging. Reducing the PET
radiotracer dose or acquisition time reduces photon counts, which can
deteriorate image quality. Recent deep-neural-network (DNN) based methods for
image-to-image translation enable the mapping of low-quality PET images
(acquired using substantially reduced dose), coupled with the associated
magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) images, to high-quality PET images. However,
such DNN methods focus on applications involving test data that match the
statistical characteristics of the training data very closely and give little
attention to evaluating the performance of these DNNs on new
out-of-distribution (OOD) acquisitions. We propose a novel DNN formulation that
models the (i) underlying sinogram-based physics of the PET imaging system and
(ii) the uncertainty in the DNN output through the per-voxel heteroscedasticity
of the residuals between the predicted and the high-quality reference images.
Our sinogram-based uncertainty-aware DNN framework, namely, suDNN, estimates a
standard-dose PET image using multimodal input in the form of (i) a
low-dose/low-count PET image and (ii) the corresponding multi-contrast MRI
images, leading to improved robustness of suDNN to OOD acquisitions. Extensive
experiments conducted on real data and several large publicly available
simulated datasets verify that suDNN yields substantially lower reconstruction
errors compared to state-of-the-art DNN methods.

generation, imitation learning has been viewed as a vital direction in the
context of robot skill learning. In contrast to unconstrained imitation
learning which ignores possible internal and external constraints arising from
environments and robot kinematics/dynamics, recent works on constrained
imitation learning allow for transferring human skills to unstructured
scenarios, further enlarging the application domain of imitation learning.
While various constraints have been studied, e.g., joint limits, obstacle
avoidance and plane constraints, the problem of nonlinear hard constraints
arising from robot kinematics/dynamics has not been well-addressed. In this
paper, we propose a framework, named Proximal Robust Optimization (PROFBO
solver), for solving a class of nonlinear optimization problems with hard
constraints. By introducing artificial points (instead of functions) and employing
the PROFBO solver, the forward and inverse kinematics of a Kuka iiwa robot are
first modeled as sets of distance-based constraints, and then the global
optimal action prediction is guaranteed during the imitation stage. Similarity,
we use regularization to model the arm's flexibility and avoide collision with
an observed, moving obstacle during the action prediction. We leverage a
partially observable motion planning framework to evaluate our proposed methods
on solving a real task, namely, picking up an object from the ground. Compared
to the baseline, our framework is shown to yield optimal performance despite
occurring collisions, improve prediction accuracy by up to 20% and reduce the
average time needed for a successful pick-up by about 15%.

  Let $n$ be the number of players and $\mathcal{X}$ be the set of possible
outcomes. A domain is a connected subset of $\mathcal{X}^n$ that contains the
equal outcome profile. A mechanism is efficient if it maps each outcome in the
domain to itself and is strategy-proof if it is a directed acyclic graph (DAC)
and no player can improve its outcome by truth-telling. We characterize the
efficient and strategy-proof domains with a version of the "angle restriction
property," which is a relaxation of the "sharp angle property" of Xie (2017).
Moreover, we show that a domain has a representation of the "represented
profile" if it is efficient and strategy-proof with the angle restriction
property.
  Finally, we introduce a new class of DACs, called the "right-angle DACs"
(RADCs), to study the social choice settings that are easily satisfied by the
RADCs. A domain is a RADC if it is efficient and strategy-proof with the
angle restriction property. We show that many domains are a RADC, and we
introduce a new characterization of the RADCs with the "local angle
restriction property."
  Our characterization of the efficient and strategy-proof domains provides a

process is an open and challenging question in biology. Recent studies classify
the topology and geometry of knotted proteins by analysing the distribution of
a protein's planar projections using topological objects called knotoids. We
approach the analysis of proteins with the same topology by introducing a
topologically inspired statistical metric between their knotoid distributions.
We detect geometric differences between trefoil proteins by characterising
their entanglement and we recover the distinction between their unsymmetric and
symmetric fold. We further detect a correlation between the distance in
configuration space of a protein and the change in its knotoid distance to its
fold. Interestingly, the change in knotoid distance is shown to be related to
the amount of energy needed to transform the unfolded state of the protein into
its folded one. Moreover, we introduce a statistical approach to distinguish the
growth in knotoid distance between unsymmetric and symmetric trefoil proteins.
We further detect a correlation between the knotoid distance and the number of
disulfide bonds in the protein. We observe that proteins with the same number
of disulfide bonds but different topology are geographically separated in
configuration space, suggesting the disulfide bonds play an important role in
the proteins geometry. Interestingly, the knotoid distance is shown to be
dependent also on the number of hydrogen bonds. We observe that proteins with
similar number of hydrogen bonds but different topology are separated in
configuration space, indicating that the hydrogen bonds play an important role
in the proteins topology. Together our results provide a support to the
hypothesis that proteins with the same topology but different geometry
unsymmetric and symmetric trefoil proteins for example share common unfolding
paths. It extends the paradigm that geometrical differences between proteins
with the same topology is mainly due to the variations in the number of
interacting residues. Besides that, it sheds light on the role of disulfide and
hydrogen bonds in the proteins geometry.
  From the methodology point of view, this work provides an example of how one
can encode structural information of proteins in a topological framework and
analyze it using tools from topology and statistics. It provides a link between
the works of [1, 2] and [3, 4] on the topology of proteins and graphs and
exactly follows their notation. It further provides a link between the works on
the statistical analysis of knotoids and the analysis of the geometrical
differences between proteins.

no consensus in the literature as to whether EDE can simultaneously solve the
Hubble tension and provide an adequate fit to the data from the cosmic
microwave background (CMB) and large-scale structure of the universe. In this
work, we deconstruct the current constraints from the Planck CMB and the
full-shape clustering data of the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey
(BOSS) to understand the origin of different conclusions in the literature. We
show that the current constraints are highly sensitive to the choice of
statistics and weighting schemes. However, when we use the $\chi^2$ statistics
and equal weight for all data points, as is commonly done in the literature,
the EDE model fails to fit the clustering data. When we use the more robust
correlation matrix to construct the $\chi^2$ statistics, the EDE model with a
wide range of fractions of the universe's duration in the EDE phase is
excluded. While when we use the account-based statistics, the EDE model is
marginally consistent with the data at ${\sim}2\sigma$ confidence level. We
also test different EDE parametrizations and models and find that the results
are highly model-dependent. Finally, we test the robustness of the constraints
and find that the EDE model fails to fit the clustering data at more than
$2\sigma$ confidence level when we increase the number of bins in the
analysis. We conclude that EDE or similar dark energy-like components in the
early universe is not able to simultaneously solve the Hubble tension and fit
the observational data adequately.
  As a reminder, the origin of the Hubble tension is yet to be fully
understood and different models including the Hubble parameter evolution have
been proposed. We, therefore, advocate a more general treatment of the Hubble
tension that does not require any specific model for the tension.

universe, especially when the first stars and structures are expected to form
around $13-12\,{\rm Gyrs}$, which is inconsistent with the EDE models where
the first stars are expected to form after $15\,{\rm Gyrs}$.

challenging capability for image editing tasks. Unlike traditional image
conditional generation that usually requires class labels for image synthesis

another by specifying the areas of interest. To achieve such capability, one may
need to condition the generators on extensive labeled data. However, annotating

ease of obtaining pixel-level hints (e.g., segmentation masks) for the images

inference network and further inject this information to the generator for
cross-space control. Extensive experiments show that our approach can effectively

smart phones and wristbands make it easy to get access to people's health
information including activities, sleep, sports, etc. Smart healthcare achieves
great success by training machine learning models on a large quantity of user
data. However, there are two critical challenges. Firstly, user data often
exists in the form of isolated islands, making it difficult to perform
aggregation without compromising privacy security. Secondly, the models trained
on the cloud fail on personalization. In this paper, we propose FedHealth, the
first federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare. FedHealth
splits traditional training into two stages: cross-user training and
cross-task training. It utilizes the transferred knowledge to adapt the
distributor (agent) to a new task with a little amount of local data, instead
of training from scratch. We evaluate FedHealth on 12 tasks of 54 subjects.
Comparised to direct learning, FedHealth achieves similar accuracy with 99% less
data. It also leads to much better personalized healthcare than federated
learning. For example, it identifies 12 incorrect activities that are
correctly classified by 90% in the direct learning. We believe FedHealth is
particularly useful for healthcare centers which have limited resources and
difficulty in collecting large volume of data.

serves two purposes. As mentioned above, it resolves the cosmological
coincidence problem. Also, our assumptions about the vacuum energy behavior
between different compactifications implies that de Sitter space is not
stable. This implies that any metastable dS vacuum will decay into lower
energy Minkowski or Robertson-Walker spacetimes, which in turn implies that
observable dark energy datasets can constrain theoretical parameters related
to spontaneous compactification.
  We also discuss the related issue of when the quintessence field becomes
accessible at a collider. We argue that it will likely occur before the
apocalyptic phase transition described above.
  Finally, we discuss our results in more detail from a phenomenological
perspective and outline some future work in greater detail.

Hadron Collider to advocate its potential relevance to establish reliable
constraints on the leptoquark parameter space and its ability to aid in correct
identification of these attractive sources of new physics. The main feature of
asymmetric pair production that genuinely distinguishes it from the usual
leptoquark pair production is given by the fact that the two leptoquarks that
are produced in proton-proton collisions through a $t$-channel lepton exchange
are not charge conjugates of each other. Hence the proposed name of asymmetric
leptoquark pair production for this type of process. We spell out prerequisite
conditions for the asymmetric leptoquark pair production mechanism to be
operational and enumerate all possible asymmetric leptoquark production
scenarios. We further substantiate genuine phenomenological potential of this
process by demonstrating that asymmetric leptoquark pair production can be
probed at the LHC also in scenarios where conventional asymmetric pair
production scenarios are not viable.
  From a theoretical perspective, asymmetric leptoquark pair production can
assist in correct identification of leptoquarks by putting separate stamps of
new physics on the final state leptoquark system. This can be of particular
importance when only single leptoquark is to be probed. It can also yield
valuable information on leptoquark mixing and how it is regulated in a given
model of new physics. From an experimental point of view, asymmetric leptoquark
pair production can be effectively probed by simply looking for events with
unequal leptoquark charges in the final state. This can be particularly
advantageous for low mass leptoquark scenarios. We have performed new
phenomenological studies for asymmetric leptoquark pair production mechanism
operating at the 13 TeV LHC in run II and run III eras for R-symmetric and
R-violating scenarios of the little hierarchy model (LHM). We have also
included new production mechanisms as well as new channels in separating the
unequal leptoquark charge events in the final states. We have also demonstrated
how di-leptoquark systems can be probed in unequally charged final states at the
LHC. Such studies have been performed for various plausible mass scenarios of
leptoquarks and universal constraints on the leptoquark parameter space from
all relevant experimental data.

particularly if they are located far away from the main data cloud. A common
method to detect outliers is based on principal component analysis (PCA) where
samples with small distances to the PCA-transformed origin are considered as
outliers. However, this method is data-set dependent and does not take into
account the underlying data distribution. For this reason, we propose a method
which constructs a latent representation of the data using robust PCA (RPCA)
and a auto-encoder (AE) and visualizes the results using a AE-generative
process called AE-manifold. Furthermore, we show that the latent representation
can be enhanced by applying adversarial auto-encoders (AAE) which captures
features on different levels of complexity. The resulting AAE-manifold could
serve as a latent representation of the data which is noise-reduced and can
detect outliers.
  We evaluate our approach on three (semi-)synthetic data sets and 12 real world
data sets. The results show that the approach detects outliers which are
completely separated from the rest of the data as well as in-the-wild outliers

This problem studies the model where the same sequence from some set is
transmitted over multiple channels, and the decoder receives the different
outputs. Assume that the transmitted sequence is at distance $d$ from some code
and there are at most $r$ errors in every channel. Then the sequence
reconstruction problem studies the codes for which the sequence can be
reconstructed reliably for all $d\geq r$.
  In our work, we study the sequence reconstruction problem for discrete
convolutional codes. We show a bound on the rate of convolutional codes that
allows reliable reconstruction for all sequences at distance $d$, provided
that $d$ is sufficiently large compared to $r$. We also show a construction
of convolutional codes that achieves this bound. Finally, we show a decoding
algorithm for convolutional codes that can be used for solving the sequence
reconstruction problem.
  Applications of our results are two channel models. The first one was
proposed by C. Zhang et al. for enabling blind communication in blind spots.
The second one is for the multi-user communication problem of C. Bodmer et al.
When solving this problem, the users are required to transmit common words at
specific time steps. Our construction and bound show that discrete
convolutional codes can be used to solve this problem for a large class of
words.
  In summary, our work establishes a connection between the sequence
reconstruction problem and discrete convolutional codes. This connection is
fundamental for solving the sequence reconstruction problem, and it also gives
useful tools for the channel model studied by C. Zhang et al. and the multi
user communication problem of C. Bodmer et al.

complex reasoning about claims made in multiple parts of a paper. In contrast,
existing information-seeking question answering datasets usually contain

a dataset of 5,049 questions over 1,585 Natural Language Processing papers.
Each question is written by an NLP practitioner who read only the title and

information-seeking QA, which our dataset is designed to facilitate.

notion of hierarchy among the objects tagged with the same primer pair and
enables efficient data updates. In contrast to prior work, in our architecture
a pair of PCR primers of length 20 does not define a single object, but an
independent storage partition, which is internally managed independently without
coordination with other partitions. This allows for transparent and efficient
data updates without the need for complex coordination among multiple partitions.
Specifically, the management of each partition is independent and does not
interfere with other partitions. We demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed
architecture by designing a simple protocol that provides the above guarantees
and has a write latency of just 15 minutes and a read latency of just 5 minutes.
We also show that our protocol is highly update-efficient. For example, to
update a 1 GB object, the new version of the object does not need to be written
to the DNA until an explicit update is explicitly initiated by the user. In
the meantime, the old version of the object can continue to be used by readers
without knowing that it is stale. Meanwhile, the new version of the object is
mirrored to a reliable disk storage by just a few kilobytes of additional
operations. The update process is fully transparent and does not affect the
readers' experience. Finally, our protocol is resilient to the failure of up to
$\sqrt{n}$ (~75%) of the 1000 nodes in the system and can recover to full
capacity within minutes.
  We have implemented a prototype of our architecture and achieved ~5 Gbps read
and ~1 Gbps write bandwidth to the DNA. Our evaluation demonstrates that our
protocol can provide data integrity in the presence of noise and error-prone
communication links.
  In summary, our proposed architecture is the first to provide transparent and
efficient data updates to a DNA storage system via PCR primers of length 20. It
defines a novel and flexible architecture that provides a strong sense of
hierarchy among objects and can achieve substantial update throughput.
Furthermore, it can provide high data integrity in the presence of noise and
error-prone communication links, reliable disk storage, and faulty nodes.
Finally, it can be combined with any DNA storage system to add the sense of

modern condensed matter theory. The unique and exotic properties of topological
states of matter allow for unidirectional gapless electron transport and
extremely accurate measurements of the Hall conductivity. Recently, new
topological effects occurring at Dirac/Weyl points have been better understood
and demonstrated using artificial materials such as photonic and phononic
crystals, metamaterials and electrical circuits. In comparison, the topological
properties of nodal lines, which are one-dimensional degeneracies in momentum
space, remain less explored. Here, we explain the theoretical concept of
topological nodal lines and review recent and ongoing progress using artificial
materials. The review includes recent demonstrations of non-Abelian topological
charges of nodal lines in momentum space and examples of nodal lines realized
in photonic and other systems. Finally, we will address the challenges involved
in both experimental demonstration and theoretical understanding of topological
nodal lines.
  In this review, we explain the theoretical concept of topological nodal
lines. We introduce topological nodal lines using a pedagogical example of a
two-dimensional kagome lattice connected to a three-dimensional honeycomb
lattice. We explain how topological nodal lines may be described using
connectivity rules and degeneracy arguments as well as using linearized
bandoretical techniques. We review recent demonstrations of nodal lines in
photonic and other systems. Finally, we address the challenges involved in both
experimental demonstration and theoretical understanding of topological nodal
lines.
  Topological phases of matter provide a promising platform to realize
exotic and enhanced electromagnetic (EM) responses. In particular, the
topological nature of EM response has been well understood and demonstrated for
Dirac/Weyl points. Recent models featuring topological nodal lines also show
interesting EM responses, but a clear understanding of the topological nature
of the EM response in the nodal line case is still missing. Here, we investigate
the topological EM response for generic nodal lines using the genetic
connectivity rule for topological nodal lines. We explain the nontrivial EM
response and its topological nature for several connectivity states realizing
topological nodal lines. We provide a clear understanding of the topological
nature of EM response in the case of nodal lines, which is also applicable to
recent models featuring nodal lines.

and self-downgrade have
recently seen increased popularity due to their simplicity, potential
performance efficiency, and low energy consumption. However, such protocols
result in memory instruction reordering, thus causing extra program behaviors
that are often not intended by the programmers. We propose a novel formal model
that captures the semantics of programs running under such protocols, and
features a set of fences that interact with the coherence layer. Using the
model, we design an algorithm to analyze the reachability and check whether a
program satisfies a given safety property with the current set of fences. We
describe a method for insertion of optimal sets of fences that ensure
correctness of the program under such protocols. The method relies on a
counter-example guided fence insertion procedure. One feature of our method is
that it can handle a variety of fences (with different costs). This diversity
makes optimization more difficult since one has to optimize the total cost of
the inserted fences, rather than just their number. To demonstrate the strength
of our approach, we have implemented a prototype and run it on a wide range of
examples and benchmarks. We have also, using simulation, evaluated the
performance of the resulting fenced programs.

3k-4 theorem states that if A and B are subsets
of the integers of size k with small sumset (of size close to 2k) then they are
very close to arithmetic progressions. Our aim in this paper is to strengthen
this by allowing only a bounded number of possible summands from one of the
sets. We show that if A and B are subsets of the integers of size k such that
for any four-element subset X of B the sumset A+X has size not much more than
2k then already this implies that A and B are very close to arithmetic
progressions.
  Another feature of our result is that we work with additive sets contained
not just integers but also (more generally) within the group Z/nZ. Our result
here is that if A and B are non-empty subsets of this group of size k with
small sumset (of size close to n-k) then they are very close to arithmetic
progressions.
  Both of these results find natural applications in Ramsey theory. To state
the simplest application: if you are given a system of n intervals of size 2
with the property that every four of them have a relatively long common
section then you are likely to find an arithmetic progression of length 3 (or,
equivalently, a triple of disjoint intervals with a long common section). This
was asked by Erdos in the 1980s and our results strengthen the conditions
assumed in the classical argument of Erdos, Szekeres and Turan which proves
this theorem. We show that these conditions can be weakened: it is enough to
assume that every four of the intervals have a relatively long common section
on one of the B-sets (instead of all of them being like that). Similar
weakening of conditions can be applied to other results in Ramsey theory.
  Finally, our results find applications to the study of Sidon sets (and, more
generally, of abstract sumsets). Our theorems suggest the following conjecture
about Sidon sets: a bounded subset of integers which "contains few summands" is
a Sidon set? We show that this conjecture, if true, implies a number of deep
results in harmonic analysis.
  The paper is concluded with a number of open problems.

induce chaos in the non-chaotic regions of the classical H\'enon-Heiles model.

semiclassical model based on Dirac's time-dependent variational principle. With

the influence of the easy negative proposals, SABRA proposes dual-path network
design for prediction. The single-shot path makes the model directly output the
relationship classification mask and avoids the loss of information in the

In this work, we present our results on the ARID dataset. Most previous works
only evaluate performance on large, well illuminated datasets like Kinetics and
HMDB51. We demonstrate that our work is able to achieve a very low error rate
while being trained on a much smaller dataset of dark videos. We also demonstrate
that our work is able to generalize to other types of corruption by achieving a
low error rate on the Cross Modal Substitution (CMS) dataset which contains
videos with noise and motion blur.
  We also propose a variant of the contrastive loss called the contrastive
silent loss. The loss is obtained by zeroing out the positive samples in the
embedded space. It leads to a nice regularization effect even when there is a
large number of frames to be used in computing the loss. It also leads to a
nice boost in validation accuracy.
  We also demonstrate that by simply increasing the temperature in the softmax
contrastive loss, we are able to achieve a nice boost in validation accuracy.
This is obtained at the cost of training convergence. The boost in validation
accuracy is however worth the loss in training convergence as it leads to a
lower error rate on test videos.
  We also observe that by simply resampling the frames to be used in computing
the loss, we are able to achieve a nice regularization effect and also a nice
boost in validation accuracy. The best results are obtained by simply sampling
one frame in every $\lambda$ frames.

the implementation of a Content
Addressable Parallel Processor using a FPGA. While Content addressable memories
have been implemented in FPGAs, to our knowledge this is the first
implementation in FPGA of Caxton C. Foster's vision of parallel processing,
particularly the notions of parallel write as well as the combining of output
values, which are usually missing in more typical CAM implementations, such as
the ones designed for network routing. The resulting CAPP is made accessible to
a host computer over a USB/UART interface, using a straightforward serial
protocol that is demonstrated using a Python-based driver.
  The CAPP comprises 16,384 words, with 48 bits per word, using 2,048 out of
6,144 available logic elements in the Xilinx Spartan-6 SX45TQ144C-2 model. At
a operational clock speed of approximately 100MHz, the CAPP can search for and
retrieve a word in just 12.6$\mu$s, and can perform 1,300,000 searches per
second, or be configured to provide 16 search results per clock cycle. In addition, the search can be configured to provide a graded degree of match, from 0 to 48, in addition to the simple boolean match that is typical of more conventional CAMs.
  The design is fully complementary CMOS, using the M4K look-up table macro,
along with several other Xilinx licensed cores, such as the Dual-Port RAM
primitive, which helps to make search results available to the USB/UART
interface while the search is being performed. The use of these established
cores, helped to simplify the design, which was put together largely from
pre-existing verilog modules. These cores also helped to provide a full set of
debugging opportunities, which was very useful during the development process.
Finally, the design is provided in a fully verilog-based structure, which should
make it relatively easy to customize or integrate with other designs.
  Overall, this is a fast, parallel, and highly capable content addressable
parallel processor, implemented entirely in FPGA logic, with no reliance on
host computer processing for search "hits".
  Keywords: Content addressable parallel processor, FPGA, verilog, C++

star-forming massive ($>10^{11}\,\rm M_{\odot}$) galaxies within the core of
the RO-1001 galaxy group at $\rm z=2.91$. Each of them displays kpc-scale
compact star-bursting cores with properties consistent with forming galaxy
bulges, embedded at the center of extended, massive stellar disks.
Surprisingly, the stellar disks are unambiguously both quiescent, and severely
lopsided in star-forming gas. This strong asymmetry suggests on-going major
major mergers, likely with a companion galaxy that is not directly visible due
to its small contribution to the total group mass. The discrete nature of the
gas asymmetry and its variation between the three galaxies suggest oscillatory
orbits, consistent with merger dynamics at higher resolution. We model their
evolution with the IllustrisTNG simulations, which also suggest three-tuples
that result in such massive central galaxies. The models further predict the
observed extended disks and the visible companion galaxies. In two of the
evolutionary scenarios the temporary collisional stabilization of the
triangulation of the three galaxies in the group is crucial to reach the
finally observed configuration. The observations and models provide strong
evidence for the role of mergers in the formation of highly star-forming, but
already quiescent massive galaxies at high-redshift.
  Finally, the large mass in extended disks in these three group galaxies and
their relation to the global distribution of the group mass suggest large
scale dark matter structure at the cluster/mass-group boundary.
  We discuss additional millimeter observations to further understand the
physical properties of the massive extended disks and the role of mergers in
their formation.

Universal Texture Zero
(UTZ) model of flavour originally presented in arXiv:1710.01741, and update
them in light of both improved experimental constraints and numerical analysis
techniques. In particular, we have developed an in-house Markov Chain Monte
Carlo (MCMC) algorithm to exhaustively explore the UTZ's viable parameter
space. We also extract predictions for a wide range of flavour and CP-violating
observables, many of which were not previously discussed in the literature. We
have seen that the UTZ remains a minimally extended Standard Model with just
three new (complex) parameters: therefore its predictions for the rest of the
particle spectrum are indistinguishable from those of the SM, to the accuracy of
the relevant experiments. The UTZ's flavour phenomenology is determined by a
single, monically increasing sequence of eigenvalues, which we discuss in some
detail. The UTZ's viability as a theory of flavour is demonstrated by the
agreement of its predictive sequence with experimental data, without the need
for any fine-tuning. We have also defined a natural extension of the UTZ, which
we call the "Extended Universal Texture Zero" (EUTZ), by introducing a fourth
new (complex) parameter. The EUTZ's viable parameter space can be visualised as
a "landscape" of possible textures, which provides an interesting context for
further phenomenological study.
  Based on the analysis presented here, we define a counting of relevant
observables which may help to critically evaluate the viability of future flavour
models. We also propose a set of simple consistency checks on the parameters and
predictions of any flavour model, which can be easily applied a posteriori.
Finally, we have developed a new approach to evaluating the viability of a flavour
model, which we call the "credibility integral", which may be useful to other
theoreticians.
  Finally, let us remark that the analysis presented here is purely
phenomenological, and does not address the issue of whether the UTZ, or any
similar theory of flavour, could be "fundamental". That question must be faced
by considering the behaviour of the theory at very small distances (i.e. at the
Planck scale), which is beyond the scope of our work.
  We have not included a comprehensive survey of existing flavour models in this
article. Such a survey can be found in the recent review paper in

detecting anomalous data
samples in streams of data. This problem poses challenges that classical and
deep anomaly detection methods are not designed to cope with, such as
conceptual drift and continuous learning. State-of-the-art flow anomaly
detection methods rely on fixed memory using hash functions or nearest
neighbors that may not be able to constrain high-frequency values as in a
moving average or remove seamless outliers and cannot be trained in an
end-to-end deep learning architecture. We present a new incremental anomaly
detection method that performs continuous density estimation based on random
Fourier features and the mechanism of quantum measurements and density matrices
that can be viewed as an exponential moving average density. It can process
potentially endless data and its update complexity is constant $O(1)$. A
systematic evaluation against 12 state-of-the-art streaming anomaly detection
algorithms using 12 streaming datasets is presented.

state-of-the-art.

court compel the respondent to enter that password into the device? In this
work, we propose a new approach to the foregone conclusion doctrine from Fisher
v US that governs the answer to this question. The Holy Grail of this line of
work would be a framework for reasoning about whether the testimony implicit in
any action is already a foregone conclusion. In this paper we attempt
something narrower. We introduce a framework for specifying actions for which
the implicit testimony is, a priori, not a foregone conclusion. Our approach
is centered around the notion of an action's \emph{degree of determinism}. We
argue that a highly deterministic action is one whose outcome is all but
guaranteed to happen regardless of the actor's input. Such an action would
typically not require the actor to perform the action in the way suggested by
the usual understanding of compulsion. On the other end of the spectrum, an
action whose outcome is highly uncertain and whose output is likely to be a
function of the actor's input would be considered largely non-deterministic,
and thus likely to constitute testimony beyond a foregone conclusion. Of central
interest, then, would be actions which balance these two extremes. We propose
a formal framework for reasoning about the degree of determinism of an action,
with the goal of identifying the actions whose testimony is not a foregone
conclusion.
  In particular, our work centers around the following question: under what
conditions is it reasonable to update on the actions of a respondent when that
respondent is compelled to perform that action in a way strongly suggested by
their pre-existing knowledge and intentions? To answer this question, we
introduce a framework for analyzing the degree to which an action is required
of a respondent. We argue that if a respondent's action is entirely required
of them -- i.e., there is little to no cost to her of submitting to the
compulsion -- then it is reasonable to update as if she had indeed chosen to
submit her evidence to the device. On the other hand, if the situation is one
in which her action is not at all required of her -- i.e., there is significant
cost to her of submitting to the compulsion -- then it is not reasonable to
update on her action.
  We apply this framework to several examples, including the cryptography
example of Fisher v US, phone password examples, safe examples, and others.

resulted in an extensive surge of interest in Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) due
to their unprecedented performance and high accuracy for different and
challenging problems of significant engineering importance. However, when such
deep learning architectures are utilized for making critical decisions such as
the ones that involve human lives (e.g., in control systems and medical
applications), it is of paramount importance to understand, trust, and in one
word "explain" the argument behind deep models' decisions. In many
applications, artificial neural networks (including DNNs) are considered as
black-box systems, which do not provide sufficient clue on their internal
processing actions. Although some recent efforts have been initiated for
providing explanation facilities for decisions made by DNNs, the area of
understanding and explaining DNNs remains largely young and in need of further
research. The first difficulty in creating explanation techniques for DNNs is
the fact that these models are complex and large in size (i.e., they are
data-driven computational systems with hundreds of thousands of learnable
parameters and nonlinear processing stages). Another challenge is that these
systems are often trained to classify different categories of examples (for
example, images of cats and dogs) and, as a result, the activation functions
output, by nature, abstract and problem-specific representations (e.g.,
visual features for image classification problems). This further complicates the
development of explanation techniques for DNNs, as it makes the ideas and
concepts that led to a particular decision abstract and difficult to understand
and model. To address these issues, we propose a novel framework for understanding
and explaining DNNs, with special emphasis on computer image recognition tasks
(using datasets such as MNIST, CIFAR-10, and STL-10). The main idea is to
learn an "explanation" (in the form of a classifier) that can generalize
different DNN models that are trained to recognize the same class of images
(e.g., cars). The "explanation" is obtained through a supervised learning
process, where the following two sources of information are used: (1) the
recorded training data (including labels and input images), and (2) the
feature maps generated by one of the DNNs on the training data. With this
information, we can learn a classifier that can identify the most important
visual features, selected by a DNN, that lead to its decisions. The

based models show good performance when trained on large amounts of labeled
data on events of interest, whereas the performance of models tends to degrade
on other events not seen during training. Therefore, a significant amount of
labeled data is required on various types of misinformation including hoaxes,
satire, and historical facts for effective detection of fake news. However, it
is a challenging and time-consuming task to annotate such data due to the need
for domain expertise. Additionally, annotating satire data requires the knowledge
of literary devices used in satire to distinguish satire from hoax and fake
news. Furthermore, collecting historical factual corruption information and
annotating them requires the knowledge of historical events to distinguish them
from the other types of misinformation. In this paper, we propose a multi-task
deep learning model that can be trained on partially labeled data, thereby
addressing the above issues. Specifically, we train a model to distinguish between
three types of misinformation (hoax, satire, and factual corruption) with three
binary labels per sample. This allows us to use existing hoax detection models
as sub-models in our framework. Furthermore, the three-label setting provides
additional information to distinguish between different types of misinformation.
We demonstrate that our model outperforms strong baseline models that use
existing hoax detection models.
  We also conduct an interesting experiment to show how the performance of our
model can be improved by providing additional information to human annotators
to reduce the need for domain expertise, resulting in 80% reduction in the
average time to annotate a sample.

a social media text dataset. The results confirm the effectiveness of our
approach, especially when compared to state-of-the-art hoax detection models

useful relational inductive bias for modeling such systems, generalization to
new system instances of the same type is less studied. In this work we trained
graph neural networks to fit time series from an example nonlinear dynamical
system, the belief propagation algorithm. We found that the networks learned
an approximation of the inverse function from hidden state to parameters, and
predicted reasonable behavior for novel observations and graphs.
Importantly, the networks did not learn an approximation to the differential

generalize better by adding inductive bias via a parametrized measurement process.

generalize to new instances of a nonlinear dynamical system.

a way of computing the Kullback-Liebler divergence between probability distributions
under the belief propagation update rule, then they would be able to learn to
predict the inverse function from the cross entropy loss. We show our experiments
demonstrating that the networks do indeed learn to predict the inverse function,
but with some qualitative differences.

) is a novel minimally invasive
treatment that is used to ablate intracranial structures to treat mesial
temporal lobe epilepsy (MTLE). Region of interest (ROI) segmentation before and
after LITT would enable automated lesion quantification to objectively assess
treatment efficacy. Deep learning techniques, such as convolutional neural
networks (CNNs) are state-of-the-art solutions for ROI segmentation, but
require large amounts of annotated data during the training. However,
collecting large datasets from emerging treatments such as LITT is impractical.
In this paper, we propose a progressive brain lesion synthesis framework
(PAVAE) to expand both the quantity and diversity of the training dataset.
Concretely, our framework consists of two sequential networks: a mask synthesis
network and a mask-guided lesion synthesis network. To better employ extrinsic
information to provide additional supervision during network training, we
design a condition embedding block (CEB) and a mask embedding block (MEB) to
encode inherent conditions of masks to the feature space. Finally, a
segmentation network is trained using raw and synthetic lesion masks to
evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed framework. Experimental results show
that our method can achieve realistic synthetic results and boost the
performance of down-stream segmentation tasks above traditional data
augmentation techniques.

of the astrobots coordination in SDSS-V by conducting various experimental and
simulated tests. We illustrate that our strategy provides a complete
coordination condition which depends on the operational characteristics of
astrobots, their configurations, and their targets. Namely, a coordination
method based on the notion of cooperative artificial potential fields is used
to generate safe and complete trajectories for astrobots. Optimal target
assignment further improves the performance of the used algorithm in terms of
faster convergences and less oscillatory movements. Both random targets and
galaxy catalog targets are employed to observe the coordination success of the
algorithm in various target distributions. The proposed method is capable of
handling all potential collisions in the course of coordination. Once the
completeness condition is fulfilled according to initial configuration of
astrobots and their targets, the algorithm reaches full convergence of
astrobots. Should one assign targets to astrobots using efficient strategies,
convergence time as well as the number of oscillations decrease in the course
of coordination. Rare incomplete scenarios are simply resolved by trivial
modifications of astrobots swarms' parameters.
  From astronomical point of view, we observe that galaxy targets with larger
redshift could have precedence over closer ones in the case of target
conflict. This historical priority of redshift introduces ordered distributions
in the plane of redshift-right ascension for observed galaxies. We call this
new order rule as redshift priority ordering (RPO). We illustrate that RPO not
only reduces spatial over-lap of observed galaxies but also provides a
convenient tool for recovery of galaxies in the plane of galactic center
right ascension versus galactic population distribution.
  In conclusion, the proposed algorithm is capable of coordinating the
astrobots in a cooperative manner for the benefit of complete observations of
targets. The algorithm is safe, efficient, and capable of handling full
astrobots collisions. Designation of targets to astrobots based on efficient
strategies further reduces the time of convergence as well as the number of
oscillations.

language based on graph transformation rules
which aims to facilitate program analysis and verification. Writing efficient
programs in such a language is challenging because graph matching is expensive.
GP 2 addresses this problem by providing rooted rules which, under mild
conditions, can be matched in constant time. Recently, we implemented a number
of changes to Bak's GP 2-to-C compiler in order to speed up graph programs. One
key improvement is a new data structure for dynamic arrays called BigArray.
This is an array of pointers to arrays of entries, successively doubling in
size. To demonstrate the speed-up achievable with the new implementation, we
present a reduction program for recognising binary DAGs which previously ran in
quadratic time but now runs in linear time when compiled with the new compiler.
We also present a program for computing the average number of white vertices in
a DAG, which compiles efficiently even though it uses a large number of
non-rooted rules.
  We discuss the choices made in optimising each aspect of the execution
environment, from the low-level design of data types to the translation of the
high-level graph transformation rules. The key to efficiency is a careful
balance between costly -- but necessarily complex -- components, such as the
dynamic array and the pattern matching algorithm, and simpler, hand-rolled,
versions of which programmers can make sparing use in order to achieve high
performance.
  Finally, we present a simple but efficient algorithm for detecting
deadlocks in DAGs, which has been traditionally implemented using a recursive
approach that is impractical for very large graphs. The implementation uses a
combination of fast rule application and a technique for efficiently generating
a topological ordering.

performance; 2) is more effective than using WikiLinks as input to the T5s;

comprehensive articles. Finally, we observe that the models pre-trained on
WikidataKG exhibit a notable reduction in the gender bias, compared to the T5
baselines.

preservation, are established by analyzing the change of geometric energy in

physical meaning of geometric energy to quantify the relationship between the

as global and local energies, are further introduced. They provide a direct

ophysical computational model of brain
regions relevant to Parkinson's Disease based on local field potential data
collected from the brain of marmoset monkeys. Parkinson's disease is a
neurodegenerative disorder, linked to the death of dopaminergic neurons at the
substantia nigra pars compacta, which affects the normal dynamics of the basal
ganglia-thalamus-cortex neuronal circuit of the brain. Although there are
multiple mechanisms underlying the disease, a complete description of those
mechanisms and molecular pathogenesis are still missing, and there is still no
cure. To address this gap, computational models that resemble neurobiological
aspects found in animal models have been proposed. In our model, we performed a
data-driven approach in which a set of biologically constrained parameters is
optimised using differential evolution. Evolved models successfully resembled
single-neuron mean firing rates and spectral signatures of local field
potentials from healthy and parkinsonian marmoset brain data. As far as we are
concerned, this is the first computational model of Parkinson's Disease based
on simultaneous electrophysiological recordings from seven brain regions of
Marmoset monkeys. Results show that the proposed model could facilitate the
investigation of the mechanisms of PD and support the development of techniques
that can indicate new therapies. It could also be applied to other
computational neuroscience works to study the dynamics of brain regions of
interest.
  We develop a biologically constrained model with adaptive time-step neurons
inspired by the Hodgkin-Huxley formalism, single-electrode current source
density, and the phase plane analysis. We show that the proposed model can
reproduce some features of the parkinsonian brain found in local field potencial
measurements, such as the changes in the spectral power of different frequency
bands (delta, alpha, beta, theta, and sigma) and the pathological oscillations
known as the "parkinsonian burst." Moreover, we show that the proposed model
can reproduce the dopamine replacement therapy effects on the parkinsonian brain
and the effects of deep brain stimulation on the subthalamic nucleus on
neural dynamics. Results indicate that the proposed model can be used to study
the mechanisms of PD and evaluate the effectiveness of different treatments on
the parkinsonian brain.
