(U/LIRGs) at $z <$ 0.04 through IFU observations with KOOLS-IFU on Seimei
Telescope. The observed targets are drawn from the Great Observatories All-sky
LIRG Survey (GOALS), covering a wide range of merger stages. We successfully
detect emission lines such as H$\beta$, [OIII]$\lambda$5007, H$\alpha$,
[NII]$\lambda\lambda$6549,6583, and [SII]$\lambda\lambda$6717,6731 with a
spectral resolution of $R$ = 15000-30000. Thanks to the high spectral
resolution, we can (1) clearly separate the emission line spectra of the
inner ($\sim$2$''$--6$''$ diameter) and outer galactic regions, (2) trace the
gas motion in the circumnuclear region (within $\sim$1$''$ radius), and (3)
quantitatively analyze the gas properties in different regions (within
$\sim$6$''$ radius). We find that the separation of the emission line spectra
is more prominent in major mergers. The [OIII] line is shifted to the blue and
red sides in the outer and inner regions, respectively. We assume a single or
double gas outflow assuming a symmetric shape and estimate the total mass
flux of the outflow. The mass flux of the outflow is stronger in the double
outflow model. We analyze the relations between the line fluxes, line widths,
and radio continuum brightness, and discuss the effects of the strong starburst
and active galactic nucleus (AGN) on the ionized gas. Finally, we compare the
observed gas properties with a high-resolution hydrodynamic simulation of one
of the major mergers in our sample, and introduce a new quantity to evaluate
the effectiveness of the simulation in reproducing the observed gas properties.
The observed gas properties and simulation results will be useful for further
modeling of dust formation and chemical evolution in U/LIRGs.

operator is constructed based on the piecewise linear interpolation by |x|. In
this paper, we first introduce a new transcendental RBF based on the hyperbolic
tangent function as a smooth approximant to f(r)=r with higher accuracy and
better convergence properties than the multiquadric. Then Wu-Schaback's
quasi-interpolation formula is rewritten using the proposed RBF. It preserves
convexity and monotonicity. We prove that the proposed scheme converges with a
rate of O(h^2). So it has a higher degree of smoothness. Some numerical

function as a smooth approximant to f(r)=r with higher accuracy and better
convergence properties than the multiquadric. We prove that the proposed RBF
is used to construct a compactly supported RBF. This RBF has uniformly
continuous derivatives up to infinity. We develop a direct local method for
solving the system of linear equations resulting from the application of the
iterative method in [G. Xu and Z. Wang, Comput. Math. Applic., 78 (2019),
123-141]. The proposed method is chosen from a class of RBFITA (RBF-Iterative
Tikhonov method for solvers of linear systems). The proposed scheme is a
monolithic method for which the iteration process is not needed. The method is
implemented for solving systems of symmetric and nonsymmetric linear systems.
Some experimental results are given to demonstrate the efficiency and accuracy

particularly, for solving Navier-Stokes equations, it indicates that the method
gives the non-uniqueness solution when the given data are not sufficient.

an approach to improving
the representation of convection in weather and climate models. This is an
attractive framework as it is fundamentally dynamical, removing some of the
assumptions of mass-flux convection schemes which are invalid at current model
resolutions. However, it is still not understood how best to close the
multi-fluid equations for atmospheric convection. In this paper we develop a
simple two-fluid, single-column model with one rising and one falling fluid. No
further modelling of sub-filter variability is included. We then apply this
model to Rayleigh-B\'{e}nard convection, showing that, with minimal closures,
the correct scaling of the heat flux (Nu) is predicted over six orders of
magnitude of buoyancy forcing (Ra). This suggests that even a very simple
two-fluid model can accurately capture the dominant coherent overturning
structures of convection.
  In the limit of large thermal expansion coefficient (Ga >~ 1000), a form of
buoyancy-locked sinking fluid is recovered, with a very narrow temperature
range, approximately equal to the difference between the temperatures of the
top and bottom boundaries. The rising fluid has a wider temperature range which
spans most of the gap between the two boundary temperatures. The narrow range of
the sinking fluid ensures a nearly constant downward velocity over a large
fraction of the domain. The counterbalancing pressure gradient force on the
mid-layer is approximately linear with height for both fluids in this limit. These
features are different from those observed in Rayleigh-B\'{e}nard convection with
strong surface tension boundaries (e.g. those of a liquid-gas interface) where
the difference between the temperatures of the two surfaces is usually much
smaller. The mass flux through the interface between the two fluids is controlled
by a balance between the pressure gradient force and the buoyancy force. The
latter is approximately linear with distance from the mid-plane for both fluids in
the vertical direction. The horizontal balance of forces is different for each
fluid. The balance on the faster moving lighter fluid is primarily between the
frictional drag and the horizontal deformation force. The slower moving denser
fluid is balanced by the deformation and the buoyancy forces. The horizontal
stretching and tilting of the ascending plume causes the rising fluid to heat up
more than the falling fluid. This coupling of horizontal and vertical heat

atoms may become genuinely entangled. We find that this task is impossible if
the cavity interacting with uncorrelated atom share classical correlations with
any other cavity. We observe that atomic state can become genuine multipartite
entangled, at least if the cavity with uncorrelated atom, is highly entangled
with any other cavity. This is an interesting and non-trivial observation and
may serve as another technique to generate multipartite entangled atoms via
JC-interactions. The findings can be realized with available experimental
setups.
  From theoretical perspective, the results present an interesting extension
of our previous work which demonstrated conditions of entanglement of two atoms
interacting via JC-interaction. This work can be viewed as extension of that
work to three atoms. The problem is complex and solved using matrix positivity
conditions and also negative eigenvalue evaluation of the reduced state
density matrix of the atoms. The methods are more involved and not as simple
as the binomial observation in the two atoms case.

correlation criteria for three atoms. In \ref b*, we discuss the conditions
which make the uncorrelated atom to become part of a genuine multipartite
entangled atom. In \ref c*, we present the atomic state formation due to cavity
entanglement with other cavities. In \ref d*, we present a specific scenario
which presents a particular pattern of entanglement. In \ref e*, we present a
specific case where an atom can become tripartite entangled with two other
atoms. In \ref f*, we present a specific scenario of three cavities where one

CMS) detector is one of two general-purpose

innermost component of the CMS tracking system. The detector which was in
operation between 2009 and 2016 has now been replaced with an upgraded one in
the beginning of 2017. During the previous shutdown period of the LHC, a
prototype readout system and a third disk was inserted into the old forward
pixel detector with eight prototype blades constructed using the new digital
read-out chips. Testing the performance of these pilot modules enabled us to
gain operational experience with the upgraded detector. In this paper, the
reconstruction and analysis of the data taken with the new modules are
presented including information on the calibration of the reconstruction
software. The hit finding efficiency and track-hit residual distributions are
also shown.

are in good agreement with simulation and with the operational experience we
gained. We also see that the physics performance of the new modules is capable
of providing good quality data.

reconstruction efficiency and hit residuals between the new modules and the
previous detector modules are shown. A small difference in the hit efficiency

Twitter provides organizations and
individuals an effective way to monitor public emotions towards them and their
competitors. As a result, sentiment analysis has become an important and
challenging task. In this work, we have collected seven publicly available and
manually annotated twitter sentiment datasets. We create a new training and
testing dataset from the collected datasets. We develop an LSTM model to
classify sentiment of a tweet and evaluate the model with the new dataset.
Experimental results show that our model achieves an accurate result of sentiment
classification.
  We also investigate the issue of limited training data in deep learning.
Inspired by recent works on very low label learning and semi-supervised learning,
we propose a new framework to learn a rich model from a small set of annotated
and a large set of unlabeled data. Experimental results on sentiment analysis
demonstrate our framework achieves better results than traditional supervised
and semi-supervised learning methods.
  Finally, we study the issue of domain shift in sentiment analysis. We collect
a new dataset that shares the same set of words but has different emotions
between the training and testing data. We propose a multi-task model to learn
both the language and domain. Experimental results show that our model achieves
better results than the baseline model.
  In summary, this work investigates sentiment analysis, limited training data,
and domain shift. We propose several frameworks and achieve better results than
state-of-the-art methods.
  This paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces the background and
related works. Section III explains the details of our frameworks for sentiment
analysis, limited training data, and domain shift. Section IV evaluates our
frameworks and state-of-the-art methods. Section V concludes this work and
proposes the future directions.

However, building a chat system is not scalable since it often requires a
considerable volume of human-human dialogue data, especially when enforcing
features such as persona, style, or safety. In this work, we study the
challenge of imposing roles on open-domain dialogue systems, with the goal of
making the systems maintain consistent roles while conversing naturally with
humans. To accomplish this, the system must satisfy a role specification that
includes certain conditions on the stated features as well as a system policy
on whether or not certain types of utterances are allowed. For this, we propose
an efficient data collection framework of gathering thousands of sentences
within only a few hours of human work. We also propose a novel loss function
that allows neural dialogue generation systems to satisfy complex conditions at
the level of both local tokens and global sentences. We leverage a set of
reinforcement learning objectives to make the system follow a certain policy
while satisfying the prescribed role specifications. Experimental results show
that our framework is able to build chat systems that can effectively maintain
multiple roles during open-domain conversations.

that only needs a few human judgments per comparison. We show that our method

The efficacies of pesticide
treatments are often evaluated by analyzing the average treatment effects and
risks. The stochastic efficiency with respect to a function is often employed
in such evaluations through ranking the certainty equivalents of each
treatment. The main challenge of using this method is gathering an adequate
number of observations to produce results with statistical power. However, in
many cases, only a limited number of trials are replicated in field
experiments, leaving an inadequate number of observations. In addition, this
method focuses only on the farmer's profit without incorporating the impact of
disease pressure on yield and profit. The objective of our study is to propose
a methodology to address the issue of an insufficient number of observations
using simulations and take into account the effect of disease pressure on yield
through a quantile regression model. We apply this method to the case of
strawberry disease management in Florida.
  For the strawberry case, the pesticide treatments considered are applications
of fungicides. We estimate separate models for the highest and average disease
pressure scenarios. We evaluate the efficiency of each treatment in reducing
losses due to disease and the profit made by farmers. The results show that for
the scenario with high disease pressure, treatments 2 to 5, which include 2
or more fungicide applications, are clearly preferred in terms of yield and
profit, while in the average disease scenario, only treatments 4 and 5 are
considered efficient. Without considering disease pressure, treatments 2 to 5
would be considered efficient in terms of profit. Our results indicate that
strategies to manage disease should be tailored to the level of disease pressure
in the area.
  Farmers in developing countries often lack information about the optimal
treatments that maximize their profits. Optimal treatment schedules are often
estimated using stochastic efficiency analyses. However, farmers often do not
have access to the large number of trial observations required to produce
results with power. In addition, current methods of analysis often focus only
on the average profit without considering the effect of disease pressure on
yield and profit. Farmers in many cases plant crops that are resistant or more
tolerant to diseases, which can affect yield and profit. Further, farmers may
want to spend less on treatments as the disease pressure decreases. Estimating
models that capture the treatment-response-yield-disease process would be more
realistic and provide scope for discussing risk and efficiency across different
levels of disease pressure. Farmers would benefit

NP-complete. We investigate and compare the computational complexity of both
decision problems restricted to some graph classes, deriving polynomial-time
algorithms, NP-completeness proofs, and initial parameterized complexity
results, including an answer to an open question in the literature for the
complexity of SG for chordal graphs.

graphs we obtain the following landmark result: if there is a polynomial-time
algorithm for this problem then all problems in NP have a polynomial-time
algorithm. We prove this by establishing a Turing-reduction from the Geodetic
Number problem, for which we prove that it is NP-hard even for bipartite
graphs, and for which we determine the exact parameterized complexity with
respect to the Geodetic Number parameter.

classification, with a polynomial-time algorithm, a semi-decision algorithm

role of the Web as a driver of polarization. In order to further our
understanding of the factors behind online polarization, in the present work we
collect and analyze Web browsing histories of tens of thousands of users

We show that online news consumption follows a polarized pattern, where users'
visits to news sources aligned with their own political leaning are
substantially increased relative to their alignment with the opposing side. In
order to disentangle the role of news consumption vs. other types of online
polarization, we ask users to block entire categories of websites (e.g., all
social media) or specific ones (e.g. Facebook). We find that polarization holds
when many types of websites are blocked, suggesting that a large part of
online polarization is due to browsing of news. We then show that the effect
dramatically diminishes when news sites are specifically blocked. We conclude
that while polarization holds when large parts of the Web are blocked, news
sites stand out as a particularly polarized category. Revealing this pattern
requires browsing history analysis across the entire Web and in conjunction
with careful measurement of time spent on various types of websites.
  Finally, our approach could be used to study polarization in other domains
than politics, such as sports or religion, and could reveal the role of
different types of online activities in the real life interactions that
contribute to polarization.

Edges and boundaries encode shape information, while textures manifest the
appearance of regions. Despite the success of Convolutional Neural Networks
(CNNs) in computer vision and medical image analysis applications,
predominantly only texture abstractions are learned, which often leads to
imprecise boundary delineations. In medical imaging, expert manual segmentation
often relies on organ boundaries; for example, to manually segment a liver, a
medical practitioner usually identifies edges first and subsequently fills in
the segmentation mask. Motivated by these observations, we propose a
plug-and-play module, dubbed Edge-Gated CNNs (EG-CNNs), that can be used with
existing encoder-decoder architectures to process both edge and texture
information. The EG-CNN learns to emphasize the edges in the encoder, to
predict crisp boundaries by an auxiliary edge supervision, and to fuse its
output with the original CNN output. We evaluate the effectiveness of the
EG-CNN with various mainstream CNNs on two publicly available datasets, BraTS
19 and KiTS 19 for brain tumor and kidney semantic segmentation. We demonstrate
how the addition of EG-CNN consistently improves segmentation accuracy and
generalization performance.

terms of enhancing boundary awareness, reducing medical image foreground
noise, improving cross-dataset generalization, and developing a simple yet

single-document transactions utilizing the WiredTiger storage engine in a
standalone node, multi-document transactions in a replica set which consists of
a primary node and several secondary nodes, and distributed transactions in a
sharded cluster which is a group of multiple replica sets, among which data is
sharded. A natural and fundamental question about MongoDB transactions is: What
transactional consistency guarantee do MongoDB Transactions in each deployment
provide? However, it lacks both concise pseudocode of MongoDB transactions in
each deployment and formal specification of the consistency guarantees which
MongoDB claimed to provide. In this work, we formally specify and verify the
transactional consistency protocols of MongoDB. Specifically, we provide a
concise pseudocode for the transactional consistency protocols in each MongoDB
deployment, namely WIREDTIGER, REPLICASET, and SHARDEDCLUSTER, based on the
official documents and source code. We then prove that WIREDTIGER, REPLICASET,
and SHARDEDCLUSTER satisfy different variants of snapshot isolation, namely
Strong-SI, Realtime-SI, and Session-SI, respectively. We also show that MongoDB
protocols can be optimized to achieve stronger consistency guarantees. Such
consistency guarantees are essential for database providers to differentiate
their products and for application developers to make informed choices about
consistency tradeoffs.
  We believe that our work is the first to formally specify and verify
non-relational, distributed databases such as the versions of MongoDB. Our work
could be used to verify other versions of MongoDB and other databases with
transactional consistency protocols similar to MongoDB.

challenging to verify, because MongoDB transactions are complex and diverse.

database like MongoDB. In this work, we outline some general methods for
verifying strong consistency protocols of databases, including checking
acquaintance of threads (or nodes), verifying lock or op-ordering protocols,
verifying queuing or ordering protocols, and checking eventual consistency
properties by statistical model checking. These methods can be used to simplify
the verification process of MongoDB protocols.

of databases. The framework generalizes the methods outlined in the above
paragraph. It can be used to simplify the verification process of MongoDB

minimization from discrete shortest paths in a spatial graph. The convergence
of such hybrid methods to global minimizers hinges on the discretization error
induced by replacing the original continuous problem by its discrete counterpart
on the graph. If the graph is obtained through radial basis function
interpolation, this error has been thoroughly analyzed for energy functionals of
Hartmann type. If the graph is obtained through linear finite elements, the
discretization error has been analyzed for Laplace operators and more recently
for the quadratic form associated with the second eigenvalue of the Laplace
operator, but under restrictive assumptions on the kernel. We aim to remove
these latter assumptions and prove a bound of order $h^2$ for the discretization
error, where $h$ is the step size of the computational domain's mesh.
Moreover, we show that this order can be achieved under minimal regularity of
the kernel, which is induced by the minimal smoothness required for the local
minimizer to be isolated. Finally, combining the results for the discrete paths
and the discretization error, we show that the cost of computing an approximate
global minimizer using a two-stage method is of order $h^2$.
  From a practical point of view, the proof of the order $h^2$ discretization
error provides a bound on the step size $h$ that guarantees that the difference
between the continuous and discrete problems is negligible. This bound can be
used to determine a suitable finite element mesh in conjunction with a method
that estimates an a posteriori error, as we show in the numerical example
Appendix A.

expanding universe is studied using
approximate analytic, and exact numerical solution of self-similar equations.
Both solutions have similar properties, which change qualitatively, depending
on the adiabatic powers $\gamma$. In the interval $1<\gamma<\gamma_{cr} \sim
1.16$ analytic and numeric solutions fill all the space without any voids and
they are rather close to each other. At larger $\gamma>\gamma_{cr}$ a pressure
becomes zero at finite radius, and a spherical void appears around the origin
in both solutions. All matter is collected in thin layer behind the shock wave
front. The structure of this layer qualitatively depends on $\gamma$. At the
inner edge of the layer the pressure is always zero, but the density on this
edge is jumping from zero to infinity at $\gamma \approx 1.4$ in both
solutions.
  Both solutions also have the second voids behind the shocks waves in the
regions of intermediate and low densities if $\gamma\approx 1.9$ and
$\gamma\approx 2.1$ in the analytic and numeric solutions, respectively. At the
inner edge of the second void in the numeric solution the pressure is zero,
and the density on this edge is also zero. This means that the matter passing
through the shock wave arrives to the second void as a flow of negative pressure
in the adiabatic process.
  At larger $\gamma$ a flow behind the shock wave becomes unstable at
numeric solution.
  Both solutions have the adiabatic wings behind the shocks waves where the
pressure and density are power functions of the radius. This gives the large
central void at $\gamma \geqslant 2$ in the analytic solution.
  Self-similar solutions of the Euler equations in the expanding universe have
been obtained in a closed form for the case of the strong shock wave formation
only for the Nicolson adiabatic index $\gamma=1.4$. The general solution for
arbitrary $\gamma$ was obtained in a closed form formally, but it is not
applicable at large $\gamma$. Therefore, our both analytic and numeric
self-similar solutions are useful for any $\gamma$.
  The critical value $\gamma_{cr}$ is similar to the one in the self-similar
solution of the blast wave, but it is not the same. It depends on the adiabatic
index.

polynomials defined as Wronskians of classic Hermite polynomials appear in a

distribution of their zeros in the complex plane. It turns out that 1D SUSY
quantum non-singular potentials come as a dressing of the negative level of
the classic Hermite polynomial by the next positive ones. We describe a structure
of such a dressing for both even and odd cases. The monodromy-free condition
along a generic contour in the complex plane turns into a discrete problem of
recurrence relations of generalized Hermite polynomials. We illustrate the idea
on the example of the 4th order Schr\"odinger operator. The case of polynomial
potentials of arbitrary degree is considered as well.

mixing angles are generated through a unique mechanism. The responsible lagrangian
is uniquely constrained by the $L_e-L_\mu-L_\tau$ symmetry. The model predicts a
large $\theta_{13}$, a quasi-degenerate neutrino spectrum and a normal hierarchy
of neutrino masses. In addition, we propose simple and feasible experiments to
test the $L_e-L_\mu-L_\tau$ symmetry and, consequently, the neutrino spectrum.

$\boldsymbol{\nu}_e$ produced via $\boldsymbol{\gamma}+\boldsymbol{N}$ interactions.

Here, we propose a hybrid measurement attack, with only linear optics, homodyne
detection, and single photon detection, to the widely used vacuum+weak decoy

implemented as a smart contract and at its peak one of the largest consumers of

all of its transactions visible on the blockchain. We take advantage of this
unprecedented transparency to gain insight into the mechanics, impact, and
participants of Forsage.

well as the (mostly nominal) losses of the vast majority of the rest of the
network. We analyze the rate of new capital being attracted to Forsage and
compare it to the rate of cash being distributed out, to understand how long
the scheme could continue to operate. We describe the geographical
distributions of Forsage participants, who they appear to be, and the
communications channels used by the scheme's promoters. Finally, we explain
the features of the smart contract that facilitate the scheme's operation as
a pyramid scheme, and how it uses "recycling" to make itself appear more
profitable than it actually is.

and highlights the dangers of such scams, especially when they use cryptocurrency
technologies. We demonstrate how automated analysis of the transaction records
of a pyramid scheme can uncover the scheme's operating mechanics, expose its
scam nature, and alert would-be participants to its dangers.
  Finally, we demonstrate how Forsage's use of smart contract technology has
allowed its promoters to present itself in a way that misleadingly appears to
be a legitimate decentralized application (a "dApp"). We thus highlight the
importance of regulating the development and operation of smart contracts to
prevent them from being used in further pyramid schemes.
  In conclusion, our work alerts potential participants to the dangers of
Forsage and shows how analysis of blockchain data can be used to expose a
pyramid scheme.

  In finite systems a transformation to the velocity gauge requires a gauge
fixing, which is in fact a projection onto a physical quantity representing the
convection velocity of electrons. For the TB model this is possible only up to
linear order in the vector potential. Going to quadratic order becomes problematic
because of the electron spin orbit coupling and nontemporal electric fields.
Moreover, the velocity gauge description is particular to linear TB models and
any kind of bare next nearest neighbor hopping will lead to unwanted gauge
coupling to the electromagnetic field in higher orders of perturbation theory.
We open the gauge choice and propose two gauge invariant ways of introducing
light-matter interaction for general TB models. These are based on the minimal
coupling scheme typical for the vector gauge but valid in both finite and
infinite systems. One of them is particularly suitable for the single-cell
nanophotonic scenario in which electron images play a crucial role and can be
incorporated directly into the model.
  We demonstrate the validity of these models by studying the electron energy
loss spectrum in a photonic crystal cavity. We show that the typical nanoscale
electron image is described by the dipole coupling in the vector gauge. This
leads to a enhancement of the cavity loss peak in the electron energy loss
spectra beyond what is expected from the dipole approximation. The dipole
coupling is not sufficient to explain the large photon mass that electrons
carry home when being transmitted through a potential barrier.
  Our results are important for the theoretical description of nanophotonic
systems and can be directly applied to any nanoscale particle coupled to light.
In particular, holes in semiconductor barriers are of high importance. We
provide a simple way to incorporate the dipole coupling to the electromagnetic
field for next nearest neighbor holes in strong electric fields.
  Finally, we provide a general procedure for constructing these models. It is
based on the canonical transformation formalism for bosonic fields. This is
particularly useful for problems involving the spin orbit coupling and magnetic
fields.

interaction in TB models. These can be used to study any problem of nanophotonic
interest. They are particularly important when electrons and holes are far

Neural Networks (CNN) and Long
Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been successfully used for process-mining tasks.
They, however, have some major limitations: 1) data quality issues: deep-learning
models are known to be sensitive to noise and missing values, factors common in
real process data; 2) small sample sizes: creating large datasets from
instrumentation sources can be challenging due to system restarts, log
freezing, or other reasons; 3) system changes: processes and systems are
constantly changing, and while changes do not usually affect the nature of the
process, they do impact the timing and logic of the behavior visible in the
logs; 4) domain knowledge integration: while machine learning has been used to
discover processes, doing so requires little knowledge of the system being
analyzed, which is rarely the case in practice; 5) change detection: while
process mining focuses on discovering processes from data, in reality, changes
need to be detected to reflect the changes in behavior; 6) initial
understanding: an understanding of the system is usually required to select the
right features (attributes) to use for analysis, which is rarely based on any
systematic approach; 7) performance improvement: while deep-learning models can
be successfully applied to process analysis, there is still a need for more
efficient approaches, learned end-to-end using direct inputs from the system
under analysis; and 8) pre-training: while some models can be trained from
scratch, pre-trained models are usually required to start the learning from a
higher level of abstraction.
  In this paper, we introduce a unified deep-learning framework that addresses
all the above limitations. The framework, based on a multi-task attention-based
encoder, is initially pre-trained in an unsupervised manner using a variational
auto-encoder (VAE) and subject to a number of constraints learned from the
system under analysis. The framework is, then, fine-tuned to a number of
specific tasks for process discovery, change detection, and understanding.
Until now, these tasks have been treated separately and there has not been a
framework that could address them in a unified manner. We apply the proposed
framework to a number of datasets and show that it outperforms the current
state-of-the-art techniques.

  Community detection is a challenging problem in various disciplines of science
and engineering. Although there are several approaches to detect communities in
a complex system, classical approaches treat the underlying system as a
staticity and do not take into account the dynamical evolution of the system. In
this paper, we propose a level set approach to detect communities from the phase
portrait of a dynamical system. The proposed approach does not need any
parameters and is able to detect half overlapping as well as hard communities.
The approach is also local and can detect leaders in a complex system. We have
tested the approach on several synthetic as well as real world systems. The
results indicate that the approach is able to detect communities from the phase
portrait of a dynamical system.

of a host star. Here, we extend our previous study on the survival of

freezethaw cycles. The model includes the effects of dust grains on the evolution

return to temperatures $T \lesssim 0 K$ with the help of dust grains in some
scenarios. This implies that interstellar panspermia could significantly fuel
the origin of life in planetary systems.

develop a crystalline structure during their journey through the hot zone. This
could provide a mechanism for the delivery of chiral organic molecules to
planets which could then lead to homochiral life. We estimate that the timescale
of these processes to be seconds or minutes in the hot zone. Thus, if
non-chiral spores enter the hot zone, they could give rise to homochiral
organisms on planets. This has a number of implications for the origin of life
that we discuss in more detail.

modifying the chemical structure of microorganisms that could lead to the
formation of more complex molecules. This could result in the delivery of
biogenic organic molecules to planets which could then lead to life as we know
it. We discuss some of the possible chemical reactions that could lead to the
formation of more complex molecules in detail.

mission planning of
unmanned aerial system swarms. Given a swarm operating in a known area, a
central command system generates measurements from the swarm. If those
measurements indicate changes to the mission situation such as target movement,
the swarm planning is updated to reflect the new situation and guidance updates
are broadcast to the swarm. The primary algorithms featured in this work are A*
pathfinding and the Generalized Labeled Multi-Bernoulli multi-target tracking
method.
  Compared to existing methods, this technique improves upon faster propagation
of new information to the swarm and reduced communication overhead. Reduced
communication overhead is achieved by having the swarm transmit their own
measurements to the command center, rather than requesting to retransmit data
already acquired by the command center. This overhead reduction allows for a
significant increase in the frequency of mission re-planning.
  A simulation comparing this work's approach with a more traditional fixed
interval re-planning strategy is presented. The results show a significant
increase in the detection of targets as well as an increase in overall mission
success.
  A physical flight test comparing this work's approach with a traditional fixed
interval re-planning strategy is also presented. The results show that the
proposed approach can improve mission success by up to 24%.
  The code for this work is publicly available at
https://github.com/tristan555/UTAMissionPlanning.
  For the purpose of peer review, the simulation and flight test data used in
this work are also publicly available at
https://tristan555.oss-bucket.com/index.html.
  For transparency, the algorithms and techniques presented in this work are not
novel and have been previously published by other authors. The purpose of this
work is to demonstrate how those algorithms can be integrated together to
achieve a novel capability, namely the autonomous re-planning of a swarm based
on native swarm sensing.
  As with any swarm flight test, considerations such as communication range
and interference did arise. Although the test demonstrated the promised
capabilities, the algorithm parameters were tuned to be robust against
communication loss. In the simulation and in future work, the algorithm's
performance will be evaluated in scenarios with intentional communication loss
and interference.
  Future work will also include the implementation of an initialization phase
for the swarm, as well as the integration with a SE 3D map. Until that work is
completed, the algorithm presented in this work will not be considered fully
developed.

processes on networks whether they are near to a transition or not. The method

investigate spreading processes on a wide spectrum of networks, both
analytically and numerically, showing that nodal activity can present complex
patterns depending on the network structure. Using annealed networks we show
that a localized state at the transition is followed by a de-localized or
super-critical state for any kind of degree distribution. On quenched networks
localized states are found on approaches to the transition from the inactive
side. We also show that the critical degree of a node, which determines its
localization, is directly proportional to its activity at the transition. Using
an epidemic model on a Los Angeles network, we show that a localized state can
be beneficial to stop the spread of a disease. Our results provide a complete
picture of localization in spreading processes on networks.

studying political polarization in political and social systems. Several
methods are used commonly to measure polarization in social networks by purely
inspecting their structure. We analyse eight of such methods and show that all
of them yield high polarization scores even for random networks with similar
density and degree distributions to typical real-world networks. Further, some
of the methods are sensitive to degree distributions and relative sizes of the
polarized groups. We propose normalization to the existing scores and a minimal
set of tests that a score should pass in order for it to be suitable for
separating polarized networks from random noise. The performance of the scores
increased by 38%-220% after normalization in a classification task of 203
networks. Further, we find that the choice of method is not as important as
normalization, after which most of the methods have better performance than the
best-performing method before normalization. This work opens up the possibility
to critically assess and compare the features and performance of different
methods for measuring structural polarization.

generate hyper-prompts: we propose HyperPrompt, a novel architecture for
prompt-based task-conditioning of self-attention in Transformers. The
hyper-prompts are end-to-end learnable via generation by a HyperNetwork.
HyperPrompt allows the network to learn task-specific feature maps where the
hyper-prompts serve as task global memories for the queries to attend to, at
the same time enabling flexible information sharing among tasks. We show that
HyperPrompt is competitive against strong multi-task learning baselines with as
few as $0.14\%$ of additional task-conditioning parameters, achieving great
parameter and computational efficiency. Through extensive empirical evaluations
on both classification and generation benchmarks, we demonstrate that
HyperPrompt can achieve superior performance against strong T5-based
Prompt-Tuning baselines, and validate that the large-scale pre-training
benefits multi-task learning with few-shot Prompt-Tuning.
  Overall, our work proposes HyperPrompt as a simple yet effective way of
parameter and computationally efficient multi-task learning using HyperNetworks
for task-conditioning in Transformers.

than a constant factor when the number of Byzantine nodes is $o(|\mathcal{V}|)$.

nodes and uses (randomized) secure multi-party computation (MPC) protocols that
are efficient even when a linear fraction of the nodes are Byzantine. The

communication overhead ($\tilde{O}(|\mathcal{W}|^{0.4})$ per node, where

fully distributed, do not have a leader or a central authority, and are
fault-tolerant (even in the presence of Byzantine nodes).

this phenomenon. Antiferromagnetic antiperovskites are one of emerging material
classes that exhibit a variety of interesting properties owing to a complex
electronic band structure and magnetic ordering. Reports on the anomalous

limited. This scarcity may be partly due to the experimental difficulty of
reliably quantifying the anomalous Nernst coefficient. Here, we report
experiments on the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite
Mn$_3$NiN thin films. Measurement of both the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects
using the same sample and measurement geometry makes it possible to directly
compare these two effects and quantify the anomalous Nernst coefficient and
conductivity in Mn$_3$NiN. We carefully evaluate the spatial distribution of
the thermal gradient in the sample and use finite element modeling to
corroborate our experimental results.
  When the current is perpendicular to the temperature gradient, the Nernst
voltage induced by thermal gradient is weak compared to the anomalous Nernst
coefficient (ANEC) when the magnetic field is zero. However, when the current
is parallel to the temperature gradient, the measured Nernst coefficient is
very small and consistent with zero, whether in a zero magnetic field or under
a finite magnetic field. The ANEC is also weak in the parallel geometry. The
weak ANEC when Nernst voltage is measured perpendicular to the direction of
current is unique in Mn$_3$NiN compared to other materials reported so far. We
fully utilize the available experimental data of the transport coefficients
and resistivity to theoretically model the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects,
and the conductivity in Mn$_3$NiN. Our theoretical model suggests that the
weakness of the ANEC when measured in the perpendicular geometry is probably
due to the small carrier scattering asymmetry.

with zero magnetization. The anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic
materials with vanishing magnetization has potential to be further investigated
in other materials classes and may have applications in designing advanced

conductivity is affected by deformations and damage. This property, known as
piezoresistivity, has been extensively leveraged for conductivity-based damage
detection via electrical resistance change methods and tomographic imaging
techniques such as electrical impedance tomography (EIT). Although these
techniques are very effective at detecting the presence of damage, they suffer
from an inability to provide precise information about damage shape, size, or
mechanism. This is particularly detrimental for laminated composites which can
suffer from complex failure modes, such as delaminations, that are difficult to
detect. To that end, we herein propose a new technique for precisely
determining damage shape and size in self-sensing composites. Our technique
makes use of a global-local imaging strategy, in which a conductivity-based
damage detection method is used in a local imaging phase to precisely refine the
known failure region to the scale of plies. We leverage the fact that these
materials are typically fabricated with a known number of layers, and use this
information along with the high spatial resolution provided by our technique to
accurately determine damage shape and size. We validate our technique on a
laminated composite specimen with a deliberately introduced delamination. The
results show that our technique can accurately determine damage shape and size
with high fidelity, and provides a significant improvement over traditional
conductivity-based detection methods.

the COVID pandemic impacts
students' ability to keep up with the pace of instruction in a university level
physics course, with a focus on the heterogeneous impact of remote learning on
different student populations. Student data is analyzed from a random sample of
two sections of university level physics course that were taught in the Spring
of 2020 with a remote learning format due to the COVID-19 pandemic and compared
to data from the same sections taught in the Fall of 2019 with a face-to-face
learning format. Results show that remote learning is strongly correlated with
lower learning progress with a mean shift of about one letter grade. Results
also show that remote learning further exacerbates the learning gap of under
represented minority students, with a mean shift of about 1.5 letter grades. The
stronger learning gap for under represented minority students is statistically
significant at the 95% confidence level. The analysis also shows that students
with lower socioeconomic status, who are defined by the percentage of students
in a student's high school receiving free lunch, tend to struggle more with the
remote format but the difference is not statistically significant at the 95%
confidence level.
  From a policy perspective, the strong evidence of the learning gap for under
represented minority students and the general mean shift due to remote learning
suggest that such student populations may benefit from extra support in online
physics courses. Teachers can also use various learning analysis tools to provide
early warning to students who are likely struggling with the course material and
provide targeted support to those students.
  It is also generally recommended that research on the effectiveness of
remote learning should control for the quality of the teaching and the quality
of the internet connection since both factors likely impact student learning
outcomes.

decoding walking-related information in the motor cortex. In this article, we
review the history and progress of BCIs for restoring walking function,
emphasizing both the technical advances and open questions that remain. We also
identify opportunities for future research, including the development of more

motor function to individuals with spinal cord injury. These systems have

important tools in evolutionary analysis, especially in phylogeny

lack of discussion or comparison for different generators. To bridge this gap,
we compare a set of phylogenetic network generators by profiling topological
summary statistics of the generated networks over the number of reticulations
and comparing the topological profiles.
  We consider four different generators, adding edges to an tree to generate a
network with a certain number of reticulations. We evaluate the topological
summary statistics, such as the number of bicharacters, the number of quartets
and the number of edges, in the generated networks and compare them to
corresponding statistics in species networks. We also validate our approach on
a dataset of species networks.
  We demonstrate that the topological profiles in generated networks are close
to the topological profiles in corresponding species networks, which suggests
that these generators can be utilized as priors in Bayesian network
reconstruction methods. We also point out that the comparison can be used as a
verification tool for new generators in the future.
  We propose a new measure, mean absolute difference, to measure the difference
between two topological profiles, and utilize it in comparing different
generators. However, the comparison is sensitive to the number of simulations and
the range of the number of reticulations. Future work is needed to determine the
number of simulations needed for a comparison and how to standardize the
topological profiles.
  We suggest that a set of generators, each representing a different level of
reticulation from trees to networks, can be utilized as a suite of methods for

search for food, find suitable
habitat, pursue prey, escape from predators, or seek a mate. The grand scale of
biodiversity contributes to the great locomotory design and mode diversity.
Various creatures make use of legs, wings, fins and other means to move through
the world. In this report, we refer to the locomotion of general biological
species as biolocomotion. We present a computational approach to detect
biolocomotion in unprocessed video.
  Significantly, the motion exhibited by the body parts of a biological entity
to navigate through an environment can be modeled by a combination of an
overall positional advance with an overlaid asymmetric oscillatory pattern, a
distinctive signature that can be used for detection of biolocomotion. We
propose an algorithm based on this distinctive signature for detection of
biolocomotion. Our approach is position-invariant, and does not require any
biological knowledge. It uses low-level features such as motion orientation
and variance, combined in a specific way, to represent the motion by a signature
capture by the positional advance and a model of the oscillatory pattern by
its symmetry. These features and models are independent of position and
therefore our approach is invariant to the position of the biological entity in
the video. We present experimental results on a variety of videos showing
different modes of biolocomotion including human, monkey, dog, cat, bird, and
fish. Our approach had a detection accuracy of 92%. It detected the
biolocomotion in all the videos of human, monkey, dog, cat, and bird, and in
three out of five videos of fish.
  We present a novel approach to detect biolocomotion from unprocessed video. A
computational model based on an insightful biological observation leads to a
novel and efficient detector of biolocomotion.
  The proposed approach is presented through a detector algorithm, and both
design and results are supported by a comprehensive analysis of a variety of
videos.
  The presented approach is general and should be able to detect any mode of
biolocomotion.
  The presented approach has the potential of being incorporated into surveillance
systems to help distinguish biological entities from non-biological moving
objects.
  The presented approach has the potential of being incorporated into motion
detection algorithms to help distinguish the motion resulting from biolocomotion
from other types of motion.

different from the albedo. We calculate the deposition coefficient of randomly
scattered, partially transparent, diffuse sources (including heat fluxes and
radiative intensities) at the boundary of an absorbing-scattering system of
finite thickness. The deposition coefficient is defined as the ratio of the
lateral flux of the radiative intensity (or heat flux) at the location of the
diffuse source to the radiative intensity (or heat flux) itself. The results
are presented for normal, oblique, and specular reflections, as well as for
periodic and uniform systems. A general expression for the deposition coefficient is obtained for arbitrary optical thickness and angle of incidence. We
provide limiting cases for the deposition coefficient for normal incident
diffuse radiation, highly absorbing or scattering systems, large systems,
systems with Planckian diffuse sources, and for normal incident heat flux.
Comparisons with the albedo are also provided.
  From the definition of the deposition coefficient, we provide a general
expression for the case of a radiative participant (both scattering and
absorbing) at the location of the diffuse source. For a typical radiative
transfer problem, the deposition coefficient for the case of a radiative
participant is close to 1 for most practical purposes. For a system with a
radiative participant at the location of a specular reflector, the deposition
coefficient for the case of a specular reflectance is also close to 1 for most
practical purposes. For other cases, the deposition coefficient provides a
convenient way to improve the accuracy of the solution by reducing the
difference between the source and the lateral flux (or heat flux). We provide
examples for carbon black and typical industrial systems.
  For a system with a radiative participant at the location of a specular
reflectant, a simple iterative method is provided to solve the equation for
the albedo (or deposition coefficient) for any optical thickness. The method
converges quickly for all practical purposes. For other cases, a simple
non-iterative method is provided to estimate the deposition coefficient (or
albedo). The estimates are close to the exact values for most practical
situations.

condensed matter and artificial systems. Here we study the topological and
localization properties in one-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model with
spatially correlated random binary disorders. It is found that random binary
disorders can induce the topological Anderson insulating phase from the trivial
insulator in various parameter regions. The topological Anderson insulators are
characterized by the disorder-averaged winding number and localized bulk states
revealed by the inverse participation ratio in both real and momentum spaces.
We show that the topological phase boundaries are consistent with the
analytical results of the self-consistent Born approach and the localization
length of zero-energy modes. The topological phases can be traced by the
disorder-averaged Berry phase curve in the renormalized parameter space. We
notice that the topological phase at strong disorder is caused by the
localized states in the bulk, which is different from the case of spatially
correlated Gaussian disorders. Our results provide more options in simulating
topological phenomena using binary disorders, which is promising for realizing
topological states in photonic and neuro-insulator systems.

works have shown how to
differentiate the solution map of a (continuous) parametrized optimization
problem, opening up the possibility of embedding mathematical optimization
problems into end-to-end learnable models. These differentiability results can
lead to significant memory savings by providing an expression for computing the
derivative without needing to unroll the steps of the forward-pass optimization
procedure during the backward pass. However, the results typically require
inverting a large Hessian matrix, which is computationally expensive when
implemented naively. In this work we study two applications of deep declarative
networks -- robust vector pooling and optimal transport -- and show how problem
structure can be exploited to obtain very efficient backward pass computations
in terms of both time and memory. Our ideas can be used as a guide for
improving the computational performance of other novel deep declarative nodes.

problem of computing the geometric mean of multiple vectors. Our experiments

important parameters, as is the case for the spreading motion of an epithelial
monolayer.

by the PHENIX Collaboration in the years from 2006 to 2011. We observe no

indicating that cold nuclear matter effects are small or absent. Hadrons
carrying a large fraction of the quark's momentum are suppressed in Au$+$Au
compared to $p$$+$$p$ and $d$$+$Au. As the momentum fraction decreases, the
yield of hadrons in Au$+$Au increases to an excess over the yield in $p$$+$$p$
collisions. The excess is at large angles and at low hadron $p_T$ and is most
pronounced for hadrons associated with lower momentum direct photons.
Comparison to theoretical calculations suggests that the hadron excess arises
from medium response to energy deposited by jets.
  Nuclear effects in the medium are similar to those found previously for
hadron-hadron correlations. The data suggest that the magnitude of the
effect is roughly proportional to the number of participants,
$N_{\rm part}$.
  These results provide new insights into the interplay between jet and
medium evolution.
  Presented theory frameworks suggest that proper treatment of
finite-time evolution and medium fragmentation go beyond the current nuclear
effects observed in data.
  Further comparison of theoretical frameworks and data will be crucial for
understanding the relationship between jet and medium evolution.
  Measurement of an excess of hadrons at large angles to the photon direction
in Au$+$Au collisions may also be the Indication of Elongation of the
fireball.
  Measurement of this excess in smaller system such as $d$$+$Au is needed to
understand the system size dependence of this effect.
  Measurement of the excess at high $p_T$ both for hadrons and photons may
provide crucial information of the energy deposited in the medium.

network theory, this work studies the extremal gain of large symmetric multiple
input multiple output (MIMO) x-nomial channels (where x can be K for multiple
input multiple output, L for linear channel or N for spatially correlated
channel), namely the extremal value of the product of the achievable rate and
the number of degrees of freedom (DoF). It is shown that the extremal gain
generally scales with the square of the number of degrees of freedom (DoF), and
achieves the same asymptotic growth rate as the sum of DoF. Thus, from the
perspective of extremal network theory, the extremal channels are the ones with
higher DoF first, then some other non-orthogonality, and lastwise a certain
transmission scheme with non-vanishing error probability. This work also shows
that our approach offers a fast way to determine the extremal channels and the
value of extremal gain, by contrast to the general practice in extremal network
theory which often requires time-consuming numerical simulations. Particular
results are also obtained for the extremal gain of Causal DoF, shared DoF, and
sum DoF. Comparisons are made between the extremal gain of causal DoF, shared
DoF, and sum DoF. Some special cases, such as the extremal gain of spatially
correlated MIMO-Gaussian channel and extremal gain of MIMO-BC (broadcast
channel) are also studied.

deal with the ground reaction force fluctuations even when the foot dimensions

  In the study reported here, the quark colors are not polarized and the
interaction in the medium is described by a contact vertex. This model is an
effective representation of the meson form factors and is regulated by the
quark masses and the coupling constant. The calculated meson elastic form
forces are seen to be well described by a monopole form factor in the low as
well as high momentum transfer regime. The charge radii obtained for the
mesons are found to be in good agreement with the results reported in the

  The present work is developed in the Rainbow-Landau gauge and hence the
quark antiquark meson form factors are seen to be clean of any gauge artifact
as they are regulated by the quark masses which are gauge invariant.
Furthermore, the meson elastic form factors are seen to be quite sensitive to
the variation of the quark masses and the interaction strength.
  Finally, it is demonstrated that the charge radii of the mesons can be
extracted purely from the meson elastic form factors at specific momentum
transfer.
  In conclusion, the present work shows that the contact interaction model
with the quark and meson dressing effects via the gap and Bethe-Salpeter
equations can well describe a range of meson elastic form factors. This model
is a effective representation of the mesons as composite objects of the
quarks.
  It is to be noted that the present work can be extended to study the light
cone form factors of the mesons by using the complex plane method of the
Bethe-Salpeter equation.

polarized and unpolarized elastic form forces.

  Information hierarchies are organizational structures that often used to organize
and present large and complex information as well as provide a mechanism for
effective human navigation. Fortunately, many statistical and computational
models exist that automatically generate hierarchies; however, the existing
 approaches do not consider linkages in information {\em networks} that are
increasingly common in real-world scenarios. Current approaches also tend to
present topics as an abstract probability distribution over words, etc rather
than as tangible nodes from the original network. Furthermore, the statistical
techniques present in many previous works are not yet scalable to process data
of the size that are being published in a hierarchical format. In this paper we
present a novel approach that automatically generates hierarchies by clustering
the pages of the original network using our non-negative matrix factorization
(NMF) based approach, HeyTree. We present an efficient algorithm with
theoretical guarantees based on the alternating update rule for the generalized
bilinear factorization model (BIFM) that is scalable to handle data of large
size including the entire MEDLINE database provided by the National Library of
Medicine. We present experimental results on several datasets including
categories from Yahoo!, BBC news articles, PubMed and Google books.

quantum system: Annealing explores equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian with
slowly changing parameters and can be exploited as a tool for solving complex
optimization problems. In contrast, quenches are sudden changes of the
Hamiltonian, producing a non-equilibrium situation. Here, we investigate the
relation between the two cases. Specifically, we show that the minimum of the
postquench gap can be predicted from the quench protocol and annealing phase
transition point. Moreover, we show that the knowledge of the quench gap can
help to better understand the role of imaginary transitions in the annealing
process.
  From the theoretical point of view, the connection between quench and anneal
evolution is not so clear. In particular it is not obvious how the quench gap
could be related to the spectral properties of the annealing Hamiltonian. To
understand this connection we considered a simple spin model, namely the
doped two-dimensional quantum Hatrree-Pauli model, for which both quench and
annealing dynamics can be studied equally well. We show that the minimum of the
quench gap, i.e., the lowest excitation energy that can be created by a
quench, contains valuable information on the dynamical process that occurs
annealing: notably, the knowledge of the quench gap allows predicting whether
an imaginary transition is needed to or can be optimized in the annealing
process.
  Moreover we show that the position of the annealing transition can be
predicted from the maximum quench gap. This is so far the most general and
non-perturbative connection between quench and anneal dynamics that we are aware
of.

particular we show that the connection between quench gap and annealing transition
is captured by the non-equilibrium correlation function that describes the
evolution of a quench excitation in the annealing Hamiltonian.
  We conclude by discussing our results from a practical perspective. In
particular we show that the connection between quench gap and annealing transition
can be exploited to optimize the annealing process by choosing the right
quench parameter.
  Finally we note that our results apply to generic Hamiltonians and protocols
and rely on neither symmetry nor perturbative assumptions on the Hamiltonian.

long history in mathematics, going back to Bachet and Lagrange. While for some
specific rings (like integers or polynomials over the rationals), there are
known methods for decomposing an element into a sum of squares, in general, for
many other important rings and fields, the problem is still widely open. In
this paper, we present an explicit algorithm for decomposing an element of the
wedge algebra (which is isomorphic to the quaternionic polynomials) as a sum of
squares. We explicitly describe all the possible combinations of Hilbert
symbols that appear in the general case of degree 4. Using this rich structure
of the wedge algebra, we are able to present a systematic algorithm for
decomposing an element as a sum of squares.
  We prove that every element of the wedge algebra has a representation as a
sum of at most 4 squares. We present an explicit algorithm for reducing an
arbitrary element of the wedge algebra (which is not a square) to a minimal
positive representation as a sum of squares (with 4 squares). This minimal
representation is unique up to the units of the algebra. The algorithm presents
a clear pattern of alternating steps of two types : adding or subtracting a
specific square (which is a uniform sum of squares) and applying a Fermat like
modular substitution (with primes 2, 7 or 41). The presentation is divided
into 3 main theorems which represent a compositional breakdown of the
decomposition.

the quadratic residueness test for prime powers. This algorithm is a natural
combination of two algorithms : one for the Eisenstein criterion and another
for the Hensel lifting. It is an interesting example of a problem (which is
known to be solvable with a degree 6 algorithm, by other famous theorems) that
is solvable with a simpler algorithm of degree 4, using the rich structure of
the wedge algebra.
  Finally, we present a natural extension of our work, to the algebras of
Bilinear Forms (which are natural generalizations of the wedge algebra). We
describe a natural extension of our results and algorithms, to these algebras
as well.

polypharmacy side effect identification, drug-drug interaction prediction and

tasks. We provide fundamental definitions, compare existing model architectures
and discuss performance metrics, datasets and evaluation protocols. In

  From a mathematical perspective, current models are based on binary relational
prediction, with the exception of one approach which we are not able to

method which operates on pairs of elements. Therefore, we provide a step-by-step
guide on how to assemble a kernel-based machine learning model which addresses
one of these tasks. We provide R code which can be used as a starting point for
new studies. In addition, we provide a summary of various datasets and metrics
which have been proposed and used in the literature. Finally, we discuss possible
applications and extensions which are not yet well represented in the field.
Specifically, multi-step learning algorithms which combine machine learning and
differential operators come to mind. Specifically, we believe that a learning
algorithm which combines kernel methods and the Kirchhoff-Frenet operator may
be able to address the prediction of sudden cardiac death, which is one of the
ten leading causes of death in the world.

to address more tasks in this domain. We would like to encourage researchers to

Learning (FL) as a canonical application. One of the main challenges of FL is
the communication bottleneck between the nodes and the parameter server. A
popular solution in the literature is to allow each node to do several local
updates on the model in each iteration before sending it back to the PS. While
this mitigates the communication bottleneck, the statistical heterogeneity of
the data owned by the different nodes has proven to delay convergence and bias
the model. In this work, we study random walk (RW) learning algorithms for
tackling the communication and data heterogeneity problems. The main idea is to
leverage available direct connections among the nodes themselves, which are
typically "cheaper" than the communication to the PS. In a random walk, the
model is thought of as a "baton" that is passed from a node to one of its
neighbors after being updated in each iteration. The challenge in designing the
RW is the data heterogeneity and the uncertainty about the data distributions.
Ideally, we would want to visit more often nodes that hold more informative
data. We cast this problem as a sleeping multi-armed bandit (MAB) to design a
near-optimal node sampling strategy that achieves variance-reduced gradient
estimates and approaches sublinear convergence rates of the classic MAB. To the
best of our knowledge, this is the first MAB formulation of RW with mixed
objectives of communication and data diversity. We complement our theoretical
results with an empirical study, showing that our approach outperforms the
state-of-the-art FL algorithms in a variety of applications.

  From a statistical perspective, medical image segmentation using deep neural
networks is about modeling the probability density function of the target
structure. The background structure is implicitly modeled by sampling from the
whole image. However, the interest region may contain other non-target
structures. Therefore, the density function of the background actually contains
multiple cluster patterns. To effectively model the background, the implicit
annotation methodology employs an auxiliary classification branch to classify
the whole image to the specific target organ/structure, and uses the output
classification map to filter the segmentation mask, rather than directly modeling
the density function of the background. This two-stage operation is the key to
disentangle the two complex pattern datasets in an end-to-end manner. Experiments
demonstrate that our proposed methodology achieves even better performance
comparing with models trained with abundant annotation.

an intuitive and generalizable pathway to quantify the relationship between
complex local atomic structure and coarse-grained materials phenomena.

applications beyond metal alloys. While developed for thermal fluctuations, our

prime workhorse of applied graph mining. Novel node embedding techniques are
often tested on a restricted set of benchmark datasets. In this paper, we
propose a new diverse social network dataset called Twitch Gamers with multiple
potential target attributes. Our analysis of the social network and node
classification experiments illustrate that Twitch Gamers is suitable for
assessing the predictive performance of novel proximity preserving and
structural role-based node embedding algorithms.
  We find that the actual predictive performance depends on both the node
embedding algorithm and the learning algorithm. Therefore, we provide a Python
implementation of Twitch Gamers with default learning algorithms to facilitate
future comparisons of novel node embedding algorithms.
  Overall, our results highlight the importance of empirical evaluations of
node embedding algorithms not only on multiple benchmark datasets but also on
diverse real-world datasets with multiple target attributes.
  Finally, we show that the social network of gamers is an incomplete sub-graph
of a larger information network that includes features and edges related to
multiple gaming activities. To our knowledge, this is the first node embedding
analysis of a social network that has been derived from a larger information
network.
  In summary, we propose a new node embedding benchmark dataset with multiple
predicted attributes, a rich information context, and an incomplete main
dataset setting. We make the full dataset available to the node embedding and
graph mining community.
  In an effort to mitigate the issue of over-engineering node embedding
algorithms, we performed a simple and transparent analysis of the node
embedding literature. The analysis revealed a research trajectory of increasing
overfitting, which motivated our choice of a diverse real-world dataset with
multiple target attributes.

failure morphology changes continuously with pulling velocity. This can be
understood as a competition between two velocity scales: the speed of
re-aggregation, in which particles relax towards a low-energy configuration
determined by viscous and capillary forces, and the difference of velocity
between neighboring particles caused by the expanding fluid. This competition
selects the cluster length, i.e., the distance between adjacent rifts. A model
based on this competition is consistent with the experimental failure patterns.

mirrored in the digital twins of our model, where the Graetz problem helps to
connect the scaling of the grains with the stretching velocity. This connection
results in a prediction of failure modes in two and three dimensions.

particles can delay failure. This is understood as an increase in the particles
diameter due to the grafted layer, which shifts the failure in three dimensions
to lower pulling velocities.

failure in two and three dimensions as well as the impact of polymers, which is
connected directly to the experimental failure patterns.

star formation suggests that the cluster is $\gtrsim$1.5 Gyr old.

complexes as surface brightness fluctuations to measure the distance to

modern encrypted databases called update pattern leakage. We formalize the
definition and security model of DP-Sync with DP update patterns. We also
proposed the framework DP-Sync, which extends existing encrypted database
schemes to DP-Sync with DP update patterns. DP-Sync guarantees that the entire
data update history over the outsourced data structure is protected by
differential privacy. This is achieved by imposing differentially-private
strategies that dictate the data owner's synchronization of local~data.
Specifically, DP-Sync comprises of two phases: (1)~private update~and~refresh
of the data structure with DP-synchronization, and (2)~query~phase with DP
search. We show several practical applications of our proposed framework DP-Sync
with DP update patterns. We also provide the implementation of our scheme with
real-world datasets and evaluate its performance.
  The main contributions of this paper are: (1)~we introduce a new type of
differential privacy called differential privacy with DP update patterns;
(2)~we propose DP-Sync, a novel framework for encrypted databases that achieves
this new privacy model; (3)~we provide several applications of DP-Sync with
practical search patterns; and (4)~we provide a comprehensive implementation and
performance evaluation of our scheme with real-world datasets.
  In conclusion, we propose a new type of leakage called update pattern leakage
and provide the framework DP-Sync that prevents such leakage. We believe that
DP-Sync provides a complete solution for data owners who want to leverage
cloud-based services while maintaining privacy of their data.
  Differential privacy (DP) has been widely adopted by many organizations to
protect their sensitive information by leaking very little about individual's
data even if the entire dataset is known. This is achieved by randomly perturbing
the data with some mechanism following a DP distribution. However, individual's
data is usually static and not likely to change over time. On the other hand,
many data owners do utilize cloud services to synchronize their local data.
Therefore, it is desirable to propose search methods over static datasets that
are generated by different individuals using private data aggregation techniques
while allowing different users to search over the data structuring for retrieving
specific information. To this end, we propose a new model called DP-Sync that
maintains entire data update history of the outsourced data structure with
differentially-private update patterns.

attitudes in a series of treatments that gradually reveal information about the

from those who have had opportunities that resulted in large outcomes when those

too little. We also explore how redistributive attitudes change in a variety of
ways, including in response to information about relative luck, changes in

while these variations move attitudes in the right direction, they do not
eliminate the large underestimation of luck's role that we observe.
  Our findings have implications for how people think about luck and merit in
society, and how these ideas influence attitudes toward redistribution. They
also have implications for policy makers seeking to use information about the
sources of outcomes to design policies that effectively address inequality.
  In particular, we find that an intervention that provides people with
information about the role of luck in a story about a person's outcome increases
attitudes toward redistributing away from that person. This suggests that
policies that provide such information -- such as policies providing
disability benefits to people who have been unlucky in terms of health or job
loss -- may be more popular than they would be otherwise. At the same time,
people still want to reward (with transfers or with respect) those who have
worked hard and been successful, even when luck has played a significant role in
their success. This suggests that any increase in redistribution resulting from
such an intervention would likely be partially offset by increased support for
transfers to reward effort.

people think about luck and merit, but also how those ideas influence attitudes
toward redistribution. This contrasts with much of the previous literature that
focuses on how people make decisions in the presence of luck and merit, while
assuming that attitudes toward redistribution are largely determined by
distribution of outcomes. We hope to spur further research on the sources of
disparities and how people think about luck and merit in order to better
understand how to reduce inequality.

multi-agent policies from pre-collected datasets, which is an important step
toward the deployment of multi-agent systems in real-world applications.
However, in practice, each individual behavior policy that generates
multi-agent joint trajectories usually has different levels of how well it
performs. e.g., an agent is a random policy while other agents are medium
policies. In the cooperative game with global reward, one agent learned by
existing offline MARL often inherits this random policy, jeopardizing the
performance of the entire team. In this paper, we investigate offline MARL with
explicit consideration on the diversity of agent-wise trajectories and propose
a novel framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) to address this
problem. Specifically, an attention-based reward decomposition network assigns
the credit to each agent through a differentiable key-value memory mechanism in
an offline manner. These decomposed credits are then used to reconstruct the
joint offline datasets into prioritized experience replay with individual
trajectories, thereafter agents can share their good trajectories and
conservatively train their policies with a graph attention network (GAT) based
critic. We evaluate our method in both discrete control (i.e., StarCraft II and
multi-agent particle environment) and continuous control (i.e, multi-agent
mujoco). The results indicate that our method achieve significantly better
results in complex and mixed offline multi-agent reinforcement learning

combined measure of knowledge and productivity, we make scientific literature
networking visible and measurable for the first time. Specifically, as revealed
by the sharp increase in the knowledge density of the literature density curve,
the knowledge density of the current literature is about 10 times that of 50
years ago. Our findings make the scientific literature "visible" for the first
time, which may help policymakers in the field of science, such as the
National Science Foundation, make decisions more effectively and accurately.
