new ancillary
services, which enable the secure and reliable operation of the electricity
system. However, assessments and policy advice regarding ancillary services and
market design lack methods to evaluate the complex interaction of markets and
services. Therefore, this paper contributes an open-source agent-based model to
test design options for ancillary services and electricity markets. The
Ancillary Services Acquisition Model (ASAM) combines the agent-based modeling
framework MESA with the toolbox Python for Power System Analysis (PyPSA). The
model provides various design parameters per market and agent-specific
strategies as well as detailed clearing algorithms for the day-ahead market,
intra-day continuous trading, redispatch, and imbalances. Moreover, ASAM
includes numerous policy performance indicators, including a novel price
mark-up indicator and novel redispatch performance indicators. A stylized
simulation scenario verified and validated the model and addressed a redispatch
design question. The results displayed the following implications from order
types in redispatch markets with multi-period all-or-none design: (1) The order
design provides few risks for market parties, as orders are fully cleared. (2)
Large orders may lead to dispatch ramps before and after the delivery period
and may cause ramp-risk mark-ups as well as additional trading of imbalances on
intra-day. (3) All-or-none design in a liquid situation leads to the
over-procurement of redispatch measures. (4) The presence of a capacity
remuneration mechanism (CRM) stabilizes prices and reduces the impact of the
over-procurement. This study contributes a purpose-built agent-based model for
the simultaneous test and validation of design options for ancillary services and
markets. The results can support the development of effective and efficient
ancillary services markets in the future.

interface within the $d$-dimensional fractured porous domain, for $d=2, 3$. Two
classes of fracture are distinguished based on the permeability magnitude ratio
between the fracture and its surrounding medium: when the permeability in the
fracture is (significantly) larger than in its surrounding medium, it is
considered as a {\it conductive} fracture; when the permeability in the
fracture is (significantly) smaller than in its surrounding medium, it is
considered as a {\it blocking} fracture. The conductive fractures are treated
using the classical hybrid-dimensional approach of the interface model where
pressure is assumed to be continuous across the fracture interfaces, while the
blocking fractures are treated using the recent Dirac-$\delta$ function
approach where normal component of Darcy velocity is assumed to be continuous
across the interface. Due to the use of Dirac-$\delta$ function approach for
the blocking fractures, our numerical scheme allows for nonconforming meshes
with respect to the blocking fractures. This is the major novelty of our model
and numerical discretization. Moreover, our numerical scheme produces locally
conservative velocity approximations and satisfies the equilibrium balance
equation in a mesh-independent way. We prove the convergence of the exact
sequence of discrete solutions. Furthermore, we provide a convergence result
for the velocity approximations. Both convergence results are proved under rather
minimal regularity assumptions on the data and, as such, is stronger than what
has been established in many earlier works on flow in fractured porous media.

model and numerical discretization.

discourse markers between sentence pairs in order to learn accurate sentence
representations, that are useful in various classification tasks. In this work,
we go one step further: using the predicted discourse relations between sentence
pairs, we learn to predict human annotations of discourse markers in an
end-to-end setting. Our results show that predicting discourse markers is a
challenging task, which requires models that capture a wide variety of
discourse relations (including relations that are rarely or never predicted
between sentence pairs in previous work). Nonetheless, we show that by predicting
a larger set of discourse markers, models learn to predict a larger set of
relations, which in turn leads to improvements in classification tasks that
require accurate sentence representations.
  We achieve these results by using a combination of weighted average scoring
(similar to mean squared error) with adversarial training, choosing a specific
but minimal set of discourse markers to predict, and by using annotations at
both sentence and document level. Finally, we also show that our models learn to
a large extent the linguistic knowledge about the language they are trained on, a
concern previously noted in the literature. We therefore release a dataset of
discourse markers annotated in the English Wiki corpus, together with a
comprehensive linguistic analysis of the discourse markers in the dataset.
  Overall, our results suggest that predicting discourse markers is a promising
direction for improving sentence representations, which in turn can lead to
better performance on classification tasks.
  Finally, we also study the role of discourse markers in a classification task
between human-annotated implicit discourse relations. We observe that predicting
discourse markers does not lead to improvements in this task, which suggests that
models need to capture more explicit linguistic structure in order to see
improvements in performance.
  We hope that our dataset and results will encourage further work on predicting
discourse markers and study the effectiveness of the methods used in the task.
Moreover, our findings under-scoring the importance of discourse markers in
classification tasks between implicit discourse relations highlights the need for
more data and better models for the implicit discourse relation classification
task.

two kinds of magnetic skyrmions, which can be created and annihilated by
monopole instantons. By careful analysis of the Wess-Zumino term in the spin

produces the destructive interference. This restricts possible perturbations of

possible phases of this system, and a direct phase transition between N\'eel

the VBS phase has degenerate ground states when $p\not\in 2\mathbb{Z}$.

spin-orbit coupling.

) have become an established part of
numerous safety-critical computer vision applications, including human robot
interactions and automated driving. Real-world implementations will need to
guarantee their robustness against hardware soft errors corrupting the
underlying platform memory. Based on the previously observed efficacy of
activation clipping techniques in strong and weak adversarial settings, we study
the robustness of CNNs against corrupt residuals in the wild. To study this,
we propose a comprehensive framework evaluating the robustness of CNNs with
state-of-the-art strength against adversarial examples, i.e., \textit{rescale}
and \textit{clip}. As a first step, we analyze the impact of activation
corruption using the Tucker decomposition technique. Building on these insights,
we study the robustness of \textit{rescale} and \textit{clip} against
counterfitted attacks. To evaluate robustness, we propose a novel set of
comparative hardness metrics to analyze the relative position of the distribution
of natural images with respect to the adversarial zone. Our results show that
both \textit{rescale} and \textit{clip} move the natural image distribution
closer to the adversarial zone. However, \textit{clip} provides more benefit than
\textit{rescale} because it activates more weights to a higher level, thus
pushing the distribution further into the adversarial zone. Finally, we study
the effect of \textit{rescale} and \textit{clip} on the decision value distribution
and analyze the trade-off between the width and height of the decision boundary.
We show that the width of the decision boundary does not change significantly,
while its height increases with the application of \textit{rescale} and
\textit{clip}. Therefore, our study offers a set of tools for evaluating the
robustness of CNNs against activation corruption and provides a set of insights
that can guide the design of hardware-safe computer vision applications.

using an auxiliary model trained on a small validation set with high-quality

infrastructure destruction. This work aims to expand an epidemiological
non-local model that successfully described the French riots of 2005 to
incorporate the topology of Santiago's subway network and explain the reported
distribution of rioting activity in the city. Although the model reproduced the
disorders' aggregated temporal evolution, it could not deliver the same
reproduction of the spatial distribution of riots. The main reason for this
failure was the network's methodology limitation, which did not retain the
geographical coordinates of the stations' connections.
  We propose the use of a spatial non-local model that successfully described
the English riots of 2011. This model combines the epidemiological approach
with aukward neighbour dynamics and could reproduce the observed distribution of
rioting activity in Santiago. Moreover, we performed two sets of numerical
simulations to study the mobility and socioeconomic aspects of the individuals
in Santiago. In a first set, we added a degree of mobility to the model by
removing connections from the network and making the individuals move to a
random station. This simulation could reproduce the movement of the riots from
the city's centre towards its periphery. In a second set, we could also study
the effect of an imbalance on the socioeconomic conditions between the stations
and how this could trigger the riots in the model.
  Finally, we propose that the studied violence in Chile and possibly other
urban areas could benefit from the development and implementation of
counter-measures based on the topology of the city's transportation network.
Although the methodology had some limitations, our approach could be applied to
other cities with a available data on the activities' temporal and spatial
distributions.
  As additional material, we provide a user-friendly interface in Python that
allows the easy implementation and visualization of the model and its
connections to a given set of spatial data.
  As a conclusion, the development and implementation of counter-measures to
prevent or mitigate urban riots, especially in cities with a complex geography
like Santiago's, could benefit from the study of a city's transportation
network and the implementation of counter measures based on it.

proved, we obtain bounds that improve the general bounds known up to date.

examples and counterexamples that allow us to better understand which of the
results obtained by G. Blekherman can be extended to other cases and which are

at high scales, the low-energy
effective $3\times 3$ leptonic mixing matrix (LMM) is in general non-unitary.
We revisit the question of what is our current knowledge of individual LMM
matrix elements, distinguishing between direct constraints on individual
matrix elements and bounds on their products. We define two equivalent
approaches to quantify the individual matrix element probabilities: a
likelihood-based method and a Bayesian method with prior rescaling. We use
these definitions to reconstruct the individual matrix element probabilities
from the 3\sigma upper bound on the difference between the largest and
second-largest eigenvalues of the product of the LEEs, derived in [1]. We
observe a marked difference between the direct bounds on the sum of the
eigenvalues and the products of pairs of eigenvalues. We argue that new
experimental constraints on magnetic moment transitions in neutrinos can
help to disentangle individual and product matrix element probabilities.
Finally, we derive a set of simple bounds on the commutator of two LEEs, which
are also applicable in scenarios of non-homogeneous CP violation in the
leptonic sector.
  We discuss the implications of our results on neutrino-driven dark matter
in the early Universe and present a simple argument that homogeneous CP
violation in the neutrino sector is disfavored at the $\sim 2\sigma$ level.
Finally, we introduce and constrain a simple model of non-homogeneous CP
violation in the leptonic sector with a neutrino-mediated component.
  We argue that future measurements of individual LEE products may help to
assess the viability of different scenarios of non-homogeneous CP violation
in the leptonic sector and, in general, constrain beyond the Standard Model
physics that could be responsible for the unitarity violation.
  Finally, we note that non-unitary LEEs have a number of implications for
dark matter and early Universe phenomenology that remain to be fully
exploited.

Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms exploit the information from camera
and inertial sensors to estimate position and translation. Recent deep learning
based VIO models attract attentions as they provide pose information in a
data-driven way, without the need of designing hand-crafted algorithms.
Existing learning based VIO models rely on recurrent models to fuse multimodal
data and process sensor signal, which are hard to train and not efficient
enough. We propose a novel learning based VIO framework with external memory
attention that effectively and efficiently combines visual and inertial
features for states estimation. Our proposed model is able to estimate pose
accurately and robustly, even in challenging scenarios, e.g., on overcast days
and water-filled ground, which are difficult for traditional VIO algorithms to
extract visual features. Experiments validate that it outperforms both
traditional and learning based VIO baselines in different scenes.
  We also visualize the proposed model's memory with visual inspection to provide insights of the model's output, which verifies that the proposed model can estimate pose accurately and robustly. For example, the memory stores the information of the ground which are difficult for traditional VIO algorithms to extract visual features on.
  Our code and data are available at https://github.com/SuZhiRong/VisualInertialOdometry.
  The framework is general and can be extended to other sensor fusion tasks by
changing the sensors' features.
  The proposed model is widely applicable as it does not depend on any specific
camera model and programming language, and it is able to provide translation
and pose (rotation) estimation.
  The model maintains good performance in different scenes, which indicates that
it is robust to the variation of scenes.
  The proposed model is able to update the memory to a stable state after a
relatively short distance (about 0.5 meter), which indicates that it is able to
remove the redundant information from the memory.
  The model is able to store the long-term information, e.g., the white line
between two parking garages, and provide accurate translation estimation.
  The model is able to provide accurate translation estimation when there is
reflection, which indicates that it is robust to the reflection noise.
  The proposed model is able to remove the redundant information and provide
accurate translation estimation when there is water splash.

Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA). The goal of FedSA is to train a
student model for a new task with the help of several decentralized teachers,
whose pre-training tasks and data are different and agnostic. Our motivation
for investigating such a problem setup stems from a recent dilemma of model
sharing. Many researchers or institutes have spent enormous resources on
training large and competent networks. Due to the privacy, security, or
intellectual property issues, they are, however, not able to share their own
pre-trained models, even if they wish to contribute to the community. The
proposed FedSA offers a solution to this dilemma. With several decentralized
teachers, FedSA learns a shared student policy that can selectively aggregate
the advice (features) from each teacher for the new task. We propose a novel
learning framework for FedSA, which involves both the teacher and student
training processes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of FedSA for several
task setups. Experimental results show that FedSA can achieve comparable or
better performance with significantly less memory cost compared to downloading
all of the teacher models.
  From a method perspective, FedSA is able to adopt various student learning
methods for the task of interest. We propose two learning protocols for FedSA,
which are able to adapt to different teacher tasks and also control the degree
of the teacher to be learned by the student. We also show that FedSA is able to
improve the existing multi-task learning further.
  Last but not least, we study some interesting issues regarding the teacher
and student in FedSA. We first experimentally analyze the relative importance
of the teachers, from the perspective of both performance and compression
ratio. We then propose an efficient variant of FedSA, which learns the student
from a teacher (instead of multiple teachers) to simplify the problem setup.

thermodynamics of many-body systems, we study if the QNEC restricts
irreversible entropy production in quenches driven by energy-momentum inflow
from an infinite memoryless bath in two-dimensional holographic theories. We
find that an increase in both entropy and temperature, as implied by the
Clausius inequality of classical thermodynamics, are necessary for the bound
to hold. We also find scenarios where the QNEC allows both an increase and a
decrease in temperature with a concomitant increase in an averaged temperature
rate. Our results provide a direct test of the causal version of the QNEC in
an out-of-equilibrium setting.
  We show that the causal QNEC implies a lower bound on the irreversible
entropy production rate in quenches where the low-frequency behavior of the
equilibrium modulus of the compressibility is captured by a pole at $p=0$.
This is because the causal QNEC, being a bound on the energy-momentum
tensor, restricts the effects of a quench-induced pressure gradient. When the
low-frequency behavior of the modulus of the compressibility is described by a
non-zero pole, the system behaves as an ideal gas, and the entropy produced
in the quench is maximized, leading to the famous H-theorem. Therefore, the
causal QNEC generalizes the ideal gas behavior to interacting holographic
theories.

the temperature in the conformally invariant case $c=\frac{3}{\pi G}$ of
two-dimensional holographic theories. This is an interesting example of a
lower bound on thermal fluctuations in out-of-equilibrium systems.
Furthermore, this result provides an interesting link between the causal QNEC
and the generalized second law of thermodynamics.
  In summary, we find that the QNEC generalizes the ideal gas behavior,
providing a non-quantum lower bound on the temperature in the conformally
invariant case. This suggests that the causal QNEC might be a classical
condition. If so, the causal QNEC would provide a fascinating connection
between the micro- and macro-physics of out-of-equilibrium systems.

Microscopy (SNOM) to probe the local dielectric properties and carrier
concentrations of wet-etched aluminum resonators on silicon, one of the most
characteristic components of the superconducting quantum processors. Using a
recently developed vector calibration technique, we extract the THz
permittivity from spectroscopy in proximity to the microwave feedline. Comparing
to silicon areas far from the etched regions and to unetched aluminum, we find
a carrier concentration increase of $\approx$50% near the silicon edges. This
increase is consistent with MOS capacitor measurements of etched silicon, and
may be useful for enhancing the efficiency of some quantum circuits. We further
find that post-thermal treatment in vacuum to remove H$_2$O gives the largest
changes in line shape and resonance frequency, with values reaching 5% and
100 MHz, respectively. We show that the line shape changes are largely captured
by a reduction in carrier concentration throughout the device. We estimate that
the vacuum treatment can give a 20$\mu$s $\mathcal{T_2}$ phase memory time,
increasing from its initial value of 1.5$\mu$s. While the vacuum treatment
increases $\kappa$ by 0.1, the increased $\mathcal{T_2}$ suggests that
quantum computing circuits based on aluminum on silicon may be resistant to
photon loss decay.

near-field THz SNOM can be used to probe material issues that lead to
decoherence in superconducting quantum circuits.

the atmosphere of Venus, and
modulation of its composition by interior-exterior cycling. The formation and
evolution of Venus's atmosphere, leading to contemporary surface conditions,
remain hotly debated topics, and involve questions that tie into many
disciplines. We explore these various inter-related mechanisms which shaped the
evolution of the atmosphere, starting with the volatile sources and sinks. We
discuss volcanic activity and its role in sequestering or adding to the atmosphere;
in particular, we highlight the role of late-stage magmatism in possibly
mitigating the atmospheric loss via photodissociation of CO2. We also discuss
possible exchanges between the atmosphere and the interior, such as alteration
of rocks in the deep crust and the possible partial melting of sub-Saharan
Venusian lithospheric mantle under high-CO2 conditions. Finally, we examine the
possible links between these long-term atmospheric evolution processes and
Venus's core, in particular the strength of its mantle through the amplitude of
the tidal heating and the secular cooling. This work aims at bringing together
different communities working on these various topics and at highlighting the
links between them.
  We propose a pseudo-budged scenario, which could have naturally occurred
during the evolution of the Venusian system. In this scenario, magmatic and
volcanic activity is significantly higher in the past (more than one order of
magnitude) than currently. This activity could have buried the rocks at the
surface (and thus protected them from interactions with the atmosphere), or
generated a crustal reservoir from which volatiles could be released in the
past, during a resurfacing event. This scenario could be linked to a late
burst of internal heat transfer, following a previous and weaker episode of
tidal heating (and possibly secular cooling), which would have triggered
magmatic and volcanic activities over several hundreds of millions of years.
Finally, this scenario could be accompanied by exchanges between the atmosphere
and the interior (e.g. rocks alterations in the deep crust and partial melting
of the mantle), which modulate the intensity of the volcanic activity.
  In any case, the evolution of Venus's atmosphere appears to be linked to
deep processes in the planet's interior. Modelling and modelling-related
experiments (e.g. thermodynamic, multi-phase) are necessary to understand and
describe these complex relationships.

surface chemistry. Chemical reactions on the surface of charged droplets are
ubiquitous in nature and can provide critical insight into more efficient
processes for industrial chemical production. Here, we demonstrate the
application of the reaction nanoscopy technique to strong-field ionized
nanodroplets of propanediol (PDO). The technique's sensitivity to the
near-field around the droplet allows for the in-situ characterization of the
average droplet size and charge. The use of ultrashort laser pulses enables
control of the amount of surface charge by the laser intensity. Moreover, we
demonstrate the surface chemical sensitivity of reaction nanoscopy by comparing
droplets of the isomers 1,2-PDO and 1,3-PDO in their ion emission and
fragmentation channels. Referencing the ion yields to gas-phase data, we find
an enhanced production of methyl cations from droplets of the 1,2-PDO isomer.
Density functional theory simulations support that this enhancement is due to
the alignment of 1,2-PDO molecules on the surface. The results pave the way
towards spatio-temporal observations of charge dynamics and surface reactions
on droplets in pump-probe studies.

encoding histological entities is imperative for computer aided cancer patient
care. To this end, several approaches have leveraged cell-graphs that encode

functionality to help quantify their relationship. Though cellular information

tissue structure. We herein treat the tissue as a hierarchical composition of
multiple types of histological entities from fine to coarse level, capturing
multivariate tissue information at multiple levels. We propose a novel
multi-level hierarchical entity-graph representation of tissue specimens to
model hierarchical compositions that encode histological entities as well as
their intra- and inter-entity level interactions. Subsequently, a graph neural
network is proposed to operate on the hierarchical entity-graph representation
to map the tissue structure to tissue functionality. Specifically, for input
histology images we utilize well-defined cells and tissue regions to build
HierArchical Cell-to-Tissue (HACT) graph representations, and devise HACT-Net,
a graph neural network, to classify such HACT representations. As part of this
work, we introduce the BReAst Carcinoma Subtyping (BRACS) dataset, a large
clinical image dataset, for testing classification of breast carcinoma subtypes
based on histology. BRACS comprises histology images annotated with breast
tumor infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) and the Invasive ductal carcinoma (IDC)
neoplasic nucleus density. In addition to breast carcinoma subtyping, we also
address the tasks of fibroblast identification and tubule density classification
from histology images. Results demonstrate that our proposed HACT representation
and classifier, HACT-Net, yields promising results compared to prior state-of-

which notably models excitation and inhibition phenomena between dimensions of
the process. In a nonparametric Bayesian estimation framework, we obtain
concentration rates of the posterior distribution on the parameters, under mild
assumptions on the prior distribution and the model. These results also lead to
convergence rates of Bayesian estimators. Another object of interest in

Bayesian methods for estimating this quantity; in particular, we prove that the

light becomes increasingly important to understand a spectral broadening
occurring with intense infrared laser pulses in various mediums. In this paper, I
discuss a theoretical model which describes a spectral broadening of pulsed
laser radiation due to the nonlinear self-focusing effect based on the
parametric approximation. With this model, I discuss the fundamental physical
processes of the spectral broadening both in the adiabatic and non-adiabatic
regimes.
  The model is developed for arbitrary laser-pulse shapes, optical materials,
and initial transverse beam profiles. In the adiabatic regime, I reveal a
precise analytical prediction of the spectral broadening in various optical
materials (e.g., air, vacuum, and traditional optical fibers) by a simple
scalar model of the self-focusing effect. In particular, I derive a precise
analytical prediction of the spectral broadening in air for laser powers up to
the multi-PW range.

simple analytical prediction of the spectral broadening in a single-shot regime,
which agrees well with numerical simulations. I demonstrate that the model
predicts a physical threshold of the spectral broadening in a single-shot regime
(1 eV/photon). In a multi-shot regime, the model predicts a well-known picture
of the spectral broadening. For the case of nanosecond laser pulses in transparent
media, I reveal a simple analytical prediction of the spectral broadening, which
agrees well with numerical simulations. I demonstrate that the analytical
prediction of the spectral broadening depends on the initial transverse beam
profile. In the case of the Gaussian beam, the analytical prediction well agrees
with the classical discussion [L. A. Ostrovsky and V. A. Petrov, JETP Lett.

gravitational lensing. To do so successfully, it is useful to explore methods

suboptimally compared to the iterative estimator in terms of the lensing
reconstruction performance. In this work, we take one step further to evaluate
the delensing performance of these estimators on mock maps that include larger
regions of strong lensing convergence. We show that the improvements in
lensing reconstruction provided by the NNs and the iterative estimator are
primarily due to improvements in the recovery of the high-scale lensing
patterns. They in turn lead to delensing residuals that are $\sim 1.5$ $\mu$

However, the iterative estimator still gives slightly smaller residuals than
the NNs in the presence of strong lensing. We also show that a simple post
processing technique (namely regressing the residuals with a NN) leads to
further improvement, bringing the performance of the NNs closer to that of the
iterative estimator. We conclude that multi-estimator combinations may be a
promising strategy for improving the delensing performance in the presence of
strong lensing.

illustrate this with the NN and iterative estimators.

MacPherson gave a local and combinatorial formula for the
Pontrjagin classes of a differential manifold. We give an expanded version of
their discussion and highlight the origins of combinatorial differential
manifolds in their work.
  Let $K_i(M)$ denote the $i$-th Pontrjagin class of a differential manifold
$M$. Gelfand and MacPherson considered the data of a combinatorial version of
the normal cycle, given by their "signed simplexes and their singular sets". A
fundamental result in their paper is that $K_1(M)$, viewed as an element of
$H^2(M;\ZZ\zeta_2)$, is completely determined by this data when the degree of
$M$ is even. We show that when the degree of $M$ is odd, $K_1(M)$ can be
computed by means of a canonical map to $H^2(M;\ZZ\zeta_2)$ which generalizes the
Beck-Cofman orientation of a combinatorial Pontrjagin class.
  We discuss the relationship between this canonical orientation and the sign
assignment given by Gelfand and MacPherson. While our discussion gives a
combinatorial formula for the Pontrjagin classes, the structure revealed
highlights the importance of the Beck-Cofman orientation in relating the two
combinatorial objects given by Gelfand and MacPherson.
  Finally, we indicate how a version of our canonical orientation gives a
formula for the Toda brackets $\tau_{2i-1}\tau_{2i-1}\tau_{2i-1}$ in
$H^{2i+1}(M;\CC)$.
  The arguments given are entirely in terms of the combinatorial differential
manifolds introduced by Gelfand and MacPherson. No knowledge of algebraic
geometry is required.

Stiefel-Whitney Classes" also uploaded to this site.

and density field information on the construction of halo mass function through
cosmological $N$-body simulations. In this direction, we train a Convolutional
Neural Network (CNN) on the initial snapshot of an only dark matter simulation
to predict the halo mass that individual particles fall into at $z=0$, in the
halo mass range of $10.5< \log(M / M_{\odot})<14$. Our results show a
negligible improvement from including the velocity in addition to the density
information when considering simulations based on the standard model of
cosmology ($\Lambda$CDM) with the amplitude of initial scalar perturbations
$A_s = 2\times10^{-9}$. In order to investigate the ellipsoidal collapse models
and to study the effect of velocity in smaller mass ranges, we increase the
initial power spectrum such that we see the effect of velocities in larger
halos which are in the resolution of our simulation. The CNN model trained on
the simulation snapshots with large $A_s$ shows a considerable improvement in
the halo mass prediction when adding the velocity field information.
Eventually, for the simulation with $A_s = 8 \times 10^{-8}$, the model trained
with only density information shows at least equally good results than the
models trained with both density and velocity information.
  From $N$-body simulations, we also investigate the Convolutional Neural
Network (CNN) models' behavior against the particle identification criteria:
the fraction of the particles which are correctly identified. We compare against
various criteria: the particles which are inside the halo virial radius,
spherical collapse radius, both, and pre-merger separation criteria. We are
looking for a set of criteria which can be used as a weight function to the
density and velocity maps to more accurately the halo structure. From our
results, we get a considerable improvement (up to 15%) by using the velocity

constructing the mass function.

better than the non-rotating one (which needs additional density information)

rapid real-time detection and classification of GW signals, and conventional
detection approaches are computationally prohibitive for the anticipated rate
of detection of next-generation GW detectors. In this work, we present the
first deep learning based results of classification of GW signals from NSBH
mergers in \textit{real} GW noise. We show that a convolutional neural network
(CNN) trained on time-series features of resampled signal waveforms can
distinguish NSBH signals from BBH and BNS signals with high accuracy in
addition to a noiser background case with an accuracy of more than 99% for
SNR of 10 and 75% for a lower SNR of 5.

and reliable in avoiding misclassification of NSBH signals with a small number
of training examples per class. These results are particularly important for
improving the efficiency of discovering and classifying GW signals in real
time.

learning architectures (including CNN, ResNet, LodgeNet, and Safe-CNN) on a
larger dataset that includes additional classes of BBH mergers with different
mass ratios to simulate the diversity of real mergers. Safe-CNN remains the
best performing model across all tests with a general improvement in test
accuracy by more than 7% as compared to the best performing baseline model.
This general improvement in accuracy is attributed to the robustness of safe
learning to the small number of training examples per class.

future NSBH mergers and highlight the need for further studies towards
increasing the diversity of the training dataset of realistic merger

urban
environments are known to spur economic productivity and innovation in cities,
while also to foster social capital and resilience of communities. However,
mobility restrictions during the pandemic have forced people to substantially
reduce urban physical encounters, raising questions on the social implications
of such behavioral changes. In this paper, we study how the income diversity of
urban encounters have changed during different periods throughout the pandemic,
using a large-scale, privacy-enhanced mobility dataset of more than one million
anonymized mobile phone users in four large US cities, collected across three
years spanning before and during the pandemic. We find that the diversity of
urban encounters have substantially decreased (by 15% to 30%) during the
pandemic and has persisted through late 2021, even though aggregated mobility
metrics have recovered to pre-pandemic levels. Counterfactual analyses show
that while the reduction of outside activities (higher rates of staying at
home) was a major factor that contributed to decreased diversity in the early
stages of the pandemic, behavioral changes including lower willingness to
explore new places and changes in visitation preferences further worsened the
long-term diversity of encounters. Our findings suggest that the pandemic could
have long-lasting negative effects on urban income diversity, and provide
implications for managing the trade-off between the stringency of COVID-19
policies and the diversity of urban encounters as we move beyond the pandemic.

scattering theory and establish its characterization by the given gerbe and the

and scattering matrix suggests a generalization to 3D and 4D theories by
extending the notions of scattering matrix and bound states. The general idea
is that the 3D/4D scattering matrix and bound states could play a role similar
to the 2D asymptotic algebra and asymptotic states. We propose a framework for

a complex task
for autonomous mobile platforms. Especially when conditions worsen, typical
sensor modalities may fail to operate optimally and subsequently provide inapt
input for safe navigation control. In this study, we present an approach for
the navigation of a dynamic indoor environment with a mobile platform with a
single or several sonar sensors using a layered control system. These sensors
can operate in conditions such as rain, fog, dust, or dirt. The different
control layers, such as collision avoidance and corridor following behavior,
are activated based on acoustic flow queues in the fusion of the sonar images.
The novelty of this work is allowing these sensors to be freely positioned on
the mobile platform and providing the framework for designing the optimal
navigational outcome based on a zoning system around the mobile platform.
Presented in this paper is the acoustic flow model used, as well as the design
of the layered controller. Next to validation in simulation, an implementation
is presented and validated in a real office environment using a real mobile
platform with one, two, or three sonar sensors in real time with 2D navigation.
Multiple sensor layouts were validated in both the simulation and real
experiments to demonstrate that the modular approach for the controller and
sensor fusion works optimally. The results of this work show stable and safe
navigation of indoor environments with dynamic objects.

shift to news consumption via social media has been one of the drivers for the
spread of misleading and deliberately wrong information, as in addition to it
of easy use there is rarely any veracity monitoring. Due to the harmful effects
of such fake news on society, the detection of these has become increasingly
important. We present an approach to the problem that combines the power of

inherent problems. Our framework, CMTR-BERT, combines multiple text
representations, with a mechanism to adapt the weights of the combination
depending on the situation, utilizing a mean squared error function for that.
But most importantly, it leverages the advantages of the BERT architecture while
simultaneously addressing one of its inherent problems, specifically, the fact
that it is not state aware, as we will explain in the introduction of this
paper. This framework is able to outperform established approaches consistently
across various datasets.

classification. It achieves state of the art results on the IIT-Hate dataset,
and is able to outperform established approaches consistently across the
NewsNet, Faktor-Net, IIT-MUM-News and HMCL datasets in fake news detection.
Furthermore, it achieves state of the art results together with a few
established techniques on the SSTS, SSTR, CMST and HMST sentiment evaluation
metrics across the AME-Bench and SRE-Bench datasets.

entropy change, via the curvature effect, has a direct connection to the

provide the details of implementation of two reduction procedures, and we then
apply them to the same test case of interest. We first implement a reduction
technique that is based on a monolithic procedure where we solve the fluid and
the solid problems all at once. We then present another reduction technique
that is based on a partitioned (or segregated) procedure: the fluid and the
solid problems are solved separately and then coupled using a fixed point
strategy. The toy problem that we consider is based on the Turek-Hron benchmark
test case, with a fluid Reynolds number Re = 100.

procedures, and we then discuss the results that we obtain by applying the
reduction techniques on the test case of interest. In particular, we focus the
discussion on the advantage of using a proper norm for the basis selection, as
for example the Gram-Schmidt process. We then move to provide a error estimate
that is valid for both the two reduction procedures. Finally, we draw some
conclusions on the results that we obtained, and we provide some future work.

mobile robots. The map is the core component to achieve this. Most map
representations rely on drift-free state estimation and provide a global metric
map to navigate. However, in large-scale real-world applications, it's hard to
prohibit drifts and compose a globally consistent map quickly. In this paper, a
novel representation named, HiTMap, is proposed to enhance the existing map
representations. The central idea is to adopt a submap-based hierarchical
topology rather than a global metric map so that only a local metric map is
maintained for obstacle avoidance which ensures the lightweight of the
representation. To guide the robots navigate into unknown spaces, frontiers are
detected and attached to the map as an attribute. We also develop a path
planning module to evaluate the feasibility and efficiency of our map
representation. The system is validated in a simulation environment and a
demonstration in the real world is conducted. In addition, the HiTMap is made
available open-source.
  From the results, the HiTMap can support safe local navigation quickly once a
frontier is detected. Besides, the drift-free HiTMap can be used as an
alternative to the conventional metric map in some cases. In conclusion, the
HiTMap is capable of enabling robots to navigate into unknown spaces with the
help of an attractive map representation.

of the proofs while showing how their differences are motivated by the varying
goals of their authors.

SIMD high-performance computing, despite the fact that many important HPC
applications have an inherent object structure. On SIMD accelerators, including
GPUs, this is mainly due to performance problems with memory allocation and
memory access: There are a few libraries that support parallel memory
allocation directly on the accelerator devices, but all of them suffer from
uncoalesed memory accesses.
  We discovered a broad class of object-oriented programs with many important
real-world applications that can be implemented efficiently on GPUs. We developed
a programming language technique to reexpress such programs in a form that runs
correctly and efficiently even when objects are stored in device memory and
accessed with coalesced memory reads and writes. We implemented this approach in
a programming language and tool, which automatically optimizes code that uses
hierarchical, composed objects into a form that runs efficiently on GPUs. Our
optimization achieves performance within 10% of hand-optimized examples while
preserving reference correctness. It also enables the use of parallel memory
allocation libraries in a way that is transparent to the programmer. We demonstrate
our approach and tool through a set of case studies, including a large, production
code benchmark that achieves a 2x performance speedup.
  Our work paves the the way for the use of object-oriented programming on
high-performance SIMD accelerators, with a focus on GPUs. We believe that our
approach can be extended to other accelerators, such as FPGAs, and that it can
be implemented in other programming languages, such as C++.

pulses, the pulse frequency has a temporal variation about its fundamental
frequency,
  which manifests to the temporal dependence of the critical density ($n_c$).
In this work we used a chirp model which is beyond the linear approximation.
For negatively (positively) chirped pulses, the high frequency component of the
pulse interacts with the target before the low frequency component (for
positively chirped pulses) or after (for negatively chirped pulses) leading to
the charge displacement in the target plasma and subsequently to the electromagnetic
wave propagation in the opposite direction of the laser propagation. This
particular feature of the negatively (positively) chirped pulses (known as the
density dispersion for the negatively chirped pulses and the density distortion
for the positively chirped pulses) leads to the enhancement of the transmission
and also to the improvement of the ion acceleration by the self-generated
electromagnetic wave.
  The model that we used for the chirped laser pulses allows a broad variation
of the pulse central frequency and also of the chirp rate, leading to a more
realistic simulation of the laser-plasma interactions.
  The results presented in this work show that the transmission and the ion
acceleration can be optimized by a proper choice of the chirp rate.
  In addition, we have observed that the threshold power for the transmission
and also for the ion acceleration decreases with the increase of the chirp rate.
This threshold decrease is attributed to the density distortion (for positively
chirped pulses) or to the density dispersion (for negatively chirped pulses) as
the high density regions of the plasma are what the electromagnetic wave
propagates against.
  Finally, we have observed that the use of the negatively chirped pulses
provides better results (in terms of the transmission and the ion acceleration)
when compared to the positively chirped pulses.
  Conclusions drawn in this work indicate that the use of the chirped laser
pulses can be very useful for the optimization of the ion acceleration
processes by the sub-wavelength targets.
  Finally, it is worthwhile to emphasize that the results presented in this
work were obtained in a one dimensional model, without any temperature in the
plasma. Future works will be done in a two/five dimensional models, with

problem: given a fixed finite graph $F$, what is the largest value of $\lambda$

variants are, in general, different, but for some choices of $F$ they are

when considering upper density, but are different when considering lower
density.

OS temperature sensor for
densely-distributed thermal monitoring in systems on chip supporting dynamic
voltage and frequency scaling. The sensor front-end exploits a sub-threshold
PMOS-based circuit to convert the local temperature into two biasing currents.
These are then used to define two oscillation frequencies, whose ratio is
proportional to absolute-temperature. Finally, the sensor back-end translates
such frequency ratio into the digital temperature code. Thanks to its
low-complexity architecture, the proposed design achieves a very compact
footprint along with low-power consumption and high accuracy in a wide
temperature range. Moreover, thanks to a simple embedded line regulation
mechanism, our sensor supports voltage-scalability. The design was prototyped
in a 180nm CMOS technology with a 0{\deg}C $-$ 100{\deg}C temperature detection
range, a very wide supply voltage operating range from 0.6V up to 1.8V and very
small silicon area occupation of just 0.021$mm^2$. Experimental measurements
performed on 20 test chips have shown very competitive figures of merit,
including a resolution of 0.24{\deg}C, an inaccuracy of $\pm$1.4{\deg}C, a
sampling rate of about 1.5kHz and an energy per conversion of 1.06nJ at
50{\deg}C.

magnetic field configurations inside stably stratified stars. These
configurations consist of mutually stabilizing toroidal and poloidal components

magnetic field components, which can be used as a starting point for further
theoretical work in the development and testing of theoretical models with the
goal of accurately describing the evolution of the magnetic field in real

long, wavy fingers in the limit of strong positive external pressure.
Topological transitions occur as the instability is fueled by increasing

variations are accurately captured by the theoretical analysis of the instability
in terms of a single variable. Finally, we provide a detailed description of the
three different scenarios in which the tension (or the external pressure) can
dominate the curvature to lead to the formation of long, wavy fingers instead of
deep folds.

difficulty is significantly reduced, and the density mask is used to indicate
the density of the nucleus, so that the position of the nucleus can be located
more efficiently and accurately. We test our proposed method on two datasets,
viz. HD-Breast and HD-Patho. The experimental results show that our proposed
method can achieve lower mASE and better perform compared to the U-Net based

) and imperative algorithms
(pseudocodes) are two well-known coexisting concepts. Then what is their
relationship? Our answer is that
  \[ imperative\ algorithms\ =\ proofs\ with\ cuts \]
  This observation leads to a generalization to pseudocodes which we call {\it
logical pseudocodes}. It is similar to natural deduction proof of computability
logic\cite{Jap03,Jap08}. Each statement in it corresponds to a proof step in
natural deduction. Therefore, the merit over pseudocode is that each statement
is guaranteed to be correct and safe with respect to the initial
specifications. It can also be seen as an extension to computability logic web
(\colw) with forward reasoning capability.
  We demonstrate the power and safety of our approach by several examples. We
also show how to utilize our approach for solving a problem called
{\it debugging}. The main benefit is that the debugged program (or algorithm)
is guaranteed to be correct with respect to the original specifications.
Besides, our algorithm can update the original program into a new one based
on the debugging steps. Therefore, the resulting program is efficient in addition to being correct.
  In addition, we observe that each step in our algorithms is closed under
compositeness. This observation leads to another benefit. The resulting
correct algorithms can be simplified by eliminating redundant steps. We show its
effectiveness by several examples.
  We also observe that each step in our algorithms is also closed under
negation. Therefore, if an equation (or problem) has a solution, then its
negation cannot have any solution and vice versa. This observation leads to a
very efficient debugging process. We show its effectiveness by several examples.
Finally, we propose a generalization of our approach for multi-agent settings.
We illustrate its usefulness by an example.

computational savings, especially when the number of states in the game is very
large. Moreover, the hierarchical structure can also capture some situations
where the opponents (e.g., an adversarial network controlled by an opponent)

solutions orders of magnitude faster than existing methods for comparison. Most
importantly, the proposed approach returns near-optimal probabilities of
capturing the opponents at the same order of time. The proposed framework is
validated in two challenging games with large action spaces: a 5,000-state game

CT denoising thanks to its superior performance despite the fast computational
time. In particular, cycleGAN has been demonstrated as a powerful unsupervised
learning scheme to improve the low-dose CT image quality without requiring
matched high-dose reference data. Unfortunately, one of the main limitations of
the cycleGAN approach is that it requires two deep neural network generators at
the training phase, although only one of them is used at the inference phase.
The secondary auxiliary generator is needed to enforce the cycle-consistency,
but the additional memory requirement and increases of the learnable parameters
are the main huddles for cycleGAN training. To address this issue, here we
propose a novel cycleGAN architecture using a single switchable generator. In
particular, a single generator is implemented using adaptive instance
normalization (AdaIN) layers so that the baseline generator converting a
low-dose CT image to a routine-dose CT image can be switched to a generator
converting high-dose to low-dose by simply changing the AdaIN code. Thanks to
the shared baseline network, the additional memory requirement and weight
increases are minimized, leading to more stable training without compromising
the image quality. Experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms
the traditional cycleGAN architecture both visually and quantitatively.
Furthermore, the proposed model is shown to generate acceptable results even
when the training data size is limited.

methods, we demonstrate a detrimental effect when using a single learned

networks. Using a single dynamics model, we see clear evidence of task

problem online from a single RGB image, whilst training our models with
entirely synthetic data. We study three main approaches: one direct regression
model that directly predicts the extrinsic matrix from an image, one sparse
correspondence model that regresses 2D keypoints and then uses PnP, and one
dense correspondence model that uses regressed depth and segmentation maps to
enable ICP pose estimation. In our experiments, we benchmark these methods
against each other and against well-established classical methods, to find the
surprising result that direct regression outperforms other approaches, and we
perform noise-sensitivity analysis to gain further insights into these results.

and projection, we can obtain sub-millimeter accuracy in just a few iterations.

invariance of linear subspaces in fractional order systems. Further, we provide

asymptotic behavior characteristic to their equilibria, while linear systems
exhibit asymptotic behavior to their linear subspaces. This observation leads
to the motivation of introducing invariant harmonic subspaces (IHS) in discrete
and fractional systems. Invariant harmonic subspaces are sets such that the
dynamic behavior of the system is asymptotically characteristic to these sets
and are analogs of linear subspaces in fractional and discrete systems. The
concept of IHS is new to the field of control theory and dynamical systems. The
observation of IHS is important in the area of model reduction. A reduced
model having only a few modes is sufficient when the systems have IHS.

linear subspaces in fractional order systems. Section IV discusses the

fractional systems.

waveform generative model named
Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) is proposed to improve the limited pitch
controllability of vanilla WaveNet (WN) using pitch-dependent dilated
convolution neural networks (PDCNNs). Specifically, as a probabilistic
autoregressive generation model with stacked dilated convolution layers, WN
achieves high-fidelity audio waveform generation. However, the pure-data-driven
nature and the lack of prior knowledge of audio signals degrade the pitch
controllability of WN. For instance, it is difficult for WN to precisely
generate the periodic components of audio signals when the given auxiliary
pitch features are not integrated into the network. To address this problem,
QPNet with PDCNNs is proposed. The proposed PDCNNs can leverage the prior
knowledge of audio signals that the periodic components of audio signals are
determined by the pitch. More specifically, the proposed PDCNNs with two
convolution layers can separately utilize the very-low-frequency (VLF) and
low-frequency (LF) components of the predicted periodic components as additional
side information to enhance the pitch controllability of WN. For example, the
LF components of the periodic components, which are more relevant than the VLF
components for the LF components of the original audio signals, can be used as
additional side information to improve the low-frequency pitch controllability
of the generated audio signals. Meanwhile, the proposed PDCNNs with two
convolution layers can also exchange the very-low-frequency (VLF) information
and the low-frequency (LF) information, which can improve the periodic
accuracy of the generated audio signals. The proposed method can be seen as
adding auxiliary pitch features to improve the pitch controllability of WN. The
proposed method is validated through the generated audio signals by WN and
QPNet at different pitches. The experimental results show that QPNet outperforms
WN in terms of pitch controllability.

  Sound source localization, i.e., the problem of estimating the 3D position of
a sound-emitting object given an audio signal, has been proven essential for
human and animals to navigate and communicate in the world. In contrast, the
corresponding problem for visual sources, i.g., objects in videos, has seen only
limited progress. Our work aims at localizing visual objects that emit sound or
animation, and are visible in a video without using manual annotations. A
practical restriction of this work is that the objects to be localized are ones
that are also visible to the human eye. A novel aspect of the work is that we
utilize crowds for automatically judging complex visual information and learning
effective localizers. We show state-of-the-art performance on two recently
published datasets.
  We propose a novel framework for sound source localization (SSL) in videos,
which uses visual clues to drive the localization process using a novel
association-based loss function. Unlike previous works that utilize the visual
features to improve the performance of the SSL model, we aim to localize the
visual object that is generating the audio signal in the video. This allows us

Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Machine Translation (MT) systems, are
prone to error propagation. End-to-end approaches use only one system to avoid
propagating error, yet are difficult to employ due to data scarcity. We explore
zero-shot translation, which enables translating a pair of languages that is
unseen during training, thus avoid the use of end-to-end ST data. Zero-shot
translation has been shown to work for multilingual machine translation, yet
has not been studied for speech translation. We attempt to build zero-shot ST
models that are trained only on ASR and MT tasks but can do ST task during
inference. The challenge is ASR and MT systems introduce different types of
errors, which are needed to be aligned to do zero-shot ST. We propose using
adversarial training with domain displacement to force ASR and MT models to
produce more suitable errors for zero-shot ST. Our experiments show that the
proposed approach is able to perform ST task without any ST data.

and the evaluation languages. We also study the issue of determining the
evaluation languages that can be zero-shot translated from a set of evaluation
languages. Our observation is that the set of evaluation languages that can be
zero-shot translated is determined by the similarity of the test languages to
the training languages. We propose a simple yet effective approach to estimate
the similarity and predict the set of evaluation languages that can be zero-
shot translated.

languages that are not even trained as MT pair during training (e.g., from
English to Korean). We propose to filter out the translations that are clearly

2-D domains is a subject of great importance for the numerical solution of
Poisson's equation and volume integral equations. Complicated domains typically
require discretization by unstructured meshes, over which the direct evaluation
of the potential by quadrature becomes costly. In this paper, we present a
simple and efficient high-order algorithm for computing Newtonian potentials,
based on the use of Green's third identity for transforming the volume integral
into a collection of boundary integrals, which can be easily handled by the
Helsing-Ojala method. As a result, the time cost of the classically expensive
near field and self-interaction computations over an unstructured mesh becomes
roughly the same as the time cost of the FMM-based far field interaction
computation. One of the key components of our algorithm is the high-order 2-D
kernel approximation scheme, which allows us to obtain highly accurate boundary
integrals with a small number of iterations of any order of accuracy $p \geq
2$. The method is implemented in a C++ library, available upon request, which
includes a simple mesh data structure, a FMM class, and utilities for
converting from a mesh function to a piecewise linear function. Some numerical
examples are provided, which demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of the
algorithm.
